02.description:
The Joint Account was charged $3,650,992.77 for an allocated portion of shorebase and LNG terminal costs. The Operator is allocating the shorebase costs using the Marine Activity Method as outlined in Model Form Interpretation 46 - Shorebase Facilities and Offshore Staging Areas (MFI-46). This method allocates a portion of shorebase costs to each location at the same percentage as that location's marine charges relative to total marine charges for each month. However, this method does not pass the 'Litmus Test for Allocation Methodologies' as discussed in MFI -46. Since the marine vessel allocations include a mileage factor, properties further away from the shorebase are consistently charged higher shorebase and LNG terminal costs which are not proportionate to actual usage. The miles traveled by the marine vessel should not be a factor in shorebase and LNG terminal costs.

An alternative method for allocation of marine terminal costs would be to use the same allocation methodology as marine standby time. The Operator allocates standby time based on vessel time at the location. Since time spent at location should closely resemble time loading and unloading at the shorebase, this same allocation methodology could be used to allocate shorebase cost more equitably. While an alternative for allocation of LNG terminal costs would be to allocate the costs based on number of voyages to the location.

The Operator is requested to determine a more equitable allocation methodology. The Joint Account should be credited for the difference between the current allocation and a fair and equitable new allocation. The new allocation methodology should be used for future shorebase allocations.

replies.text:
The terminal costs are allocated based on total marine spend which is inclusive of direct vessel costs, lead-in standby allocation, and fuel. Basically if the total costs for the GoM Marine spend was $10M and a single asset spends $1M they would receive 10% of the terminal spend so mileage is not really a factor. It still comes down to how the boat is managed as a whole. For example - Perdido which is farther away could use 1 boat per week for 2 voyages and spend $1M and an asset in the East could use 2 boats per week and complete 5 voyages and spend $1M. Each would get 10% of the terminal allocation.

As also stated prior, the alternative is to go under the old operating model with a shore base that is closer and add $12M - $17M to the portfolio. At some point the distance is a cost of doing business in an area that lack infrastructure and growth.

This exception is denied.

The Accounting Procedure at Exhibit 'C', Section III Overhead states that,

replies.text:
Scott Armature stored critical equipment for motors in their climate controlled facility, and they are responsible for furnishing the VFD's (Variable Frequency Drivers) and motors when required that enable us to continue operations. They are also responsible for inspecting and maintaining this critical equipment in their facility. They are procuring business critical equipment, and without these services, it would not be possible to carry out safe and reliable operations and production at Perdido would be at risk. The items have very long lead times, typically around 25 weeks.

COPAS MFI 38 Materials Manual page 15 J. Maintenance and Preservation Costs states the following:

Warehouse operation, storage fees and maintenance expenses represent the operator's cost of storing (in a wholly owned warehouse) and handling material 1) may not be readily available in current market conditions for immediate use, 2) is frequently used, or 3) is otherwise held as surplus.

Services provided by 3rd parties for the co-owned material is not intended to be covered by the overhead rate.

Credit is denied.

replies.text:
Scott Armature stored critical equipment for motors in their climate controlled facility, and they are responsible for furnishing the VFD's (Variable Frequency Drivers) and motors when required that enable us to continue operations. They are also responsible for inspecting and maintaining this critical equipment in their facility. They are procuring business critical equipment, and without these services, it would not be possible to carry out safe and reliable operations and production at Perdido would be at risk. The items have very long lead times, typically around 25 weeks.

COPAS MFI 38 Materials Manual page 15 J. Maintenance and Preservation Costs states the following:

Warehouse operation, storage fees and maintenance expenses represent the operator's cost of storing (in a wholly owned warehouse) and handling material 1) may not be readily available in current market conditions for immediate use, 2) is frequently used, or 3) is otherwise held as surplus.

Services provided by 3rd parties for the co-owned material is not intended to be covered by the overhead rate.

Credit is denied.

The Operator cites COPAS MFI 38 in its response. However, this same document states in its introduction (page 3): "The provisions in this MFI do not supersede or override the provisions of any accounting procedure that is part of an existing agreement. The joint operating agreement and accounting procedure for a particular property will always take precedence". Therefore, the Confidential Settlement Agreement between SOI and Chevron supersedes COPAS provisions.

Clause 3.7 of the Settlement Agreement specifically limit third-party storage charges to 6 months and states:

Third Party Storage, Warehouse Facilities - For approved projects, the labor and facilities costs and any consignment fee directly incurred for preservation, maintenance, and storage for jointly owned equipment or materials for Joint Operations may be charged to the Joint Account as a direct charge. The chargeable amounts are limited to periods of six (6) months or less occurring prior to execution of the project or as agreed to by the Parties. This time period is considered temporary staging for a specific project. After use of the material or equipment for the Joint Operation is completed, the equipment or material storage costs will no longer be charged to the Joint Account unless the Parties have agreed in writing that the material or equipment is a critical spare.

Chevron is not disputing the criticality of the services provided. However, the Settlement Agreement requires that charges above six months be agreed in writing by the parties.

The claim is maintained. The Operator is requested to provide supporting documentation that the storage costs are in line with the terms of the agreement or credit the Joint Account $64,915.46 ($57,447.31 plus 13% overhead of $7,468.15) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.
This exception is currently being reviewed.

Chevron appreciates the Operator granting the claim for Randy Guliozo. However, the Company believes that the operator did not respond fully to its request. Exhibit C, section 2 C states:

OTL is chargeable to the joint account for planners, schedulers, plan execution supporters and others working on drilling, completions, facility maintenance, well maintenance operations and turnaround activities whose function was previously performed offshore/onsite but have been relocated onshore but excluding any non-technical personnel engaged in dedicated administrative support of such activities.

In addition, Exhibit C also states in section 3 C:

OTL is chargeable to the joint account for planners, schedulers, plan execution supporters and others working on drilling, completions, facility maintenance, well maintenance operations and turnaround activities whose function was previously performed offshore/onsite but have been relocated onshore but excluding any non-technical personnel engaged in dedicated administrative support of such activities.

Per the provisions of the settlement agreement, Exhibit C, section 2 and 3, the Operator has not provided sufficient information to substantiate that Geoffrey Checkan is not a "non-technical personnel engaged in dedicated administrative support of such activities". In addition, the Operator should evidence that the position was previously performed offshore/onsite but has been relocated onshore.

The remaining claim is maintained, and the Operator is requested to provide documentation that the services were previously located onsite, but subsequently moved offsite or credit the Joint Account $60,626.01 ($53,651.34 plus 13% overhead of $6,974.67) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

The response from the Auditor is noting Exhibit C, section 2.C and 3.C in error, each with the same paragraph. The Operator was not able to find the repeated 2.C reference, as section 2 is the definition of "Technical Employees".

As noted in the Operators prior response and as per Geoffrey Checkan, he handles the technical issues related to chemical engineering (as well as offshore visits) and chemical changeouts including how to maximize production, based on operating variables and chemical optimization. Administrative personnel do not handle these technical issues nor do they travel offshore to the asset. The following statement still stands, per the Billing Standards of the Settlement Agreement between Shell and Chevron effective January 1, 2019, Exhibit C, section 3.C applies for these direct billable charges.

In addition, the Operator states the following:

1. The settlement agreement intent is the same as recent COPAS accounting procedures/MFIs and uses the term 'function'. COPAS focus is on function of the role and not location of the role. Proving the role used to be offshore doesn't add any value because t he focus is on the function of the role.

19.description:
Semar, LLC Tidewater Marine, LLC Harvey Gulf International Marine

Voyages: 20191757, 20191425, 20191367, 20190291, 20190184, 20190826

The Joint Account and the Perdido Regional Host (PRH) Shared OPEX Cost Center- O.US.132.PER.001.71300-09 (LOGM) were charged for an allocated portion of marine voyages on various invoices. Each of the voyages made stops at Perdido as well as other locations not in Alaminos Canyon.

The vessel and fuel costs for each trip are allocated using hours at location (loading and unloading time plus rig standby time) times the mileage from shorebase. This allocation method is not equitable because the mileage factor disproportionately distributes more costs to the locations further away.

An allocation method using hours at the location without a mileage factor and underway time with a mileage factor would be more equitable. Using this method, the Joint Account was overcharged $197,187.55.

The Joint Account should be credited $204,892.04 ($170,760.88 plus 2.5% overhead, and $26,426.67 plus 13% overhead) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
The challenge of mileage is one that appears to be present when there are significant difference in the locations and primarily those between our eastern operations in Mississippi Canyon and our western/southwestern operations in Alaminos Canyon (Perdido field). The specifics below are on 6 voyages over a duration of 2019 where the stops were at different mileage locations. An important data point is that on an annual basis we share an average of 70 voyages per year between Perdido and other assets throughout our portfolio.

We have also witnessed our total operating expense from a marine perspective on Perdido drop by about 20% YOY since 2018 and from an activity based perspective it is down close to 50% on a cost per ton metric. This is also inclusive of the decisions made to consolidate from Galveston previously in 2016-2017 that reduced annual operating costs by ~$17M and those values have remained consistent through further commercial review of our marine and terminal category management review.

With regards to the 6 voyages in challenge, we view those as opportunity costs that benefits Shell and our partners. These voyages were shared with other locations and thus saved costs for Perdido along with reducing our portfolio exposure from hiring an additional boat or creating an NPT event. Both of those outcomes could have had further cost implications to these projects through the possibility of added pooled costs in our marine category.

It appears that challenge to mileage is only being applied in uncommon occurrences being that less than 2% of all shared voyages on an annual basis traveling to the Perdido field have been challenged. Moreover, we are not aware of any other equity partners challenging this methodology which further suggests that it meets the litmus test for our allocation processes being equitable over the audit period.

Credit is denied.

## C.Planners & Schedulers, maintenance and turnaround, rig administration

OTL is chargeable to the joint account for planners, schedulers, plan execution supporters and others working on drilling, completions, facility maintenance, well maintenance operations and turnaround activities whose function was previously performed offshore/onsite but have been relocated onshore but excluding any non-technical personnel engaged in dedicated administrative support of such activities.

Per the provisions of the settlement agreement, Exhibit C, section 2 and 3, which you referred to in your response, the Operator has not provided sufficient information to substantiate that the work performed onshore/offsite by Keystone Engineering was previously performed offshore/onsite but has been relocated onshore. Exhibit C, section 3 C states:

OTL is chargeable to the joint account for planners, schedulers, plan execution supporters and others working on drilling, completions, facility maintenance, well maintenance operations and turnaround activities whose function was previously performed offshore/onsite but have been relocated onshore but excluding any non-technical personnel engaged in dedicated administrative support of such activities.

The claim is maintained, and the Operator is requested to provide documentation that the services provided were previously located onsite, but subsequently moved offsite or credit the Joint Account $68,125.56 ($60,288.11 plus 13% overhead of $7,837.45) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

The response from the Auditor is noting Exhibit C, section 2 and 3 in error. The Operator referenced "the billing standards of the Settlement Agreement between Chevron and Shell effective January 1, 2019, exhibit C, section 3.C these charges are direct billable."

In addition, the Operator states the following:

1. The settlement agreement intent is the same as recent COPAS accounting procedures/MFIs and uses the term 'function'. COPAS focus is on function of the role and not location of the role. Proving the role used to be offshore doesn't add any value because the focus is on the function of the role.
2. The settlement agreement states the roles function used to be offshore and is now performed onshore. The settlement agreement doesn't state Shell must prove the role was offshore. Stating the roles used to be offshore and are now onshore is already acknowledged by Chevron signing the agreement and no further proof is needed.

These points have been communicated to the Chevron Joint Venture Audit Manager. This exception is denied.

No credit is due.

Section 3.5 of the settlement agreement, which deals with Field Computer and Communication Systems, allows 'scheduling and maintenance software systems when used by billable personnel for preventive maintenance or management of the Joint Property.' The su pporting documents provided by the Operator do not allow Chevron to assess the billability of the personnel using these systems.

The Settlement Agreement adds further clarity and insight on specific subjects in conjunction with other applicable guidance. As noted by the Operator, MFI-44, section II, C - "Software costs include - Support Costs - troubleshooting, upgrading, maintaining, and reconfiguring to accommodate physical changes to the wells and equipment over time." and "Examples of Computer Applications (Table 1)" therefore these charges are maintained as direct billable.

The Yokogawa system as a whole is the entire interface that operations uses to control the process and keep it safe, it is absolutely critical to be able to operate Perdido.

The Operator cites COPAS MFI 38 in its response. However, this same document states in its introduction (page 3): "The provisions in this MFI do not supersede or override the provisions of any accounting procedure that is part of an existing agreement. The joint operating agreement and accounting procedure for a particular property will always take precedence". Therefore, the Confidential Settlement Agreement between SOI and Chevron supersedes COPAS provisions.

Clause 3.7 of the Settlement Agreement specifically limit third-party storage charges to 6 months and states:

Third Party Storage, Warehouse Facilities - For approved projects, the labor and facilities costs and any consignment fee directly incurred for preservation, maintenance, and storage for jointly owned equipment or materials for Joint Operations may be charged to the Joint Account as a direct charge. The chargeable amounts are limited to periods of six (6) months or less occurring prior to execution of the project or as agreed to by the Parties. This time period is considered temporary staging for a specific project. After use of the material or equipment for the Joint Operation is completed, the equipment or material storage costs will no longer be charged to the Joint Account unless the Parties have agreed in writing that the material or equipment is a critical spare.

The Confidential Agreement requires that charges above six months be agreed in writing by the parties. Therefore, the claim is maintained. The Operator references the Settlement Agreement/Billing Standards between the co-owners and Operator, effective January1, 2019, Exhibit C, 3.A Regulatory Activity. The clause states that:

"OTL is chargeable to the joint account for activities required to comply with any governmental agency, authority, commission, political subdivision, or any other governmental body or entity, including but not limited to the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE), and any applicable law or regulation..."

In addition, the clause requires that the Operator that 'OTL charges related to the above regulatory activities must be adequately and properly documented by the Operator, identifying the specific activity of the individual(s), and will reference specific program elements as described in the Federal Register'.

The Operator has not provided evidence of these activities being mandated by a governmental body. In addition, the justifications provided indicates that these activities are mere improvements, which are beyond the scope of the referred clause.

In addition, the Operator references Settlement Agreement/Billing Standards 3.C Planners & Schedulers, maintenance and turnaround, rig administration. The same clause requires the Operator to charge only for 'activities whose function was previously performed offshore/onsite but have been relocated onshore but excluding any non-technical personnel engaged in dedicated administrative support of such activities'.

Chevron claims that the Operator has not complied with the requirements of the Settlements agreement and maintains the claim. The Operator is requested to provide documentation that the charges comply with the Settlement Agreement or credit the Joint Account the remaining amount of $983,417.69 ($870,281.14 plus 13% overhead of $113,136.55) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

The Operator states the following:

1. The settlement agreement intent is the same as recent COPAS accounting procedures/MFIs and uses the term 'function'. COPAS focus is on function of the role and not location of the role. Proving the role used to be offshore doesn't add any value because the focus is on the function of the role.
2. The settlement agreement states the roles function used to be offshore and is now performed onshore. The settlement agreement doesn't state Shell must prove the role was offshore. Stating the roles used to be offshore and are now onshore is already acknowledged by Chevron signing the agreement and no further proof is needed.

These points have been communicated to the Chevron Joint Venture Audit Manager. This exception is denied.

No credit is due.

This role has historically been an offshore role, and is heavily involved with ordering the equipment and parts offshore for robust materials planning and ordering purposes so that the jobs are performed in timely and orderly fashion. This expense is chargeable to the Joint Account as it is equivalent to the planning function for rigs offshore.

Wells Records Management Focal - This role polices and gathers critical Well Files at the end of the Well and stores them in a Wells library. Examples of these files are detailed well schematics, fluids reports, cementing reports, well prognosis. Many of the files are stored as a requirement to retain the information should a process safety incident occur and utilized by field personnel offshore.

Deepwater Cost Planner - Creates requisitions and builds networks so that purchase orders can be created so that service company can provide services and equipment. As noted, this role is heavily integrated with planning function and getting equipment ordered in timely fashion with the vendors that are involved with wells and the rigs.

Deepwater Logistics Coordinator - Logistics Coordinator works offshore on the rigs, getting personnel and equipment to and from the rigs for wells and drillships. They organize and setup the helicopters, boats, and other transportation methods for this movement so that the jobs offshore are able to be carried out.

BoM Tech - is responsible for managing the materials related to the wells and all the tangible equipment that Shell purchases. The BoM Tech keeps track of what is being installed in the well and any surplus that is left over to prevent surplus, as well as utilizing and transferring leftover equipment from other wells that can be used at Perdido.

Deepwater Wells Operations Technologist - Supports rigs, carries out daily QA/QC of EDM data each morning before the reports go out, followed by supporting secondary report creation, creating reports for the rig ranging from cementing and fluids reports to equipment installation reports as tangibles are installed, which is a BSEE requirement. For example, if we are using drilling fluidlike Mud, we have to specify details of the slurry. If we are cementing some casing in the well, we have to specify slurry details and volume. This is required reporting from BSEE.

Per the billing standards of the Settlement Agreement between Chevron and Shell effective January 1, 2019, Exhibit C definitions for OTL and Technical Employees as well as section 3.C apply for these direct billable charges, therefore this exception is denied.

Credit is denied.

## C. Planners & Schedulers, maintenance and turnaround, rig administration

OTL is chargeable to the joint account for planners, schedulers, plan execution supporters and others working on drilling, completions, facility maintenance, well maintenance operations and turnaround activities whose function was previously performed offshore/onsite but have been relocated onshore but excluding any non-technical personnel engaged in dedicated administrative support of such activities.

Per the provisions of the settlement agreement, Exhibit C, section 2 and 3, which you referred to in your response, the Operator has not provided sufficient information to substantiate that the work performed onshore/offsite by Keystone Engineering was previously performed offshore/onsite but has been relocated onshore. Exhibit C, section 3 C states:

OTL is chargeable to the joint account for planners, schedulers, plan execution supporters and others working on drilling, completions, facility maintenance, well maintenance operations and turnaround activities whose function was previously performed offshore/onsite but have been relocated onshore but excluding any non-technical personnel engaged in dedicated administrative support of such activities.

The claim is maintained, and the Operator is requested to provide documentation that the services provided were previously located onsite, but subsequently moved offsite or credit the Joint Account $110,484.73 ($98,528.45 plus various overhead of $11,956.28) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

The response from the Auditor is noting Exhibit C, section 2 and 3 in error. The Operator referenced "the billing standards of the Settlement Agreement between Chevron and Shell effective January 1, 2019, exhibit C, section 3.C these charges are direct billable." Also, the Auditor is noting Keystone Engineering whereas this exception is in regards to Petroleum Co-Ordinators, Inc invoices.

In addition, the Operator states the following:

1. The settlement agreement intent is the same as recent COPAS accounting procedures/MFIs and uses the term 'function'. COPAS focus is on function of the role and not location of the role. Proving the role used to be offshore doesn't add any value because the focus is on the function of the role.
2. The settlement agreement states the roles function used to be offshore and is now performed onshore. The settlement agreement doesn't state Shell must prove the role was offshore. Stating the roles used to be offshore and are now onshore is already acknowledged by Chevron signing the agreement and no further proof is needed.

These points have been communicated to the Chevron Joint Venture Audit Manager. This exception is denied.

No credit is due.

55.short_description: COUA - Opex Matrix - Documentation - SAP Upgrade
55.description:
The Joint Account was charged $180,391.54 for 2018 SAP upgrade cost for improvement to SAP modules for asset materials management (MM), and corrective and preventive maintenance (PM). Information Request (IR) #71 was submitted requesting the Operator provide all invoice support utilized in the allocation, as well as a breakout of the amount between materials management and preventive maintenance. Exception is taken to the entire charge since a split cannot be determined as to charges for preventative maintenance, and those associated with materials management.

Per MFI 44, purchasing and inventory management systems are covered under administrative overhead. Administrative systems (SAP MM) are not chargeable even when used by field personnel. Based on the monthly allocation percentages for the PRH OPEX Cost Center, $153,424.27 of expenditures were billed to the Great White Joint Account.

The Joint Account should be credited $173,369.43 ($153,424.27 plus 13% overhead of $19,945.16) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
These costs are associated with SAP Software Maintenance and Usage. We have an established allocation system for assigning charges where the users offshore on Perdido are billed based on per user charge. SAP does not bill us by individual modules. The charges include various Blueprint components (Global Blueprint Projects, Staff Cost, Blueprint Infra Cost, SAP M&S License, Managed service Contract etc.).

These costs follow MFI 44. Field Computer and communication Systems. The PM and MM modules are used by the field personnel for Maintenance Scheduling. SAP is not an isolated accounting system. In addition, as per the billing standards of the Settlement Agreement between Chevron and Shell effective January 1, 2019 section 3.5.a, "Scheduling and maintenance software systems when used by billable personnel for preventive maintenance or management of the Joint Property, including but not limited to SOI's SAP Plant Maintenance Module (also referred to as "PM"), and successor systems may be billed to the joint account as direct charges."

Please review the "SAP Billing - Cost Sharing Process Overview" White Papers for information on how SAP Billing is conducted.

Credit is denied.

The Joint Account was charged $949,978.35 from six FMC Technologies invoices on milestone payments of Tree PMPE services. Exception is taken for offsite services of project engineering and project management, and other Onshore services in the amount of $949,978.35.

The Accounting Procedure at Exhibit 'C', Section III Overhead, Paragraph (ii.) states that,

The salaries, wages and Personal Expenses of Technical Employees and/or costs of professional consulting services and contract services of technical personnel either temporarily or permanently assigned to and directly employed in the operation of the Joint Property: (x) shall be covered by the overhead rates.

The Joint Account should be credited $973,727.81 ($949,978.35 plus 2.5% overhead of $23,749.46) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
FMC was hired by Shell to perform services required as part of the refurbishment, mobilization and change-out projects. As part of those projects, Shell contracts FMC to prepare/test and manage many equipment interfaces. In order for other FMC personnel to be offshore they have many techs, billing, and drafters that help the project operate. Shell requires drawings and pre-job testing for all equipment that will be utilized offshore. Shell has no control over where those ancillary services are performed.

Many of the other services on the FMC Invoices, such as shop labor and planning, are ancillary activities to the overall project for which FMC was hired. Many of these services were performed in the vendor's yard (i.e. shop labor, inspection and testing). COPAS MFI-21 states that work performed at the site of construction yards is considered onsite.

Credit is denied.

- (1) "Shorebase Facilities shall mean onshore support facilities that during drilling, development, maintenance and producing operations provide such services to the Joint Pop rat ns sns t is ent debarkation point for drilling and production personnel and services; communication, scheduling and dispatching center; other associated functions benefiting the Joint Property."

The Operator cites COPAS MFI 38 in its response. However, this same document states in its introduction (page 3): "The provisions in this MFI do not supersede or override the provisions of any accounting procedure that is part of an existing agreement. The joint operating agreement and accounting procedure for a particular property will always take precedence". Therefore, the Confidential Settlement Agreement between SOI and Chevron supersedes COPAS provisions.

Clause 3.7 of the Settlement Agreement specifically limit third-party storage charges to 6 months and states:

Third Party Storage, Warehouse Facilities - For approved projects, the labor and facilities costs and any consignment fee directly incurred for preservation, maintenance, and storage for jointly owned equipment or materials for Joint Operations maybe charged to the Joint Account as a direct charge. The chargeable amounts are limited to periods of six (6) months or less occurring prior to execution of the project or as agreed to by the Parties. This time period is considered temporary staging for a specific project. After use of the material or equipment for the Joint Operation is completed, the equipment or material storage costs will no longer be charged to the Joint Account unless the Parties have agreed in writing that the material or equipment isa critical spare.

The Confidential Agreement requires that charges above six months be agreed in writing by the parties. Therefore, the claim is maintained. The Operator is requested to provide supporting documentation that the storage costs are in line with the terms of the agreement or credit the Joint Account $140,430.46 ($124,274.74 plus 13% overhead of $16,155.72) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

85.short_description: Coding Error - GW to Rig Use Agreement
85.description:
The Great White Joint Account was charged a total of $2,902,265.19 from various invoices for the Mooring Line - Rig Idle (AFE #P.US.GWH.EI.19.002.0991A) while on well #GA021. Since the severed Host mooring line was what caused/necessitated the H&P 205 rig idle in 2Q 2019 (as opposed to anything relating to GA021 operations), the rig idle was charged to Great White in error and should have instead been allocated to the Perdido Host in accordance with the Rig Usage Agreement (RUA) between the Perdido Host Owners and the Great White Producers.

Article 3 (Operations of the Host), Section 7 (Emergency Operations), Paragraph 5 of the RUA states,

In all cases where the cause of the emergency situation is clearly identified and is directly attributable solely either to the Rig Activities during Host Time, or to the Host or related upstream pipelines at any time, the Host Owners shall be responsible for all costs to remedy or alleviate the emergency situation.

The Joint Account should be credited $2,902,265.19 with a reference to Chevron's audit number and ex ception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text: As per Commercial Operations, the rig was on GA021 before the mooring line event. Rig idle is addressed in the Rig Usage Agreement for H&P Drilling Rig 205, section 1.12 'Great White Time shall mean all periods of time (measured in days and whole hours) during which the Rig is engaged in, including but not limited to preparing for, conducting, completing and concluding Rig Activities on behalf of the Producers, using the AFE referenced in the daily Rig morning report as the primary indication of Great White Rig Activities. Great White Time shall also include Rig Activities under Section 5.4 of this Agreement as well as the following periods of time when they are initiated for or occur during Great White Rig Activity: (a) time during which Rig repairs are conducted; (b) time during storm evacuation; (c) time during interruption of Great White Rig Activity for any reason including Force Majeure events, other than as set forth in the 2nd Priority and the 4th Priority in Section 2.2.1 of this Agreement; (d) time during suspensions under Section 3.4 of this Agreement; and (e) time during compliance with any law, order, rule, or regulation, governmental action or delay in granting permits or permit approvals as needed for Great White Rig Activity, or inability to secure permits or permit approvals as needed for Great White Rig Activity.' Force Majeure was declared by the Host, but none of the exceptions were triggered in the definition of Great White Time (as noted above); therefore repair time remains as Great White Time. Furthermore, Section 3.7.7 in the Rig Usage Agreement expressly states and clarifies that all of Article 3 (which includes the Section 3.7.5 referenced by t he auditor) is not intended to address Rig Idle Time; rather 'Article 3 addresses only the costs incurred by the Host Operator to remedy or alleviate an emergency situation such that the danger to people and property has been alleviated,' which Rig Idle is not.

01.short_description: Affiliate Payroll – Supervision Above First Level
01.description: The Joint Account was charged $86,619.56 from multiple Shell International Exploration & Production invoices for two personnel above first level supervision which is covered by overhead. The Accounting Procedure attached to and made a part of the Joint Operating Agreement, Exhibit C, Section III Overhead states, As compensation for administrative, supervision, office services and warehousing costs, Operator shall charge the Joint Account in accordance with this Section III. Under Section II. Direct Charges, only First level supervision is allowed. The Joint Account should be credited $87,918.85 ($86,619.56 plus 1.5% overhead of $1,299.29) with a reference to Chevron’s audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text: The purpose of the AFE issued was for: "Inspection, recovery, and replacement of Regional Host Perdido #6 Mooring Line due to damage from outside vessel downlines coming in contact with structure. Recovery and repair work required through regulatory to uphold asset intergrity and allow rig to be moved to continue with drilling activity." The project was classified as Major Construction and the timewriting for William Hoffman and John Sexton was for Technical Services provided on the Mooring Line Recovery Project, not for supervisory above first level. Therefore, direct billable per the COUA for Perdido. Affiliate services for a Major Construction project are referred to in the Addendum to Exhibit "C" Accounting Procedure Statement of Clarification and Intent SECTION III, PARAGRAPH 2.B: In order to clarify "engineering, design and drafting costs" chargeable under Exhibit “C”, Section III, Overhead, Paragraph 2. Overhead-Major Construction, the following shall apply: b. AFFILIATE SERVICES An Affiliate of the Operator or a Non-Operator providing service at the request of a Integrated Project Team, or for the direct benefit of a Major Construction project, shall be chargeable direct to the Joint Account, regardless of the location of the service provider, or the site at which the work is conducted. Affiliate employees and contract services of the Affiliate shall be charged a Gulf of Mexico all inclusive standard rate of Two-hundred forty dollars ($240.00) per hour. Such rate shall be applied to the actual hours of services provided to the Joint Account under the terms of the Agreement for any Affiliate Personnel, which shall be deemed to include Affiliate’s employees and Affiliate’s third party contractors, regardless of the job classification of such Affiliate Personnel, or the actual salary, wages, incentive compensation, burden and benefits Affiliate’s Personnel may receive individually. William Hoffman - The damage to the mooring line occurred during the jumper installation. Because of the offshore construction work associated with the repair, Mr. Hoffman coordinated the offshore construction work associated with the repair of the mooring line. John Sexton was responsible for reviewing the causal investigation on mooring line and providing support and input on the investigation from HSSE Discipline. Credit is denied.

012.description:
COVID 19 impacts have been felt across the world and industry. The result has been an agile approach by Operators to deal with the uncertainty, while enhancing safety and treatment for employees and contractors. A white paper published by the Operator states, "Shell implemented several measures to preserve the health and safety of people supporting the assets coowned with other companies. The measures benefit the joint operations of the joint property and are billable to all co-owners."

Cont inuing from the white paper, "In order to react quickly, several costs were paid through Shell's overhead and is subsequently being allocated in an equitable and fair methodology." During the audit, Auditors were able to locate source documents and confirm them to be COVID related. These charges were subsequently allocated to the Great White Joint account. The source documentation provided in SAP was unclear how the allocations were calculated.

Great White information requests 39 and 41 were submitted based upon specific allocations from August and December 2020. These IRs requested documentation regarding the percentages or methodologies used to allocate high-level COVID charges to the various wells operated by Shell. These IRs remained open at the conclusion of fieldwork.

The Operator is requested to provide documentation detailing the percentages or methodologies used for the COVID allocations to the Joint Account. Additionally, the Auditors request the Operator to provide any information on whether they received Federal COVID subsidies and passed those on to the Joint Account. Chevron reserves the right to issue additional exceptions, if warranted, after reviewing the Operator's response.

replies.text:
Please see attached for supporting documentation:

The file 'Ex 12 Supporting' addresses IR 39.

The file 'JADE Lines\_COVID 2 back to auditor' addresses IR 41.

Methodologies used for the COVID allocation to the Joint Account have been provided. As per the Senior Finance Advisor, Shell did not receive Federal COVID subsidies.

No credit is due.

The amount of $453,500.00 as noted in this exception (and IR #46) was posted to the Joint Account in December 2020. It was then fully reversed by a reclass entry in March 2021, as noted in the attached JADE line. No further credit is due.

The amount of $433,621.61 as noted in this exception (and IR #47) is for various invoices which have been attached. No credit is due.

The amount of $453,500.00 as noted in this exception (and IR #46) was posted to the Joint Account in December 2020. It was then fully reversed by a reclass entry in March 2021, as noted in the attached JADE line. No further credit is due.

The amount of $433,621.61 as noted in this exception (and IR #47) is for various invoices which have been attached. No credit is due.

The auditor has reviewed the March 2021 reverse reclass journal entry. This portion of the exception is closed. The remaining $433,621.61 remains open. Upon review of the invoices provided by Shell the auditor was unable to substantiate the location of the services. Furthermore, the auditor noted that the Schlumberger invoices indicated charges for a 'Dummy Well'. Please provide evidence supporting the location of the services provided.

Shell Int'l Exploration Prod'n Inc (SIEP), a Shell affiliate, validated the:

Schlumberger 3rd party charges against the project scope details (gas make-up; live-oil recombination; recombined live oil validation (partial PVT, AOP); OSDC testing without DLC (done separately); Live-oil OSDC with DLC to evaluate critical velocity). These are referenced on the SIEP invoices as noted in the attached supporting documentation. In addition, the Schlumberger invoices noted by the Auditor also included a reference to the Perdido fields. Also attached to the 3rd party invoices are approvals, verifying the work, from Shell to the vendor with specific details for the project. Schlumberger invoices of $154,271.41 - no credit is due.

DuneFront 3rd party charges are related to the wells' productivity as Packpro, as per the Principal Production Technologist, is an engineering modeling software package that was used for designing and installing the gravel packs for the wells in the Great White/Perdido area, namely GD-004, GD-005, GD-006, and GD-007. The charges will not reference specific wells because it is expected that this Packpro software is utilized on all Great White/Perdido assets that have an Openhole gravel pack, as per the Wells Engineering Manager. DuneFront invoices of $75,000.00 - no credit is due.

University of Houston 3rd party charges for a study to gain better insights of lightweight proppant transport in a horizontal open hole gravel pack for the Great White assets, as per the project scope of 4 open hole completions in Frio Phase II project needing horizontal OH gravel packing. As per the Team Lead, these charges are for physical testing done to validate the modeling on the GD-007/006/004/005. University of Houston invoices of $200,179.00 - no credit is due.

002.short_description: Rig Rate Discrepancies- Pontus
002.description:
SOI Finance Inc. charged the joint account for a series of internal invoices initially issued by Transocean during 2020. The rates charged by SOI are greater than the initial invoices issued by Transocean. Furthermore, Shell and BP entered an agreement in 2019 which included a schedule of rates chargeable for activity associated with the Pontus. On all the SOI invoices for 2020, the daily rate charges to the joint account is $531,089. Per the schedule in the settlement agreement, this rate should be $476,000.

Based on the information received, the joint account has been overcharged $55,089 per day. A partner direct JADE was provided as part of the initial documents for this audit; however the transactions do not contain sufficient information validate actual rate applied after credits.

In a separate request to Operator on 9.24.21, the audit team requested more details regarding the rig rate entries listed on the partner direct JADE. Querying the SAP document numbers from this JADE, we were only able to see a note indicating "Entries for rig services due to settlement agreement."

We have requested a reconciliation showing the breakdown of the initial charges billed via SOI in 2020 and the adjustments applied, to achieve the rates per the terms of the settlement agreement.

Absent a reconciliation, BP requests credit for the difference charged vs. agreed per settlement, per day of drilling activity. Amount TBD.

001.description:
The Operator billed the Great White Joint Account $80,464,741.17 for SOI Finance Inc invoices related to services of the drilling rig Transocean Deepwater Pontus for the period of June 13 thru November 30, 2020.

The amount billed to the Joint Account was calculated based on a rate of $531,089.00/day, which was specified by a contract assignment between SOI Finance Inc and Shell Offshore, Inc (SOI).

A review of the invoices and the contract amendments indicated that the amounts charged to SOI Finance from the owner of the Deepwater Pontus, Transocean, were based on an operating rate of $475,089/day. The rate increase created an additional billing to the Joint Account of $8,484,483.49 during the invoice period.

SOI Finance and SOI are related entities. There is no provision in the Joint Operating Agreement for a related entity, operator, its parent company, or an affiliate to markup a billing or invoice.

Request for remaining credit is denied.

The billing period shown on the invoice includes days of preparation, travel, standby, and COVID quarantine. However, the Non-Operator has included these days in the calculation of 5 consecutive workdays, which is incorrect and not supported by UOA and COPAS MFI-48 Application and Calculation of Drilling Overhead.

(2) (b), which states that such charges shall be applied for the period from date workover operations commence through date of rig or other unit release. replies.text:
The Operator has stated that " Prepping activity, travel days, and standby time do not count as being 'on the well' and are excluded from the 5 consecutive workdays rule." . This is contrary to MFI-21 which states that recompletion and workover operations lasting for five or more consecutive workdays qualify for Drilling Overhead:

业

## 1. FIXED RATE BASIS (WELL BASIS)

The fixed rate overhead provisions in the COPAS 2005 Accounting Procedure are essentially the same as the 1984 and 1986 forms, to help standardize accounting amongst these forms. Accordingly, drilling and producing overhead under the fixed rate basis are assessed as follows:

## Drilling Overhead

- The drilling rate in the agreement is a rate per well.
- The drilling rate is expressed as a monthly rate that is pro-rated based on the number of drilling days.
- Drilling overhead starts when (1) the well is spud, for onshore wells, or (2) the equipment arrives on location, for offshore wells.
- Drilling overhead ceases when the drilling or completion equipment is released, whichever is later.
- Drilling overhead is not charged when operations are suspended for 15 or more consecutive calendar days.
- Drilling overhead applies to recompletion or workover operations lasting five or more consecutive work days.
- Drilling overhead applies to abandonment operationslasting five or more consecutive work days.

## 2. PERCENTAGE BASIS

The percentage based overhead provisions in the COPAS 2005 Accounting Procedure are essentially the same as the 1984 and 1986 forms. Each form provide for development and operating percentage based overhead, and the language is very similar. Highlights of the percentage overhead provisions are as follows:

## Development Rate

Applies to:

- Drilling, re-drilling, sidetracking, or deepening operations
- Plugging back or workover operations lasting five (5) or more consecutive work days
- Abandonment of a well that was not completed as a producer
- Preliminary expenditures necessary to prepare for drilling
- Fixed asset projects that do not qualify for major construction or catastrophe overhead.

As the activities mentioned qualify for Drilling Overhead (2.5%), the Operator is requested to grant the remainder of credit due on this exception.

replies.text:
The Operator has stated that " Prepping activity, travel days, and standby time do not count as being 'on the well' and are excluded from the 5 consecutive workdays rule." . This is contrary to MFI-21 which states that recompletion and workover operations lasting for five or more consecutive work days qualify for Drilling Overhead:

## 1. FIXED RATE BASIS (WELL BASIS)

The fixed rate overhead provisions in the COPAS 2005 Accounting Procedure are essentially the same as the 1984 and 1986 forms, to help standardize accounting amongst these forms. Accordingly, drilling and producing overhead under the fixed rate basis are assessed as follows:

## Drilling Overhead

- The drilling rate in the agreement is a rate per well.
- The drilling rate is expressed as a monthly rate that is pro-rated based on the number of drilling days.
- Drilling overhead starts when (1) the well is spud, for onshore wells, or (2) the equipment arrives on location, for offshore wells.
- Drilling overhead ceases when the drilling or completion equipment is released, whichever is later.
- Drilling overhead is not charged when operations are suspended for 15 or more consecutive calendardays.
- Drilling overhead applies to recompletion or workover operations lasting five or more consecutive work days.
- Drilling overhead applies to abandonment operations lasting five or more consecutive workdays.

## 2. PERCENTAGE BASIS

The percentage based overhead provisions in the COPAS 2005 Accounting Procedure are essentially the same as the 1984 and 1986 forms. Each form provide for development and operating percentage based overhead, and the language is very similar. Highlights of the percentage overhead provisions are as follows:

## Development Rate

Applies to:

- Drilling, re-drilling, sidetracking, or deepening operations
- Plugging back or workover operations lasting five (5)or more consecutive work sday
- Abandonment of a well that was not completed as a producer
- Preliminary expenditures necessary to prepare for drilling
- Fixed asset projects that do not qualify for major construction or catastrophe overhead.

As the activities mentioned qualify for Drilling Overhead (2.5%), the Operator is requested to grant the remainder of credit due on this exception.

Accordingly, the Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $487,150.93 for the excess Overhead charged.

replies.text:
Credit Denied.

The Operator's Accounting classification does not dictate the Overhead to be applied to the costs. It is the Overhead section of the Accounting Procedure and the scope of work. The scope of work was presented in the AFE's.

Application of Overhead - Percentage Basis shall be as follows :

For the purpose of determining charges on a percentage basis under Paragraph 1B of this Section III, Development shall include all cost in connection with drilling, re-drilling, or deepening of any or all wells, and shall also include any remedial operation requiring a period of five (5) consecutive work days or more on any or all wells; also, preliminary expenditures necessary in preparation for drilling and expenditures incurred in abandoning when the well is not completed as a producer, and original cost of construction or installation of Fixed Assets , the expansion of fixed assets and any other project clearly discernible as a fixed asset, except Major Construction as defined in Paragraph 2 of this Section III. All other costs shall be considered as Operating except that Catastrophe costs shall be assessed overhead as provided in Section III, Paragraph 3.

The Overhead in the Auditor's pivot table is incorrect. The Auditor included JV Burden as Overhead. Below is the pivot table without the JV burden account.

For WBS C.US.MR2.PD.18.005.1230A - MB17 LLE Well Head Instrumentation, there were two different overheads charged (Jan-October 2020 Producing) and Nov-Dec 2020 Development. There was an adjusting entry made in Nov 2020 giving $235,330.38 TG credit for the percentage overhead that was overbilled. Attached is SAP document 129921257 made in 11/2020 to account A7970160 JV Adjustment BI Overhead.

For WBS C.US.WEB.PD.19.002.0942A MC806-003 Drilling LLAFE, the Auditor included Account A6560050 Rent Co-owned Facilities - Renter BI. This is a revenue account and overhead are not calculated on revenue accounts. Account A8399830 IT Recovery Costs-BI did not attract overhead, and the Joint Account is adjusted accordingly. Taking these accounts into consideration., the overhead charged to the Joint Account is correct.

For the WBS's that have in their description "Turnaround",

- The Operator made an internal decision to start capitalizing turn arounds, which does not impact the accounting classification and treatment of co-owners or the OH rate.
- Co -owners are accustomed to associating 'C' type AFE's with capital and a lower OH rate, but the activity itself is what drives the OH rate - not our accounting rules.
- This is consistent with how BP as Operator bills Shell the Operating OH rate for turnaround activity at NaKika. For the WBS's that have in their description "Commissioning/Unload"

While there is nothing in COPAS or the JOA/UOA Accounting Procedures that specifically addresses the well commissioning and unload costs, all the technical work is performed by Operations and is considered Operating costs and therefore, should be charged based on the Operating Overhead rate.

By definition, the execution of well unloads falls under 'other cost'.

Per COPAS MFI 21, 'Operating costs are chargeable costs other than those classified as D evelopment, Major Construction, Catastrophe or Project Team and are subject to the Operating Overhead Percentage application'.

Per COPAS 1986 Accounting Procedure (Exhibit C of JOA/UOA), if Percentage Based Overhead is selected under Section III (Overhead), then according to Section III, B (2), all other costs are considered Operating costs.

Application of Overhead - Percentage Basis shall be as follows: For the purpose of determining charges on a percentage basis under Paragraph 1B of this Section III, Development shall include all cost in connection with drilling, re-drilling, or deepening of any or all wells, and shall also include any remedial operation requiring a period of five (5) consecutive work days or more on any or all wells; also, preliminary expenditures necessary in preparation for drilling and expenditures incurred in abandoning when the well is not completed as a producer, and original cost of construction or installation of Fixed Assets, the expansion of fixed assets and any other project clearly discernible as a fixed asset, except Major Construction as defined in Paragraph 2 of this Section III. All other costs shall be considered as Operating except that Catastrophe costs shall be assessed overhead as provided in Section III, Paragraph 3.

replies.text:
The Operator, in its response stated that " Co-owners are accustomed to associating 'C' type AFE's with capital and a lower OH rate, but the activity itself is what drives the OH rate - not our accounting rules".

According to the Mars Unit Operating Agreement, Article 8, Expenditures, section 8.2 Authorization, the Operator shall be allowed exceed the original AFE limit by 10%. As noted in the Exhibit "C" Accounting Procedure, the Development Rate is 2.5%, and the Operating Rate is 13%, and the difference between the two is 10.5% which exceeds the Operator's allowance under the Unit Operating Agreement.

On any given current Shell AFE, there is not a box/field which Shell informs the Co-Owners what overhead rate will be applied to the particular cost/WBS in question. (See finding PF0001). The Co-Owners therefore rely on the Operator's classification of a project as a "C/P/O" type WBS in order to determine the Overhead rate to be expected, as the Co-Owners are not informed elsewhere by the Operator. Therefore, when the Operator informs the Co-owners on the AFE that the classification will be as Capital Development 2.5%, however charges the Operating Expense rate of 13% they have by default exceeded the 10% AFE threshold as stated in the UOA.

These AFEs which have exceeded the stated expenditure threshold due to incorrect overhead category are therefore not approved and should be credited to the Joint Account, unless the Operator can provide evidence of additional approval of the Participating Parties.

- 8.2 Authonzation. Operator shall neither make any singleexpenditure nor undertake any project costinę in excess of Three Hundred Thousand Dollars ($300,000) for platform or major facilities expenditures, and One Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars (S150,000) for all other types of expenditures, without prior approval of the Participating Parties and shall submit an "Authority for Expenditure" (AFE) to the Participating Parties for all such expenditures or projects. Operator shall be allowed to expend up to ten percent (10%)above the AFE amount without obtaining additional approval of the Participating Parties. Operator shall furmnish written information to all the Participating Parties on any single expenditure or project costing in excess of Twenty Five Thousand Dollars (S25,000). Subject to any election provided in Articles 10, 12 and 13 hereof, approval of an Appraisal or a Development Step-Out Well (drilled as an expendable well shall include approval of all necessary expenditures for drilling and logging to Objective Depth, and approval of Development Well or a Development Step-Out Well (not drilled as an expendable well) shall include approval of all necessary expenditures through installation of the wellhead. In the event of an emergency, and notwithstanding the foregoing, Operator may immediately make such expendituresas in its opinion as a reasonable and prudent operator, are required to deal with the emergency. Operator shall report to the Participating Parties, as promptly as possible, the nature of the emergency and action taken.

replies.text:
Credit denied.

The contract provision of that Operator shall be allowed to expend up to 10% above the AFE amount without obtaining additional approval of the Participating Parties from section 8.2 Authorization of Article 8. Expenditures from the Mars UOA quoted by the auditor is for the Operator to obtain additional approval from the co-owner when the actual spending had exceeded 10% of the approved amount of an AFE. Except for auditor's assumption, there is no proof that the expenditure of an AFE has exceeded the 10% of the approved amount. The contract provision quoted by the auditor is not to be used as the basis for the determination of overhead rate for an AFE.

As stated in IR-008 during field audit (see below), the Overhead section of the Accounting Procedure and the scope of work dictate the Overhead rate to be applied to the costs. The scope of work was presented in the AFE's.

Application of Overhead - Percentage Basis shall be as follows :

By definition, the execution of well unloads falls under 'other cost'.

Per COPAS MFI 21, 'Operating costs are chargeable costs other than those classified as Development, Major Construction, Catastrophe or Project Team and are subject to the Operating Overhead Percentage application'.

Per COPAS 1986 Accounting Procedure (Exhibit C of JOA/UOA), if Percentage Based Overhead is selected under Section III (Overhead), then according to Section III, B (2), all other costs are considered Operating costs.

The Operator, in its response stated that " Coowners are accustomed to associating 'C' type AFE's with capital and a lower OH rate, but the activity itself is what drives the OH rate - not our accounting rules".

According to the Mars Unit Operating Agreement, Article 8, Expenditures, section 8.2 Authorization, the Operator shall be allowed exceed the original AFE limit by 10%. As noted in the Exhibit "C" Accounting Procedure, the Development Rate is 2.5%, and the Operating Rate is 13%, and the difference between the two is 10.5% which exceeds the Operator's allowance under the Unit Operating Agreement.

On any given current Shell AFE, there is not a box/field which Shell informs the Co-Owners what overhead rate will be applied to the particular cost/WBS in question. (See finding PF0001). The Co-Owners therefore rely on the Operator's classification of a project as a "C/P/O" type WBS in order to determine the Overhead rate to be expected, as the Co-Owners are not informed elsewhere by the Operator. Therefore, when the Operator informs the Co-owners on the AFE that the classification will be as Capital Development 2.5%, however charges the Operating Expense rate of 13% they have by default exceeded the 10% AFE threshold as stated in the UOA.

These AFEs which have exceeded the stated expenditure threshold due to incorrect overhead category are therefore not approved and should be credited to the Joint Account, unless the Operator can provide evidence of additional approval of the Participating Parties.

8.2 Authonzaton. Operator shall neithermakeany singleexpenditurenor undertakeany project costing in excessof Three Hundred Thousand Dollars (S300,000) for platform or major facilities expenditures, and One Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars (S150,000) for all other types of expenditures, without prior approval of the Paricipating Parties and shall submit an "Authority for Expenditure" (AFE) to the Participating Parties for all such expenditures or projects. Operator shall be allowed to expend up to ten percent (10%)above the AFE amount without obtaining additional approval of the Participating Parties. Operator shall furmish written information to all the Participating Parties on any singleexpenditure or project costing in excess of Twenty Five Thousand Dollars (S25,000). Subject to any election provided in Articles 10, 12 and 13 hereof, approval of an Appraisal or a Development Step-Out Well (drilled as an expendable well shall includeapproval of all necessary expenditures for drilling and logging to Objective Depth, and approval of Development Well or a Development Step-Out Well (not drilled as an expendable well) shall include approval of all necessary expenditures through installation of the wellhead. In the event of an emergency, and notwithstanding the foregoing, Operator ma immediately make such expendituresas in its opinion as a reasonableand prudent operator, are required to deal with the emergency. Operator shall report to the Participating Parties, as promptly as possible, the nature of the emergency and action taken.

The Operator charged the Joint Account $ 535,844.31 on various Sumitomo Corporation Of Americas invoices for SCM Fee Consignment charges. This is a management fee and is not a direct cost of the material but an additional fee to house the material and ensure it is available when needed.

Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreement states: As compensation for administrative, supervision, office services and warehousing costs, Operator shall charge the Joint Account in accordance with this Section III.'

Additionally, AG 19, Section IV.3.C states 'Actual costs may include costs of (I) Material, (2) making it suitable for use, and (3) transportation from the point of acquisition to the Joint Property including loading and unloading. Not included are storage or carrying costs."

The Operator is requested to reimburse joint account for$535,844.31 plus overhead of 2.5%.

replies.text:
Credit denied. The consignment fee is neither warehouse nor storage fee. The Operator does not own any of goods/ products or inventory at vendor's facility. The contract provision described in Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreemen t (UOA)stated does not apply here.

Per UOA, Exhibit 'C' Section II Direct Charges, 4. Material, Material purchased or furnished by Operator for use on the Joint Property as provided under Section IV. Only such material shall be purchased for or transferred to the Joint Property as may be required for immediate use and is reasonably practical and consistent with efficient and economical operations. The accumulation of surplus stocks shall be avoided.

In compliance to and support of this contract provision of having the material ready for immediate use and prevent the accumulation of surplus stocks, this consignment fee have the vendor to agree to invoice for the full amounts of goods/ products until they have been shipped offshore for installation/consumption. Any items not used/ consumed/installed can be returned to vendor for credit. And the Joint Account will pay for items which are used in the well only.

The Fee in question is not a direct cost of the Material; it is a fee paid separately to the vendor. According to MFI-38, direct material purchases "... should be charged to the joint account at the final price paid for the material." The SCM fee is not a cost of the material, nor is it a service associated with the material (such as coating, inspection or transportation). Therefore, it should be credited to the Joint Account. Full credit remains due.

III. MATERIALS PRICING

## A. Direct Purchase Pricing

The operator generally is responsible for providing materials to be used by joint operations. The operator can provide these materials in several ways. The simplest way of providing materials, from an accounting standpoint, is via a Direct Purchase. A Direct Purchase occurs when an agreement is created between the operator and a third party to provide materials for a specific project or a property. The operator can make a direct purchase of either new or used materials.

Direct Purchases should be charged to the joint account at the final price paid for the material. This is inclusive of all discounts received by the operator from the third party, as well as any costs for any special features or services associated with the material, such as coating, inspection and transportation. The operator should make a good faith effort to obtain the best possible value for the joint account. Refer to COPAS MFI-23, Discounts, for specific guidance on accounting for discounts and rebates.

## From the Consignment Fee Contract:

## 4. SCMFEE

SCM fees are subject to review and adjustment based on forecast accuracy and inventory turn performance. SCM Fees will be applied to the DDP price quoted to COMPANY for a particular item at time of mill order placement as per below. For a first 12 month period, the initial SCM fee shall be applied. The inventory turn will be measured during that period and the SCM fee for the next 6 months shall be determined based on a trailing 12-month inventory turn rate per below table. Inventory turns shall be calculated utilizing only those items that belong to the respective category. This process will repeat every six months as part of the overall inventory management review process. Any variation in 3-month LIBOR rates outside the range of 0.5%-1.5% shall be discussed between COMPANY and CONTRACTOR during the review meetings to determine how SCM fees shall be adjusted.

As this fee represents the cost of warehousing, it is covered by Overhead, and full credit remains due.

According to MFI-38, direct material purchases "... should be charged to the joint account at the final price paid for the material." III. MATERIALS PRICING

## A. Direct Purchase Pricing

The operator generally is responsible for providing materials to be used by joint operations. The operator can provide these materials in several ways. The simplest way of providing materials, from an accounting standpoint, is via a Direct Purchase. A Direct Purchase occurs when an agreement is created between the operator and a third party to provide materials for a specific project or a property. The operator can make a direct purchase of either new or used materials.

Direct Purchases should be charged to the joint account at the final price paid for the material. This is inclusive of all discounts received by the operator from the third party, as well as any costs for any special features or services associated with the material, such as coating, inspection and transportation. The operator should make a good faith effort to obtain the best possible value for the joint account. Refer to COPAS MFI-23, Discounts, for specific guidance on accounting for discounts and rebates.

005.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $4,296,128.86 for materials on Mars A21 according to the provided JADE lines. Upon review, it appears that these items were not ran in the well per the support provided on Information Requests IR001, IR005, IR065, and IR076, which were raised during the fieldwork.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $4,296,128.86 for the materials plus 2.5% overhead for a credit of $4,403,532.08.

table_references.summary:
## Summary

This table presents a well materials/tubular goods reconciliation, tracking footage charged versus what was actually set in a well. A total of 1,517.01 feet (33 joints) were charged at **$99.33 per foot** ($150,682.60 total), while only 711.38 feet were confirmed run in the well (704.34 feet per iWells report plus 0.01 thread loss adjustment). This resulted in an **over-charge of 805.6 feet**, generating a **credit back to the joint account of $80,021.83**.

replies.text:
Following the transfer, a total of 298 joints of 8 5/8" casing were received at the well site, amounting to 12,840.91 feet - an average of 43.09 feet per joint. Of these, 296 joints totaling 12,215 feet were installed, with an average length of 41.27 feet per joint.

The discrepancy in footage per joint is attributed to unrecognized waste or loss of casing during installation. To account for this loss in the reconciliation, the joint count is undercharged by 36 feet, equating to $3,912.34. The operator has waived this undercharge.

This exception is considered resolved and should be closed.

replies.text: Based on the Operator's own statement in the previous rebuttal, 12,840.91 feet were charged, and only 12,215 feet were installed. Adding 1% thread loss (122.16ft) brings the installed footage up to 12,337.82 including thread loss. This means that 503.09 feet are in excess (12,840.91 - 12,337.82 = 503.09). Considering a price of $108.75 per foot, the Joint Account should therefore be credited $54,711.04 plus 2.5% Overhead.

## Summary

This table contains casing component data for two Intermediate Liner Casing strings in a well. The first string has a nominal OD of **11.75 inches**, set at **21,477 ft** on **11/27/2021**, consisting of three components including threadlocked casing and a guide shoe. The second string has a nominal OD of **7.625 inches**, set at a deeper depth of **25,067 ft** on **12/17/2021**, and contains numerous components including hangers, seal bores, pup joints, float collars, and guide shoes, predominantly made of **Q125 ISO grade** pipe weighing **39 lb/ft** with an OD/ID of **7.63/6.63 inches**.

replies.text:
Credit denied. It is uncertain why the auditor had removed the transfer activities from his reconciliation as it shown in his snip. The reconciliation is to perform by well, by WBS and by material type/ size even for transfer made within Mars. Instead of removing and ignoring material transferred made from Well MA04 to P11 or MB03, etc., the auditor is recommended to provide a reconciliation at Well P11 or MB03 or follow up the transfer in the subsequent year of audit.

The credits of $212,556.28 of inter well transfers have already been issued. Please refer to the Operator's reconciliation and CJI3 work sheet provided in the initial Operator's response. Therefore, the total footage charged is not at 16,454.92 FT shown by the auditor. It should be at 13,128.01 FT.

[table 2]

Per the reconciliation, the difference in this reconciliation is three joints. It is within the acceptable variance. No adjustment will be made to the Joint Account.

The footage discrepancy represents the discrepancy between the FT per joint of material charged vs FT per Joint set in well. There is a difference of 1.53 FT per Joint. Apparently, the discrepancy could be attributed from having different technique or method used in measurement for various activities. Therefore, it is appropriate to place the focus of the reconciliation on the total number of Joints charged in vs. the total number of Joints set in well.

It records 92 joints totaling **4,220.87 feet** charged at an average price of **$52.94/foot**, resulting in a total charged amount of **$223,456.06**. After reconciling against actual footage set in the well (3,264.82 feet, adjusted to 3,297.47 feet with thread loss), there is an overcharge discrepancy of **923.4 feet**, resulting in a **credit of $48,885.59** to the joint account.

It records footage, amounts charged, and average price per foot across 72 total joints covering **3,316.60 feet**, with a total amount charged of **$179,716.48** at an average price of **$54.19 per foot**. Key reconciliation figures show a footage discrepancy of **51.78 feet** and a credit/charge to the joint account of **($1,769.11)**, with actual footage set in the well reported as **3,264.82 feet** per iWells.

Credit denied. It is uncertain why the auditor had removed the transfer activities from his reconciliation as it shown in his snip. The reconciliation is to perform by well, by WBS and by material type/ size even for transfer made within Mars. Instead of removing and ignoring material transferred made from inter Wells, the auditor is recommended to provide a reconciliation at each well or follow up the transfer in the subsequent year of audit.

The credits of $44,361.18 of transfers/ disposal have already been issued. Please refer to the Operator's reconciliation and CJI3 work sheet provided in the initial Operator's response. Therefore, the total footage charged is not at 4,220.87 FT shown by the auditor. Instead, it is at 3,316.60 FT.

[table 2]

Per the reconciliation, total 72 joints charged have been installed. Therefore, no adjustment will be made to the Joint Account.

The footage discrepancy represents the discrepancy between the FT per joint of material charged vs FT per Joint set in well. There is a difference of 0.72 FT per Joint. Apparently, the discrepancy could be attributed from having different technique or method used in measurement for various activities. Therefore, it is appropriate to place the focus of the reconciliation on the total number of Joints charged in vs. the total number of Joints set in well.

Job Summary:

The Operations Engineer is primarily responsible for supporting and coordinating activities of workers and equipment engaged in drilling oil and gas wells and support the local office, yard activities, and customer from an engineering / technical standpoint.

- Defines project objectives; develops operating plan; including manpower requirements, in compliance with management decisions related with the rig site and operations.

- Analyzes rig inspections and submits rig condition reports

- Monitors the condition of drilling rigs and equipment to ensure preventative maintenance procedures are followed.
- Serves as liaison with customer and Company personnel on engineering / technical rig operations.

The Operator charged the Joint Account $61,000.26 for the following Shell Offshore Inc (SOI) invoices as shown on the attached JADE lines. These were the subject of IR #27 during fieldwork.

|   SOI Invoice | Invoice Date   | Amount     |
|---------------|----------------|------------|
|    1800413259 | 2/17/2020      | $30,500.13 |
|    1800413251 | 2/14/2020      | $21,203.62 |

An examination of invoice #1800413251 shows that the Operator was only billed for $21,203.62 by SOI for materials issued for Transocean Poseidon. However, the joint account was charged for $30,500.13 as shown on the JADE. Thus, the joint account was overcharged by $9,296.51.

Invoice #1800413259 pertains to services provided by DNV GL for DNV GL Class costs. Per the contract attached to the invoice, Transocean is to pick up the first $100,000 of these costs and SOI is to pick up the remaining costs. A total of $128,240.46 was billed by DNV GL to Transocean of which $28,240.46 was for the account of SOI. SOI rebilled this $28,240.46 plus an 8% handling fee for a total of $30,500.13 to the Operator. It appears that this charge benefits 4 Shell rigs as shown on the email attached from Transocean staff and per Operator response. In the email, Transocean had noted that they will allocate their $100,000 share of the costs to 4 Shell rigs. Operator representative has confirmed the same understanding. Thus, the joint account was overcharged by $ 22,875.10 or 3/4 of the total $30,500.13 rebilled to the Operator.

Please credit the Joint account for $32,171.61 ($ 9,296.51+$ 22,875.10) plus 13% overhead for a total of $36,353.92.

table_references.summary: This table tracks pipe/tubing inventory transactions between vendors (primarily Tenaris Global Services and Vallourec USA Corporation) and internal transfers (Shell MTR) across multiple well locations. It records footage amounts, quantities in joints (JTs), and associated charges, with per-foot prices ranging from $58.91 to $98.53. The total charged comes to **$850,026.67** across **10,791.40 feet (249 joints)**, with a minor footage discrepancy of 20.38 feet and a resulting credit/charge to the joint account of **($1,588.42)**.

This table is a **tubular reconciliation report** for Shell's audit (2021SOV_E109) covering well OLYMPUS MB-003 on the Mars property, tracking 7.625" casing (39.00, Q125RY) transactions across multiple voucher references from vendors including OUREC USA Corporation and Naris Global Services. It lists approximately 15 line-item transactions with footage amounts (both positive and negative, indicating charges and credits/reversals) at average prices of **$59.10–$59.36 per foot**, with one entry at $56.40/ft, totaling **7,346.92 feet charged at $410,701.84**. The reconciliation concludes that only 3,723.58 feet were actually set in the well (3,760.82 ft adjusted for 1% thread loss), resulting in a **credit of $200,467.51** owed back to the joint account due to overcharging.
