56.description: Document 06/2021-13035866 charged various Appomattox WBS $7,015.387.17 for use of the Operator owned 400°F Capping Stack at a rate of $25,624.19 per day. The Operator's rate calculation is based on the costs of ownership and operation as provided in Section II, Paragraph 7A of the Appomattox Accounting Procedure and includes operating expenses, insurance, taxes, and interest on investment less accumulated depreciation. The Umbrella Agreement of 09/28/2018 in Paragraph 2.4 and in Exhibit 5 also provides that the rental rate "... is calculated per the Appomattox UOA, specifically the Accounting Procedure Exhibit "C", section II Direct charges paragraph 7 ... ." Information Request 38 submitted questions concerning the calculation and application of the capping stack rental rate components. The Operator's response to Information Request (IR)-038 stated, "The daily rate for the Capping Stack up to this year is $25,624 per day, with market rate plus other assumptions of Maintenance, Insurance, depreciation, and property tax subject to location have also been considered." The response did not address the specific questions concerning the components of the rate calculation. Also, "market factors" and "market rate" as mentioned in the response have no bearing on the rate calculation as described in the Accounting Procedure and the Umbrella Agreement. The auditor's review indicated the following four discrepancies in the rental calculation and application: 1. The daily rental rate of $25,624.19 has been used in activity years 2019, 2020 and 2021 to charge for use of the Capping Stack. Since the Interest on Investment component of the billing rate calculation is determined by applying the interest rate of 8% to the net book value (gross investment amount less accumulated depreciation) of the capping stack, the rental rate should decline each year as the gross investment is depreciated. 2. The daily rental rate calculation included a Maintenance expense component which used an estimated rate of 12% of gross investment to recover the Operator's costs of warehouse maintenance and storage. The estimated 12% maintenance rate results in annual maintenance costs of $3,749,881 (12% X $31,249,011 gross investment) which appear to be very high. The Maintenance component should be based on the Operator's actual costs. Without the Operator's actual cost information, the auditor has used a maintenance rate of 6% in the auditor's determination of a revised rental rate pending receipt of actual maintenance cost information. 3. The capping stack rental rate calculation included a Property Tax component which was calculated using an estimated rate of 1.5% for Louisiana property taxes on gross investment. The response to IR-038 stated the capping stack was stored in the MWCC facility in Ingleside, Texas. The property tax should be based on the actual property taxes paid and the physical location of the equipment when it is rendered for property tax valuation. 4. The rental rate calculations included Property Tax and Insurance components. These costs were determined by applying estimated rates for each component to the capping stack's gross investment. Since the asset declines in value as it ages, the estimated rates should be applied to the asset's gross investment less accumulated depreciation. The auditor used the property tax rate Page 59 of 63 used by the Operator in the auditor's revised rental rate calculations. This rate should be adjusted to the rates actually paid as noted in discrepancy (3) above. The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account for the incorrect capping stack rental rate as detailed in the workpapers provided to the Operator. Credit of $3,050,874.59 is requested plus 2.5% Development Overhead. Credit Requested $ 3,050,874.59 Overhead $ 76,271.86 Exception Total $ 3,127,146.45

replies.text: Credit Denied. The Capping Stack is considered as major equipment. A market rate analysis was conducted by the business in 2018 to determine the day rates and interest rates . Since there has not been any new general assumptions since, the day rates and interest rates have stayed static. As noted in the 2022 audit, Information Request #38… The ownership of the Capping Stack has been transferred to Marine Well Containment Company (MWCC) in 2021. Prior to 2021, It was stored in the MWCC facility in Ingleside, Texas. MWCC also oversees the quarterly function testing for Shell. The Capping Stack is considered as major equipment; hence market factors have been considered in arriving at the day rate. The daily rate for the Capping Stack is $25,624 per day and there have been no rate adjustments since 2019. The rate is calculated based on the below. The is $25,624 /day charge is compared to the internal market analysis done by the business. The daily rental rate of $25,624.19 (which was the day rate in 2019) was applied since it is lower than the Shell Suggested Rate of $30,378.08 (see screen shot of table below). The property tax rate of 1.5% is indeed correct for the Louisiana property tax; however, the Texas property rate is 2.5% and this rate should have been applied instead. For this claim, the Operator has decided not to do a retroactive adjustment for the difference in the property tax rates.

60.description: WBS C.US.APT.PD.14.004.1230E, Well Systems, was charged a total of $3,375,715.61 through seven Transocean invoices as detailed on tab 'Exc 60.1 JADE.' These invoices relate to the installation and operation of the Managed Pressure Drilling (MPD) system on the drill rig Proteus. The full amount of each invoice was charged to the WBS. The auditor also observed in WBS C.US.APT.PD.14.004.1230E similar MPD system charges related to the drill rig Poseidon. Those MPD costs were subsequently transferred out to WBS P.US.RTD.EB.21.001.1510A, Transocean Poseidon MPD Upgrade accumulator (See Exception No 7 of this Audit Report). The absence of similar treatment for the Proteus MPD charges led the auditor to submit Information Request (IR) No 24.1. The Operator responded with "there is no Proteus MPD upgrade accumulator, as it was agreed that Appomattox Wells Systems budget was available to fund the upgrade, and the upgrade was driven by the Appomattox well technical requirements." (Exc 60.3\_IR No 24 Response). However, the auditor obtained a Scout's Web Delivery System Report for the Shell-operated Llano LL6 well (outside the Appomattox footprint) which shows the Proteus onsite in 2022 and the use of MPD equipment (Exc 60.4\_Scout Report). The auditor submitted a follow-up question to IR No 24.1 requesting the Operator confirm whether the MPD equipment was used at Llano LL6 well and if so, then would a Proteus MPD upgrade accumulator be appropriate to allocate the MPD charges to all wells benefitting from the equipment’s use. At the time this Audit Report was issued, the Operator had yet to respond to the follow-up question. The Operator is requested to credit WBS C.US.APT.PD.14.004.1230E in the amount of $3,375,715.61 plus 2.5% Development Overhead or explain why an accumulator is not appropriate considering the MPD equipment being used outside the Appomattox footprint. Credit Requested $ 3,375,715.61 Overhead $ 84,392.89 Exception Total $ 3,460,108.50

replies.text: Credit denied. The MPD equipment on the Proteus was commissioned on 12 th February 2021. Had Shell created a rig accumulator for this piece of equipment, it would have only been allocated from that day forward to the end of the 5 year rig assignment with SEPWES which ended on 5 th May 2021. Shell’s accumulator process is to allocate the cost over the existing rig assignment. Had this occurred, there would have only been 2 wells drilled to pay for this equipment upgrade (AC-003 and IW-001). See below sequence for these dates (in reverse order).

002.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account the full invoice amount for two Noble Drilling invoices; $47,741.07 for Noble invoice 90016883 dated 12/19/2018 and $11,229.28 for Noble invoice 90017128 dated 3/27/2019. These invoices were the subject of Information Request 20 issued to the Operator during the fieldwork.

Invoice 883 is for the removal of a bracket/umbilical frame/padeye that was installed on the Noble Don Taylor rig at some point in the campaign. Invoice 128 is for a replacement gasket assembly.

These costs were incurred immediately prior to the rig idle and release period. As these parts were utilized in the drilling of other wells besides Crosby, it is unfair to burden the Joint Account with the full invoice value.

The Operator is requested to allocate this invoice across all projects and wells drilled since the bracket was installed.

Credit due the Joint Account: $58,970.35 plus 2.5% Overhead.

The Noble Drilling invoice no. 90016883 dated 12/19/2018 for $47,741.07 is for third party rebill for service rendered from 8/20/2018 to 8/24/2018. The service time periods have been captured under Page 6 and page 69 of the supports attached behind this invoice.

The Noble Drilling invoice no. 90017128 dated 3/27/2019 for $11,229.28 is for the reimbursement of gasket replaced on 7/4/2018. Please see invoice page 4, 5, and 6 for detail. It shows the gasket was used on 7/4/2018 with an estimated value of $11,006.40 and get reimbursed based on the actual invoice from Cameron.

Therefore, these two charges were made correctly. Credit request is denied

As stated in the Operator's initial response, The rig of Don Taylor was on Crosby #5 from 7/2/2018 to 8/24/2018. The two invoices in question were to obtain reimbursement for third party service and gasket replacement which were damaged during the operation of Crosby #5. Please refer to the supports of rig schedule and two invoices provided prior. Per COPAS MFI-56 Rig Related Costs, XIII. Rig Repairs, Chargeability of Rig Repairs, snip below, these costs are directly chargeable to the Joint Account.

## Chargeability of Rig Repairs

Generally speaking, costs for repairs due to damages caused by operations on a specific property are direc chargeable to the property whose operations caused the damage. For example, some Rig equipment, su as Blow-Out Preventers, may require frequent inspections that reveal a need for unexpected repairs. Co

13

Additionally, the auditor's rebuttal "The main invoice (snip below) was for removal of a derrick hang-off which is a part that was utilized by all wells during the drilling campaign. The gasket in question similarly should not be charged entirely to Crosby." is not supported by COPAS MFI-56 Rig Related Costs. Per COPAS MFI-56 Rig Related Costs, XIII. Rig Repairs, Chargeability of Rig Repairs, 2nd paragraph, snip below, the costs in question are directly chargeable to all wells using the repaired equipment over the remaining life of the Rig Contract. Accordingly, it is correct to charge the Crosby Joint Account directly for these costs.

Costs for repairs not caused by operations on a specific property are a part of the overall compensation due the drilling contractor and are directly chargeable to all wells using the repaired equipment over the remaining life of the Rig Contract. These costs are directly chargeable to the joint account under the Labor, Transportation, Services or other pertinent provisions of the applicable accounting procedures except the D o ad o s o - s o dDn o ond provides that such costs are directly chargeable to the joint account under the Equipment and Facilities Furnished by Parties, Affiliates provisions. Refer to Appendices B, C, D and F. Methods of allocating these costs include a daily or monthly rate or a flat rate per well, based on the Company's reasonable and consistent procedures. Refer to the Allocation section for further discussion.

Regarding SOI Invoice 90016883, the services provided here is the removal of a derrick hangoff. This is not a repair. It is removal of an accessory attached to the rig before returning the rig. This overhang had served/benefitted all the properties served by the rig and therefore its removal cost should be allocated to all the properties benefitted.

Regarding SOI Inv 90017128, the cost relates to a gasket repair which was made on July 4, 2018. As noted on the rig schedule, the Don Taylor started working on Crosby on July 2, 2018. Thus, there is a high degree of likelihood that the damage occurred prior to serving Crosby. This credit remains due until the Operator demonstrates that the damage to the gasket occurred between July 2-4 while the Don Taylor was at Crosby.

Credit of $58,970.35 plus 2.5% overhead remains due.

003.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $4,829,076.98 in accumulator costs for rig mobilization, upgrades. These were the subject of Information Request 23 issued to the Operator during the fieldwork.

The Globetrotter II rig charged $4,815,199.16 in costs using an allocation basis of 477 days according to the NGT II Accumulator Consolidated workbook included with this IR, which matches the JADE charges. According to the Noble Fleet Status report, also provided, the contract with Shell should be 1705 days. (Jan 1 2019 to Sept 1 2023).

Additionally, the workbooks used to make the charges used a budget figure, not the actual costs, and no true-up was provided by the Operator. The budgeted mobilization figure used is $21,300,000 vs actual cost of $19,538,249. The budgeted upgrades figure used is $11,050,000 vs actual cost of $161,656. The Operator did not provide information regarding any potential true-up during the audit fieldwork.

A revised accumulator sheet has been prepared to accompany this exception using the corrected contract length which leads to a dayrate of $11,459.38/day for mobilization and $94.81/day for the modifications. Using the corrected dayrates, multiplied by 71 days of rig usage equals a charge of $820,347.94 which is what should have been charged to the Joint Account. The total overcharge to the Joint Account is ($4,815,199.16-$820,347.94)=$3,994,851.22 plus overhead.

The Don Taylor rig charged $13,877.82 in budget to actuals true-up costs on a basis of 474 days according to the provided accumulator workbook. Upon review, the letter agreement from Shell to Noble (see invoice 5103011571) is dated 12/9/2016 which is when Shell agreed to the BSEE required modifications. Keeping the contract termination date unadjusted, the revised accumulator start date leads to an amortization period of 624 days and a reduction in the dayrate from $2,494.78/day to $1,895.07/day.

According to the revised calculations in the workbook, the Joint Account should have received a credit of $18,506.29 instead of a charge. This means the total overcharge to the Joint Account is ($13,877.82+$18,506.29)=$32,384.11 plus overhead.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $4,027,235.33 plus 2.5% overhead.

replies.text:
I. Regarding the cost allocation of mobilization and upgrade of NOBLE GLOBETROTTER II (NGT2) rig, it isinappropriate for the auditor to use 1705 days (Jan 1 2019 to Sept 1 2023) as an basis of allocation from Noble Fleet status report obtained from the website and to ignore the facts presented by the rig schedule and LOA which documents have been provided to the auditor during the field audit.

The NGT2 was mobilized to the US GoM in July 2019 from Bulgaria. The official SOI assignment date began on 26th July 2019. The assignment was for a term of 18 months, and therefore would end on the 25th January 2020. The rig incurred a number of days between 26th July and 10 October 2019 for intake and upgrades before it could begin work in the GoM. It began drilling the first well on 11th October, therefore the allocation period between 11 October 2019 and 29 January 2021 (477 days) is the period in which all drilling activities occurred during the assignment period. It is correct to use 477 days as a basis to calculate the dayrate. The credit claim of $3,994,851.22 plus overhead is denied.

II. Regarding the Don Taylor rig, the true up/ unwind of Well Control Accumulator of Don Taylor rig, the charge of $13,877.82 in actuals true-up calculated on the basis of 474 days has been done correctly. The purpose of this accumulator is to bring rig into compliance with BSEE CFR 250.730 to 250.739 well control ruling regarding Oil and Gas and sulfur operations in the outer continental self-blowout preventer system and well control. These upgrades and tests benefit the remaining rig activities. Since the accumulator was not approve and set up until 5/8/2017, it is correct to allocate this well control cost on the basis of 474 days from 5/8/2017 to 8/24/2018. To allocate this cost starting from 12/9/2016 as suggested by the auditor is inappropriate since no wells received any benefit from well control activities until 5/8/2017. Therefore, the claim of ($13,877.82 + $18,506.29) = $32,384.11 plus overhead is denied.

MFI 53 notes the following in its discussion of rig-related costs:

Rig-related costs also include all costs for commissioning and mobilization of a rig, including, but not limited to, sea trials and transportation of the rig from its construction site to the Gulf of Mexico.

Generally speaking, Rig-Related Costs are borne by the properties that benefit. For costs such as construction, commissioning, and mobilization, that includes all the properties served over the life of the agreement with the rig owner.

Thus, it is incorrect for the Operator to use the time period when NGT2 is drilling at Crosby to allocate Mobilization costs. These mobilization costs should be allocated over the life of the agreement with the rig owner. In this case, NGT2 is leased to Shell for 1705 days and therefore mobilization costs should be allocated over this period to all properties benefitting from the service of this rig during this time. In addition to this, the Operator has not addressed the issue of using budget amounts instead of actual amounts for allocation.

MFI 56 Section VI notes the following regarding rig modifications:

Rig modifications include, but are not limited to, changes made to meet: government regulations, technical requirements or specifications to make the rig suitable for drilling in a particular area or under certain drilling conditions; the Company's needs or standards, or to perform specific operations functions.

Often Rig Modifications benefit all wells drilled over the remaining life of the Rig Contract, but they could benefit only a subset of wells.

The Operator's use of 474 days based on the approval date of the accumulator is clearly erroneous. The accumulator is merely an accounting tool to collect and distribute costs and its approval date should not factor into the allocation period.

The Letter Agreement dated December 9, 2016 noted that the deadline for compliance with the BSEE requirements was July 28, 2016. Noble had requested for and was granted a departure not to exceed Dec 28, 2016. Shell and Noble agreed on Dec 9, 2016 to comply with these.

Furthermore, the timesheet backup attached to Noble invoice # 90016087 (dated 5/8/2017) shows that work to comply with these BSEE requirements started as early as July, 2016. This makes sense in light of the December 2016 deadline for compliance.

Thus, the work done to be in compliance with these BSEE requirements would have started to benefit wells by Dec 9, 2016 and not the date that the accumulator was set up on 5/8/2017. If the BSEE work did not benefit the wells until 5/8/2017, this would have implied that Shell and Noble were out of compliance with BSEE regulations for at least 4 months.

Given the above facts and guidance from MFI 56, we stand by our original exception that Don Taylor modification costs should be allocated over 624 days instead of 474 days.

Total credit of $4,027,235.33 plus 2.5% overhead remains due.

The JADE lines provided by the auditor are incomplete. The standard JADE line provided by the Operator to the auditor has 42 columns. However, there are only 29 columns in the JADE provided by the auditor. The auditor had removed information from Column A to column P. The data of Account no., WBS, cost objects, and other pertinent information of the first 16 columns are missing. When proper JADE line entries are not provided, it causes extra work and create additional burden on Operator to review the audit claim. The Operator has the right to deny the claim until the auditor can provide any missing information.

FMC Invoice No. 92528375 references Purchase Order No. 4513643912 (PO)) previously provided to the Auditor. The delivery location for this PO is Crosby-Central Receiving in Morgan City, LA. During field audit work it was explained to the Auditor regarding the Operator's practice to utilize hardware already in-progress in order to meet installation schedules. When the Crosby CA7 well was put into execution mode the Operator made the decision to allocate hardware from the Europa EA3 project which was already in-progress. The Operator can do this

due to the standard nature of the hardware utilized in our portfolio. Therefore, Crosby CA7 received hardware in time to meet the installation schedule and the Crosby CA 7 hardware is charged to Europa EA3 at a later time as its schedule permits. Please see the attached email from engineer Jared for detail.

In the email response provided by the Operator's employee, Mr. Jared Spritzer dated 4/8/2021, he noted that " Crosby CA7 received the following to make schedule that were funded by others...Subsea X-mas Tree, SCM, Choke, Tubing Hanger"

Conceptually the Non-Operator does not take issue with utilizing parts from other projects in the "mix and match" fashion as alluded to in Mr. Spritzer's email in order to make schedule deadlines and accelerate work activities.

The Non-Operator wants to ensure: 1. The correct price was paid for the parts, and 2. that the parts in question were in-fact installed. The pricing concern is especially important as the parts in question are rebuilt parts and will not necessarily carry a uniform price due to different levels of work required in the overhaul process which varies from part to part.

The Operator is therefore requested to:

1. Furnish evidence that the Xmas Tree in question was installed on the well (schematic/drawing with serial # reference)
2. Provide invoices for the installed Xmas Tree and other parts (which were charged to other wells) so that the Non-Operator can verify the price paid for the Europa parts is the same.

The system for managing M&T rental charges was changed in 2019, from Lindros to the current PowerBI based system. The attached 2020 MT Rates file includes a prior usage report that demonstrates the day rates of 2019 for equipment prior to the transition and establishment of standard rates (per equipment type).These day rates were based on asset value and 10 years depreciation period for 'Subsea - Special' tooling that is explained in the GOM Subsea tab of the spreadsheet, a long with calculations.

When transitioning to the PowerBI system the rental rates were simplified for the highest value equipment, which were grouped into the major categories we're using now and in particular resulted in the standard rates:

- OWIRS = $9 0,000/day
- THRA = $9,900/day
- IWOCS Reel = $9,000/day
- IWOCS HPU = $2,963/day

a snapshot of the 2019 (Lindros) rental rates for some of our major equipment. Using the 10yr depreciation basis it appears that day rate for OWIRS was prohibitive at $191k and was part of the rationale for reducing to $90k.

The IWOCS Reels range in calculated day rates between $6.6 - $12.6k, and the HPUs range from $2.3 - $3.4k. My crude accounting math puts the simplified rates at approximately the average for the rates that would be calculated using the previous method. From a standpoint of costs incurred by Shell (for preservation, maintenance, and storage), there is negligible difference between unique tools.

[table 1]

While we understand the move towards aggregating and simplifying the rates for equipment categories, it is not clear how the dayrates shown on the Operator's response had been derived. For example, the Operator's response shows that IWOCS 6 with a historical cost of $4,586,668 has been assigned a dayrate of $11,512.54. The Operator's response seems to imply that the dayrate is derived by assuming a life of 10 years for the equipment. Thus, for this piece of equipment, the dayrate would have been $4,586,668/(10*365) or $ 1,256.62 and not $11,512.54.

Please explain how dayrates noted on the exception are derived or credit remains due.

013.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $ 30,241.20 on various Sumitomo Corporation Of Americas invoices for SCM Fee Consignment charges. This is a management fee and is not a direct cost of the material but an additional fee to house the material and ensure it is available when needed.

Furthermore, FI document 5103297287 does not have the right Sumitomo Corporation invoice attached and could potentially include SCM charges as well.

Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreement states: As compensation for administrative, supervision, office services and warehousing costs, Operator shall charge the Joint Account in accordance with this Section III.'

Additionally, AG 19, Section IV.3.C states 'Actual costs may include costs of (I) Material, (2) making it suitable for use, and (3) transportation from the point of acquisition to the Joint Property including loading and unloading. Not included are storage or carrying costs."

Based on material reconciliation attached, there is also evidence that materials in excess of requirements, and which were subject to the consignment fee, were not repurchased by Sumitomo from Crosby.

The Operator is requested to reimburse joint account for $30,997.23 including overhead.

014.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $61,029.94 for timewriting from IQN employee Justin Phillips, according to the provided JADE lines. In a review of helicopter logs, it was noted that Justin Phillips had not been at Crosby after 3/9/2019. The Joint Account was charged $ 46,914.48 for Justin Phillips' contract labor for time periods subsequent to 3/9/2019. In information request 45, the Operator was requested to provide an explanation as to why Justin Phillips' time was charged to Crosby during time periods when helicopter logs show him to be elsewhere. The operator's response did not address this time discrepancy.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account for $48,087.34 including overhead for contractor labor charges not pertaining to Crosby.

replies.text: Credit denied. Since the claim of this exception is under $50K, it is to be waived and closed in according to letter from BP dated June 18, 2020.
This exception is closed.

015.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $199,000.00 according to the attached JADE line which appears to be a material transfer. In Information Request 39 the Operator was requested to provide documentation of the original cost of the material to confirm that there had not been mark-up or other additional cost on the material.

The Operator is requested to provide support of the price charged or credit the Joint Account $199,000.00 plus 2.5% overhead for the undocumented charge.

attachments: IR-39 CT159 STAR to Crosby 5 Wellhead (1).xlsm

replies.text: Credit denied. Material transferred thru material transfer is not a new purchase. It is used, rebuilt or repaired. Depending on the condition of the material, the price won't be the original purchase price. The wellhead material in question is purchased from BP for ultimate use at Crosby 5. The material transfer is for the STAR BP Wellhead transfer to Crosby 5. The auditor could verify this purchase price from BP if he or she is concerned about any mark-up on the price. Since the material has been used and installed for the Joint property of Crosby 5. No credit is due to the Joint Account.

The auditor is aware that the price charged may not be the original purchase price for the wellhead. We are asking for the basis by which the $199k was charged to the Joint Account. Please provide documentation to substantiate the basis of this charge.

Otherwise, the credit to the Joint Account remains due.

01.description:
The Operator charged the Crosby Joint Account $103,193.70 for LOOP Cavern charges as noted on the provided JADE. The Operator was requested to explain these charges, and to show bp consent to these charges (AFE or otherwise) which was unable to be provided. This was the subject of IR 16 issued to the Operator during the course of fieldwork.

As noted in bp's response to exception 04 from the prior Crosby audit (Shell 2019SOV\_E114 or bp 2019 -112) bp notes its explicit opposition to Shell's use of the ancillary cavern for the Mars corridor during the period of August 2017 through April 2019. As the charges in question here occurred during this period, please refer to the 2019 audit report for bp's ration ale for this exception.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $103,193.70 plus 2.5% OH.

02.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account the full invoice amount for two Noble Drilling invoices; $47,741.07 for Noble invoice 90016883 dated 12/19/2018 and $11,229.28 for Noble invoice 90017128 dated 3/27/2019.

These invoices were the subject of Information Request 20 issued to the Operator during the fieldwork. Invoice 883 is for the removal of a bracket/umbilical frame/padeye that was installed on the Noble Don Taylor rig at some point in the campaign. Invoice 128 is for a replacement gasket assembly.

These costs were incurred immediately prior to the rig idle and release period. As these parts were utilized in the drilling of other wells besides Crosby, it is unfair to burden the Joint Account with the full invoice value. The Operator is requested to allocate this invoice across all projects and wells drilled since the bracket was installed.

Credit due the Joint Account: $58,970.35 plus 2.5% Overhead.

replies.text:
According to the rig schedule of Don Taylor, the rig was on Crosby #5 from 7/2/2018 to 8/24/2018. The two invoices in question were to obtain reimbursement for third party service and gasket replacement incurred during the operation of Crosby #5.

The Noble Drilling invoice no. 90016883 dated 12/19/2018 for $47,741.07 is for third party rebill for service rendered from 8/20/2018 to 8/24/2018. The service time periods have been captured under Page 6 and page 69 of the supports attached behind this invoice.

The Noble Drilling invoice no. 90017128 dated 3/27/2019 for $11,229.28 is for the reimbursement of gasket replaced on 7/4/2018. Please see invoice page 4, 5, and 6 for detail. It shows the gasket was used on 7/4/2018 with an estimated value of $11,006.4 and get reimbursed based on the actual invoice from Cameron.

Therefore, these two charges were made correctly. Credit request is denied.

replies.text:
Per the attached Noble Fleet Status report issued on 12/13/2018, the Operator had exercised its contractual right to idle the Don Taylor rig for the remainder of the contract or 183 days ending February 25, 2019. This means that the rig was idled from Aug 21, 2018 to Feb 25, 2019. As Operator noted in its response, services billed on SOI invoice # 90016883 for $47,741.07 were performed on 8/20/2018-8/24/2018 for derrick overhang removal. These services were performed one day before and during the idle period.

Furthermore, replacement of Cameron gasket billed on SOI invoice #90017128 for $ 11,229.28 appears to have been performed sometime in July or August of 2018 as the original Cameron invoice provided by the Operator was dated Feb 19, 2019 and attached an Exhibit A which referenced dayrates for July and August 2018. In its response, the Operator referenced July 4 as the date of service but this is merely the date of the rebilling form and not the service date. Thus, the Operator is requested to allocate these costs to the relevant wells and properties benefitted by these services. Credit due the Joint Account: $58,970.35 plus 2.5% Overhead

Credit denied.

As stated in the Operator's initial response, The rig of Don Taylor was on Crosby #5 from 7/2/2018 to 8/24/2018. The two invoices in question were to obtain reimbursement for third party service and gasket replacement which were damaged during the operation of Crosby #5. Please refer to the supports of rig schedule and two invoices provided prior. Per COPAS MFI-56 Rig Related Costs, XIII. Rig Repairs, Chargeability of Rig Repairs, snip below, these costs are directly chargeable to the Joint Account.

## Chargeability of Rig Repairs

Generally speaking, costs for repairs due to damages caused by operations on a specific property a chargeable to the property whose operations caused the damage. For example, some Rig equipı as Blow-Out Preventers, may require frequent inspections that reveal a need for unexpected repa

13

Additionally, the auditor's rebuttal "The main invoice (snip below) was for removal of a derrick hang-off which is a part that was utilized by all wells during the drilling campaign. The gasket in question similarly should not be charged entirely to Crosby." is not supported by COPAS MFI-56 Rog Re;ated Costs. Per COPAS MFI-56 Rig Related Costs, XIII. Rig Repairs, Chargeability of Rig Repairs, 2nd paragraph, snip below, the costs in question are directly chargeable to all wells using the repaired equipment over the remaining life of the Rig Contract. Accordingly, it is correct to charge the Crosby Joint Account directly for these costs.

Costs for repairs not caused by operations on a specific property are a part of the overall compen: the drilling contractor and are directly chargeable to all wells using the repaired equipment remaining life of the Rig Contract. These costs are directly chargeable to the joint account under t Transportation, Services or other pertinent provisions of the applicable accounting procedures DWAP. The DWAP definition of Rig-Related Costs includes repair costs paid by the Com provides that such costs are directly chargeable to the joint account under the Equipment and Furnished by Parties, Affiliates provisions. Refer to Appendices B, C, D and F. Methods of these costs include a daily or monthly rate or a flat rate per well, based on the Company's reaso consistent procedures. Refer to the Allocation section for further discussion.

The Operator charged the Joint Account $4,829,076.98 in accumulator costs for rig mobilization, upgrades. These were the subject of Information Request 23 issued to the Operator during the fieldwork. NGT II Accumulator Consolidated workbook included with this IR, which matches the JADE charges. According

The Globetrotter II rig charged $4,815,199.16 in costs using an allocation basis of 477 days according to the to the Noble Fleet Status report, also provided, the contract with Shell should be 1705 days. (Jan 1 2019 to Sept 1 2023).

Additionally, the workbooks used to make the charges used a budget figure, not the actual costs, and no trueup was provided by the Operator. The budgeted mobilization figure used is $21,300,000 vs actual cost of $19,538,249. The budgeted upgrades figure used is $11,050,000 vs actual cost of $161,656. The Operator did not provide information regarding any potential true-up during the audit fieldwork.

A revised accumulator sheet has been prepared to accompany this exception using the corrected contract length which leads to a dayrate of $11,459.38/day for mobilization and $94.81/day for the modifications. Using the corrected dayrates, multiplied by 71 days of rig usage equals a charge of $820,347.94 which is what should have been charged to the Joint Account. The total

overcharge to the Joint Account is ($4,815,199.16-$820,347.94) =$3,994,851.22 plus overhead.

The Don Taylor rig charged $13,877.82 in budget to actuals true-up costs on a basis of 474 days according to the provided accumulator workbook. Upon review, the letter agreement from Shell to Noble (see invoice 5103011571) is dated 12/9/2016 which is when Shell agreed to the BSEE required modifications. Keeping the contract termination date unadjusted, the revised accumulator start date leads to an amortization period of 624 days and a reduction in the dayrate from $2,494.78/day to $1,895.07/day.

According to the revised calculations in the workbook, the Joint Account should have received a credit of $18,506.29 instead of a charge. This means the total overcharge to the Joint Account is ($13,877.82+$18,506.29) =$32,384.11 plus overhead.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $4,027,235.33 plus 2.5% overhead.

replies.text:
I. Regarding the cost allocation of mobilization and upgrade of NOBLE GLOBETROTTER II (NGT2) rig, it is inappropriate for the auditor to use 1705 days (Jan 1 2019 to Sept 1 2023) as an basis of allocation from Noble Fleet status report obtained from the website and to ignore the facts presented by the rig schedule and LOA which documents have been provided to the auditor during the field audit.

The NGT2 was mobilized to the US GoM in July 2019 from Bulgaria. The official SOI assignment date began on 26th July 2019. The assignment was for a term of 18 months, and therefore would end on the 25th January 2020. The rig incurred a number of days between 26th July and 10 October 2019 for intake and upgrades before it could begin work in the GoM. It began drilling the first well on 11th October, therefore the allocation period between 11 October 2019 and 29 January 2021 (477 days) is the period in which all drilling activities occurred during the assignment period. It is correct to use 477 days as a basis to calculate the day rate. The credit claim of $3,994,851.22 plus overhead is denied.

II. Regarding the Don Taylor rig, the true up/ unwind of Well Control Accumulator of Don Taylor rig, the charge of $13,877.82 in actuals true-up calculated on the basis of 474 days has been done correctly. The purpose of this accumulator is to bring rig into compliance with BSEE CFR 250.730 to 250.739 well control ruling regarding Oil and Gas and sulfur operations in the outer continental self-blowout preventer system and well control. These upgrades and tests benefit the remaining rig activities. Since the accumulator was not approve and set up until 5/8/2017, it is correct to allocate this well control cost on the basis of 474 days from 5/8/2017 to 8/24/2018. To allocate this cost starting from 12/9/2016 as suggested by the auditor is inappropriate since no wells received any benefit from well control activities until 5/8/2017. Therefore, the claim of ($13,877.82 + $18,506.29) = $32,384.11 plus overhead is denied.

replies.text: MFI 53 notes the following in its discussion of rig-related costs: Rig-related costs also include all costs for commissioning and mobilization of a rig, including, but not limited to, sea trials and transportation of the rig from its construction site to the Gulf of Mexico. Generally speaking, Rig-Related Costs are borne by the properties that benefit. For costs such as construction, commissioning, and mobilization, that includes all the properties served over the life of the agreement with the rig owner. Thus, it is incorrect for the Operator to use the time period when NGT2 is drilling at Crosby to allocate Mobilization costs. These mobilization costs should be allocated over the life of the agreement with the rig owner. In this case, NGT2 is leased to Shell for 1705 days and therefore mobilization costs should be allocated over this period to all properties benefitting from the service of this rig during this time. In addition to this, the Operator has not addressed the issue of using budget amounts instead of actual amounts for allocation. MFI 56 Section VI notes the following regarding rig modifications: Rig modifications include, but are not limited to, changes made to meet: government regulations, technical requirements or specifications to make the rig suitable for drilling in a particular area or under certain drilling conditions; the Company's needs or standards, or to perform specific operations functions. Often Rig Modifications benefit all wells drilled over the remaining life of the Rig Contract, but they could benefit only a subset of wells. The Operator's use of 474 days based on the approval date of the accumulator is clearly erroneous. The accumulator is merely an accounting tool to collect and distribute costs and its approval date should not factor into the allocation period. The Letter Agreement dated December 9, 2016 noted that the deadline for compliance with the BSEE requirements was July 28, 2016. Noble had requested for and was granted a departure not to exceed Dec 28, 2016. Shell and Noble agreed on Dec 9, 2016 to comply with these. Furthermore, the timesheet backup attached to Noble invoice # 90016087 (dated 5/8/2017) shows that work to comply with these BSEE requirements started as early as July, 2016. This makes sense in light of the December 2016 deadline for compliance. Thus, the work done to be in compliance with these BSEE requirements would have started to benefit wells by Dec 9, 2016 and not the date that the accumulator was set up on 5/8/2017. If the BSEE work did not benefit the wells until 5/8/2017, this would have implied that Shell and Noble were out of compliance with BSEE regulations for at least 4 months. Given the above facts and guidance from MFI 56, we stand by our original exception that Don Taylor modification costs should be allocated over 624 days instead of 474 days. Total credit of $4,027,235.33 plus 2.5% overhead remains due.

The JADE lines provided by the auditor are incomplete. The standard JADE line provided by the Operator to the auditor has 42 columns. The data of Account no., WBS, cost objects, and other pertinent information of the first 16 columns are missing. When proper JADE line entries are not provided, it causes extra work and create additional burden on Operator to review the audit claim. The Operator has the right to deny the claim until the auditor can provide any missing information.

FMC Invoice No. 92528375 references Purchase Order No. 4513643912 (PO)) previously provided to the Auditor. The delivery location for this PO is Crosby-Central Receiving in Morgan City, LA. During field audit work it was explained to the Auditor regarding the Operator's practice to utilize hardware already in-progress in order to meet installation schedules. When the Crosby CA7 well was put into execution mode the Operator made the decision to allocate hardware from the Europa EA3 project which was already in-progress. The Operator can do this due to the standard nature of the hardware utilized in our portfolio. Therefore, Crosby CA7 received hardware in time to meet the installation schedule and the Crosby CA 7 hardware is charged to Europa EA3 at a later time as its schedule permits.

Please see the attached email from engineer Jared for detail.

I. Regarding the cost allocation of mobilization and upgrade of NOBLE GLOBETROTTER II (NGT2) rig, it is inappropriate for the auditor to use 1705 days (Jan 1 2019 to Sept 1 2023) as an basis of allocation from Noble Fleet status report obtained from the website and to ignore the facts presented by the rig schedule and LOA which documents have been provided to the auditor during the field audit.

The NGT2 was mobilized to the US GoM in July 2019 from Bulgaria. The official SOI assignment date began on 26th July 2019. The assignment was for a term of 18 months, and therefore would end on the 25th January 2020. The rig incurred a number of days between 26th July and 10 October 2019 for intake and upgrades before it could begin work in the GoM. It began drilling the first well on 11th October, therefore the allocation period between 11 October 2019 and 29 January 2021 (477 days) is the period in which all drilling activities occurred during the assignment period. It is correct to use 477 days as a basis to calculate the day rate. The credit claim of $3,994,851.22 plus overhead is denied.

II. Regarding the Don Taylor rig, the true up/ unwind of Well Control Accumulator of Don Taylor rig, the charge of $13,877.82 in actuals true-up calculated on the basis of 474 days has been done correctly. The purpose of this accumulator is to bring rig into compliance with BSEE CFR 250.730 to 250.739 well control ruling regarding Oil and Gas and sulfur operations in the outer continental self blowout preventer system and well control. These upgrades and tests benefit the remaining rig activities. Since the accumulator was not approve and set up until 5/8/2017, it is correct to allocate this well control cost on the basis of 474 days from 5/8/2017 to 8/24/2018. To allocate this cost starting from 12/9/2016 as suggested by the auditor is inappropriate since no wells received any benefit from well control activities until 5/8/2017. Therefore, the claim of ($13,877.82 + $18,506.29) = $32,384.11 plus overhead is denied.

replies.text: MFI 53 notes the following in its discussion of rig-related costs: Rig-related costs also include all costs for commissioning and mobilization of a rig, including, but not limited to, sea trials and transportation of the rig from its construction site to the Gulf of Mexico. Generally speaking, Rig-Related Costs are borne by the properties that benefit. For costs such as construction, commissioning, and mobilization, that includes all the properties served over the life of the agreement with the rig owner. Thus, it is incorrect for the Operator to use the time period when NGT2 is drilling at Crosby to allocate Mobilization costs. These mobilization costs should be allocated over the life of the agreement with the rig owner. In this case, NGT2 is leased to Shell for 1705 days and therefore mobilization costs should be allocated over this period to all properties benefitting from the service of this rig during this time. In addition to this, the Operator has not addressed the issue of using budget amounts instead of actual amounts for allocation. MFI 56 Section VI notes the following regarding rig modifications: Rig modifications include, but are not limited to, changes made to meet: government regulations, technical requirements or specifications to make the rig suitable for drilling in a particular area or under certain drilling conditions; the Company's needs or standards, or to perform specific operations functions. Often Rig Modifications benefit all wells drilled over the remaining life of the Rig Contract, but they could benefit only a subset of wells. The Operator's use of 474 days based on the approval date of the accumulator is clearly erroneous. The accumulator is merely an accounting tool to collect and distribute costs and its approval date should not factor into the allocation period. The Letter Agreement dated December 9, 2016 noted that the deadline for compliance with the BSEE requirements was July 28, 2016. Noble had requested for and was granted a departure not to exceed Dec 28, 2016. Shell and Noble agreed on Dec 9, 2016 to comply with these. Furthermore, the timesheet backup attached to Noble invoice # 90016087 (dated 5/8/2017) shows that work to comply with these BSEE requirements started as early as July, 2016. This makes sense in light of the December 2016 deadline for compliance. Thus, the work done to be in compliance with these BSEE requirements would have started to benefit wells by Dec 9, 2016 and not the date that the accumulator was set up on 5/8/2017. If the BSEE work did not benefit the wells until 5/8/2017, this would have implied that Shell and Noble were out of compliance with BSEE regulations for at least 4 months. Given the above facts and guidance from MFI 56, we stand by our original exception that Don Taylor modification costs should be allocated over 624 days instead of 474 days. Total credit of $4,027,235.33 plus 2.5% overhead remains due.

The auditor acknowledges that the issue related to the allocation period will be subject to management/commercial agreement. However, please also note that the accumulator for NGTII used budgeted amounts rather than actual costs as of the period audited. There should be no disagreement that actual costs should be used instead of budgeted costs in calculating the dayrate to be applied.

A revised NGTII accumulator sheet has been prepared using the allocation period of 477 days used by the Operator but correcting for actual costs as of the audit period. This calculation leads to a revised dayrate of $40,960.69/day for mobilization and $338.90/day for the modifications. Using these dayrates based on actual costs, multiplied by 71 days of rig usage equals a charge of $2,932,270.89 which is what should have been charged to the Joint Account. Thus, to correct for actual costs only (but using the Operator's allocation period), the overcharge to the Joint Account is ($4,815,199.16-$2,932,270.89)= $1,882,928.27 plus overhead. This overcharge due to using budgeted amounts rather than actual spend is due now, with the remainder of the original credit requested to be paid once an agreement has been reached regarding the allocation period.

Credit due remains at $4,127,916.21 with $ 1,930,001.48 ($1,881,928.27 plus 2.5% overhead) due now.

Don Taylor Rig - True-Up II Explanation:

The true-up/unwind of the Well Control Accumulator for the Don Taylor rig has been accurately calculated. The charge of $13,877.82 reflects the actual figures over a period of 474 days. This accumulator was installed to ensure compliance with BSEE regulations CFR 250.730 to 250.739, which govern well control and blowout preventer systems for oil, gas, and sulfur operations on the Outer Continental Shelf. 05.description:
The Joint Account was charged for the following invoices which appear to be coding errors:

| Vendor               |   Inv Doc # | Invoice #    |     Amount | Comments                       |
|----------------------|-------------|--------------|------------|--------------------------------|
| FMC TECHNOLOGIES INC |  5103628395 | 92528375     | 953,737.00 | XT for Europa                  |
| DNV GL USA INC       |  5103622311 | 870010123590 |   6,000.00 | for various other Shell assets |
| DANOS LLC            |  5103575990 | IN218392     |   5,681.34 | for Perdido                    |
| DANOS LLC            |  5103569497 | IN217182     |   3,039.36 | for Perdido                    |
| DANOS LLC            |  5103563629 | IN215738     |   2,854.32 | for Perdido                    |
| DANOS LLC            |  5103563631 | IN215737     |   2,854.32 | for Perdido                    |
| Total                |             |              | 974,166.34 |                                |

This was raised to the Operator in Information Request 14 issued during the fieldwork.

FMC Technologies Inv 92481956 shows that the joint account had been charged for refurbishment of XT from Glider. The Master Flo Valve Invoice #0000606127 also shows work on the same Glider XT. Thus, it appears that the refurbished XT used on Crosby is from Glider and not from Europa.

Credit due to Joint Account of $974,166.34 plus 2.5% of OH for total due of $998,520.50.

Credit denied.

The JADE lines provided by the auditor are incomplete. The standard JADE line provided by the Operator to the auditor has 42 columns. However, there are only 29 columns in the JADE provided by the auditor. The auditor had removed information from Column A to column P. When proper JADE line entries are not provided, it causes extra work and create additional burden on Operator to review the audit claim. The Operator has the right to deny the claim until the auditor can provide any missing information.

FMC Invoice No. 92528375 references Purchase Order No. 4513643912 (PO)) previously provided to the Auditor. The delivery location for this PO is Crosby-Central Receiving in Morgan City, LA. During field audit work it was explained to the Auditor regarding the Operator's practice to utilize hardware already in-progress in order to meet installation schedules. When the Crosby CA7 well was put into execution mode the Operator made the decision to allocate hardware from the Europa EA3 project which was already in-progress. The Operator can do this due to the standard nature of the hardware utilized in our portfolio. Therefore, Crosby CA7 received hardware in time to meet the installation schedule and the Crosby CA 7 hardware is charged to Europa EA3 at a later time as its schedule permits.

Please see the attached email from engineer Jared for detail.

replies.text:
In the email response provided by the Operator's employee, Mr. Jared Spritzer dated 4/8/2021, he noted that "Crosby CA7 received the following to make schedule that were funded by others...Subsea X-mas Tree, SCM, Choke, Tubing Hanger"

Conceptually the Non-Operator does not take issue with utilizing parts from other projects in the "mix and match" fashion as alluded to in Mr. Spritzer's email in order to make schedule deadlines and accelerate work activities.

The Non-Operator wants to ensure: 1. The correct price was paid for the parts, and 2. that the parts in question were in-fact installed. The pricing concern is especially important as the parts in question are rebuilt parts and will not necessarily carry a uniform price due to different levels of work required in the overhaul process which varies from part to part.

The Operator is therefore requested to:

1. Furnish evidence that the Xmas Tree in question was installed on the well (schematic/drawing with serial # reference)
2. Provide invoices for the installed Xmas Tree and other parts (which were charged to other wells) so that the NonOperator can verify the price paid for the Europa parts is the same.

In order to evidence the installation of the Xmas Tree on Crosby, the Operator provided a snippet from an excel file which shows the material number, equipment number, and serial number of the items installed. We compared this excel excerpt to the FMC invoice # 92528375 which also shows the material no. and equipment no. of the refurbished parts from Europa A6. We noted that there is a mismatch between parts no. and equipment no. between the FMC invoice vs. the excel excerpt for Material P1000077259. (line noted in green was matched to FMC invoice, while item marked with red circle shows mismatch of equipment number). Furthermore, we were unable to find the other 2 parts referenced on the FMC invoice to the excel snippet that the Operator provided. Therefore, we were unable to confirm that the items charged to Crosby per the FMC invoice were installed on the Joint Property. Please provide corroborating evidence of installation that is consistent with the information on the FMC invoice.

replies.text:
The credit claim of $998,520.50 has been denied. According to the materiality threshold for exception of less than $50K established by BP letter of June 6, 2020, it had been agreed and adopted by BP-SOI during Face-to-Face Meeting in February 2022 that small exception should not be raised. However, many small unrelated claims had been combined with the claim of FMC Technologies Inv 92481956 for the refurbishment of XT in this exception which has violated the purpose of this agreement.

For example, the claim of coding error of $6,000 from DNV GL USA Inc. had been for various assets is incorrect. DNV GL USA Inc. has been hired to perform the review of valve for regulatory compliance at $6000 per well for 14 different assets. Please see below screen shot of PO 4513427328. The item no. 80 is for well of Crosby C7. Therefore, there is no coding error.

- TH: P137806-1021 | EQ#10205884 (Recovered from Europa A6)

Based on the result of the review of the claim of coding error of $6,000 from DNV GL USA Inc. it has been determined that there was no error in the coding. Therefore, no further review will be performed for the other four invoices with small charges. They are recommended to be closed.

Regarding the claim of miscoding of $953,737 of FMC Technologies Inv 92481956 for the refurbishment of XT, it has been determined that this charge represents the first installment for a contract value at $3,368,038.00 1. There are payments made in 2021 and 2022 subsequently which would have been covered by 2023 field audit of Crosby. It is inconclusive to address this in 2021 audit. Additionally, a new serial number is assigned to refurbished equipment. It is inappropriate for the Non-Operator trying to match the serial number from the invoice of 92481956 for the equipment removed from Europa to the new serial number provided from the screen shot of the material installed provided in rebuttal 2. The equipment has been installed. Therefore, this claim is denied.

A copy of Purchase Order (PO) 4513643912 was provided to the co-owner with the initial audit response. This PO is primarily for subsea engineering services for XT, XT CAP, and Hanger Refurbishment. It includes details for items 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60. The charge of $953,737 falls under item 40, which covers XT, XT CAP, and Hanger refurbishment, totaling $2,805,108. The charge in question is the first milestone payment due upon receipt of the order. It is also included in the Shell CTR Proposal Summary attached to invoice no. 92528375.

Number: FRM-0000021201

Preparer: Tyler

Reviewer: Nirvish Urs, Justin R

Approver: Nicl

The non-operator is encouraged to review the AFE of WBS C.US.CRO. PD.19.003.1233A approved by BP and PO 4513643912. This AFE aims to develop an economically undeveloped reservoir with a slim hole sidetrack CA-7 wellbore, potentially delaying the full field abandonment of Crosby.

As explained during the audit fieldwork; to optimize resources and reduce costs, the Operator adopts the following process:

1. Farming Subsea Hardware: Hardware from wells that are no longer produced is retrieved. This includes components like chokes, valves, and other subsea equipment.
2. Refurbishment and Reinstallation: The retrieved hardware undergoes refurbishment or repair. Once refurbished, it is reinstalled on other wells that need functioning equipment

When the Crosby CA7 well was put into execution mode, the Operator decided to allocate hardware from the in-progress Europa EA3 project. This ensured that Crosby CA7 received the necessary hardware in time to meet the installation schedule. Consequently, the Crosby CA7 well is charged for the subsea engineering service charges related to the XT refurbishment from Europa A6 for Europa A3.

The project was completed in 2023. The refurbished equipment was installed in the Crosby CA7 well and assigned new serial and equipment numbers associated with Crosby CA7. The Operator has already verified and provided the table below to show that the material was installed in the Joint Property.

[table 3]

The AFE and the use of XT from the Europa A6 Refurbishment for Europa A3 to Crosby CA7 Well are for the benefit of the Crosby Joint Account. The cost of this XT refurbishment is within the approved AFE. Therefore, $953,737 was correctly charged to the Joint Account.

The charge in question was the first installment for a contract value of $3,368,038.00 1. Additional payments were made in 2021 and 2022 which would have been included in the 2023 audit of Crosby. It is inconclusive to address this in the 2021 audit. Additionally, a new serial number is assigned to refurbished equipment. It is inappropriate for the non-operator to try to match the serial number from invoice of 92481956 for the equipment removed from Europa to the new serial number provided from the screenshot of the installed material provided in rebuttal 2. The equipment has been installed. Therefore, this claim is denied.

## 2. The request for credit for coding error of $6,000 from DNV GL USA Inc. plus overhead is denied.

The evidence was previously provided in Rebuttal 3. DNV GL USA Inc. was hired to perform the review of valves for regulatory compliance at $6000 per well for 14 different Wells. Please see the screenshot of PO 4513427328 provided in Rebuttal 3 and again in this response. Line item 80 of this PO is for Crosby C7 well. Therefore, there is no coding error. Credit denied.

Steve Schatz is Logistics Coordinator 5, and 50% of his time is dedicated to supporting the Crosby operation. This is evidenced by his timesheet and allocation, which are attached to each Danos LLC invoice.

1. The detail of $70,627.39 is shown below which including $30K related to CCIM services, and the remainder balance of $40,627.39 for the 3rd party contractor and inspection services. The supports of each document have been attached for review in case these files have not been download by auditors during the field audit.

[table 1]

The CCIM is the capability center information management. The CCIM team supported the Crosby project from Q4 2019 thru Q1 2021. $3,000 a month is the standard cost IM charges for this type of project. The project services provided by the IM team on Crosby included:

- Setting up a Document Management and Document Control (DCDM) system - Assai
- Setting up a Project Team Space in Share point for information collaboration throughout the project
- Access management to the different electronic systems based on information security classifications
- Interfacing with contractors and suppliers to assure consistency in information standards used by all parties, converted to Shell standards, as required, and received and quality checked all information deliverables
- Developing Master Document Registers (MDR), Document Distribution Matrixes (DDM), and review/approval workflows to ensure all information is received and reviewed/approved by proper authorities.
- Managed the PCAP process, including building PCAP into Assai and linking to the proper documents demonstrating the Control Points
- Identified and escalated delays in the document review/approval workflows
- Developed dashboards and reports to provide insight to information status and quality
- Participated in regular reviews with project teams, and project leads, to ensure the information quality.
- Interfaced with project teams to answer questions and concerns regarding information deliverables
- Building P2A handover in Assai, mapping project deliverables to asset handover requirements, and tracking status
- Along with asset IM team, executed the P2A handover of the information deliverables

Per letter agreement between SOI and BP dated February 13, 2019, 1.Billing Disputes, d. Data Repository Systems, e. Field Computer and Communication Systems i. Scheduling and maintenance Software Systems, iii. Labor to install field communications system, these charges of CCIM services are chargeable to the Joint Account directly. Please see the attached file for the detail explanation of the 3rd party charges.

replies.text:
Credit denied. Please see the Operator's responses below:

a. Please provide 3rd party invoices related to the $30,000 in CCIM charges. Furthermore, letter agreement dated Feb. 13, 20219 only allows costs related to data repository systems and scheduling and maintenance systems if they are related to the preventative maintenance or management of the Joint Property. Please explain how CCIM supports preventative maintenance for the Joint Property.

As indicated in prior response, $3,000 a month is the standard cost IM charges for this type of project. The 3rd party invoices are attached. The IM team ensures the quality of the information that is delivered by our different equipment vendors/contracts, and ensures a complete handover of the critical documents and data to the asset, thus ensuring that operation and maintenance teams have the information they need for any maintenance activities.

b. For the items noted below, please provide job titles and job descriptions of each employee/contractor and an explanation as to how the work they performed supports compliance with CFR 250.1910 and CFR 250.1916.

In regard to $4,010.00, as stated in prior response and described in the invoice, they are for 3rd party quality inspection services, Sr. Inspector service and shop/site inspector services. $ 2,640.4 ($193+$2447.2) from SGS north America Ins was for Scholz, Herbert who is a Shop/Site inspector; $420 from QNC Inc. was for Vasquez, Douglas who is a senior Inspector; $950 from Bureau Veritas North American, Inc. was for Hebert, Lane, who is a Quality Assurance Engineer. They worked from vendor locations. They provide instructions to ensure the mechanical integrity and safe operation of equipment through inspection, testing, and quality assurance which is required by CFR 250.1916.

In regard to $9,483.49, it is from Genesis Inc. for Bing Bal who is a staff engineer/specialist of Genesis. He was to support Marine Construction/ Jumper project. He was responsible to provide technical expertise to pipeline jumpers for subsea project, manage delivery schedule and permitting of the jumpers, work scope with fabrication contractors and installation contractors, manage technical interface issues between disciplines, manage and promote safety culture and practices with contractors to ensure safe installation , and participate in peer reviews, technical challenge, HAZID and HAZOP.

In regard to $23,342.46, $639.90 was T&E cost for Bing Bal, $22,486.06 was T&E cost for Meng, Weihong, who was an offshore/flowline jumpers specialist supporting Marine construction/Jumper project in 2018. In according to Shell manager who had oversight over their service had confirmed that Meng and Bing worked almost solely offshore on projects. These travel and expense costs are correct and consistent with the GoM project scope during that time period (2018).

[table 3]

Below are the detail information regarding CFR 250.1910 and 250.1916, please review them and provide reasons why the effort from quality inspection assurance, shop/site inspectors and specialist and engineers in supporting marine construction /jumper are not meeting the compliance regulatory requirement of CFR 250.1910 and 250.1916.

CFR 250.1910 - What safety and environmental information is required?

- (a) You must require that SEMS program safety and environmental information be developed and maintained for any facility that is subject to the SEMS program.
- (b) SEMS program safety and environmental information must include:
- (1) Information that provides the basis for implementing all SEMS program elements, including the requirements of hazard analysis (§ 250.1911);
- (2) process design information including, as appropriate, a simplified process flow diagram and acceptable upper and lower limits, where applicable, for items such as temperature, pressure, flow and composition; and
- (3) mechanical design information including, as appropriate, piping and instrument diagrams; electrical area classifications; equipment arrangement drawings; design basis of the relief system; description of alarm, shutdown, and interlock systems; description of well control systems; and design basis for passive and active fire protection features and systems and emergency evacuation procedures.

CFR § 250.1916 What criteria for mechanical integrity must my SEMS program meet?

You must develop and implement written procedures that provide instructions to ensure the mechanical integrity and safe operation of equipment through inspection, testing, and quality assurance. The purpose of mechanical integrity is to ensure that equipment is fit for service . Your mechanical integrity program must encompass all equipment and systems used to prevent or mitigate uncontrolled releases of hydrocarbons, toxic substances, or other materials that may cause environmental or safety consequences. These procedures must address the following:

- (a) The design, procurement, fabrication, installation, calibration, and maintenance of your equipment and systems in accordance with the manufacturer's design and material specifications.
- (b) The training of each employee involved in maintaining your equipment and systems so that your employees can implement your mechanical integrity program.
- (c) The frequency of inspections and tests of your equipment and systems. The frequency of inspections and tests must be in accordance with BSEE regulations and meet the manufacturer's recommendations. Inspections and tests can be performed more frequently if determined to be necessary by prior operating experience.
- (d) The documentation of each inspection and test that has been performed on your equipment and systems. This documentation must identify the date of the inspection or test; include the name and position, and the signature of the person who performed the inspection or test; include the serial number or other identifier of the equipment on which the inspection or test was performed; include a description of the inspection or test performed; and the results of the inspection test.
- (e) The correction of deficiencies associated with equipment and systems that are outside the manufacturer's recommended limits. Such corrections must be made before further use of the equipment and system.
- (f) The installation of new equipment and constructing systems. The procedures must address the application for which they will be used.
- (g) The modification of existing equipment and systems. The procedures must ensure that they are modified for the application for which they will be used.
- (h) The verification that inspections and tests are being performed. The procedures must be appropriate to ensure that equipment and systems are installed consistent with design specifications and the manufacturer's instructions.
- (i) The assurance that maintenance materials, spare parts, and equipment are suitable for the applications for which they will be used.

replies.text:
The system for managing M&T rental charges was changed in 2019, from Lindros to the current PowerBI based system. The attached 2020 MT Rates file includes a prior usage report that demonstrates the day rates of 2019 for equipment prior to the transition and establishment of standard rates (per equipment type). These day rates were based on asset value and 10 years depreciation period for 'Subsea - Special' tooling that is explained in the GOM Subsea tab of the spreadsheet, along with calculations.

When transitioning to the PowerBI system the rental rates were simplified for the highest value equipment, which were grouped into the major categories we're using now and in particular resulted in the standa rd rates:

- OWIRS = $90,000/day
- THRA = $9,900/day
- IWOCS Reel = $9,000/day
- IWOCS HPU = $2,963/day

a snapshot of the 2019 (Lindros) rental rates for some of our major equipment. Using the 10yr depreciation basis it appears that day rate for OWIRS was prohibitive at $191k and was part of the rationale for reducing to $90k.

The IWOCS Reels range in calculated day rates between $6.6 - $12.6k, and the HPUs range from $2.3 - $3.4k. My crude accounting math puts the simplified rates at approximately the average for the rates that would be calculated using the previous method. From a standpoint of costs incurred by Shell (for preservation, maintenance, and storage), there is negligible difference between unique tools.

[table 1]

replies.text:
In our last rebuttal, we had noted that we were able to ascertain that the rental rates for all equipment sampled were reasonable, except for the THRA. We requested the Operator to demonstrate how the THRA day rate of $9,900 was calculated.

In its response, the Operator recommends that the historical cost of the THRA should be "updated to $3,000,000" in the calculation of the day rate in order to obtain a day rate of $9,900. However, the Operator did not provide the basis for this recommendation nor any evidence to support an amended historical cost. Please provide evidence that shows that the historical cost for the THRA should be $3,000,000.

Furthermore, in examining the screenshot of the day rate calculation provided by the Operator in its latest response, we noted that there had been a change in the calculation of maintenance costs to be included in the day rate calculation. The screenshot shows using a $401.75/day maintenance cost while the original documentation provided to us (see attached file called "Exc 12-2020 MT Rates with auditor highlights to equipment grouping", tab " GOM subsea") shows that maintenance cost included in the calculation is 29.5% per $1,000 of historical cost. It appears that there had also been a change in the day rate calculation methodology as shown on the screenshot provided above. Please explain why the maintenance cost included in the methodology has been changed in the Operator's latest response.

Thus, the auditors are still unable to ascertain whether the day rate of $9,900 for the THRA is reasonable.

Given that we have received additional documentation since the issuance of the initial audit report, we are changing thisexception from TBD to monetary. We have quantified the exception related to the outstanding issue of the day rate for theTHRA to be $673,200 plus 2.5% overhead or a total of $690,645. (please refer to file called "Exc 12 Quantification").

Please provide the above requested documentation or credit the Joint account $690,645.

replies.text:
To address the non-operator's questions regarding the acquisition cost of $3,000,000 used for THRA and the day rate of $401.75 used in the calculation of maintenance costs, please see the comments below.

As previously explained, the M&T rental charges management system was changed in 2019, transitioning from Lindros to Power BI. This change resulted in simplified rental rates for the highest value equipment, including the major categories of OWIRS, THRA, IWOCS Reel, and IWOCS HPU, leading to the standard rates.

Two files, the 2020 MT Rates file and the M&T Costs file, were provided to the non-operator in our initial response. The 2020 MT Rates file contains historical costs and the calculation of rental rates under the Lindros system. This information is provided for background purposes to the auditor, but the calculation of the rental rate under Lindros is no longer valid.

To demonstrate that the difference in rental rates between the Lindros system and Power BI is minimal, we used the estimated cost of $3,000,000 for THRA and the FMC storage cost of $108,000 per THRA annually, along with T&E per THRA of $45,833.33, as obtained from the M&T Costs file. Instead of using the 29.5% warehouse maintenance rate in the formula, the FMC storage cost is used to calculate the daily rental rate of THRA. The $401.75 is calculated as follows: ($108,000 + $45,833.33) / 365 days = $401.75 per day for maintenance costs. However, it should be noted that 180 days should be used for the calculation of the day rate since subsea equipment is not used 365 days a year and is specialized in nature.

As shown in Rebuttal 3, when the initial cost of $3,000,000 and the $401.75/day maintenance cost are used in the calculation of the rental rate of THRA, the difference is $55.75 ($9,955.75/day from Lindros vs. $9,900/day charged).

Please refer to the two files provided in the initial response for details. The request for credit is denied.

This exception was discussed during Feb 2025 Shell/bp face to face meeting. Shell has agreed to investigate and provide documentation for the cost of ownership and operation of THRA, specifically, the basis for the $3m cost used and the deviation from the 29.5% maintenance rate used to calculate the day rate for this piece of equipment.

replies.text:
As noted here and on exception 18 of the 2020 Mars audit (SOV-E101), this is a management fee which allows the Operator to call off materials as needed. This type of fee is considered overhead and should not be directly charged. Given that this is a recurring issue, the $50k threshold does not apply. Credit remains due.

Credit is denied. Per UOA, Exhibit 'C' Section II Direct Charges, 4. Material, Material purchased or furnished by Operator fo r use on the Joint Property as provided under Section IV. Only such materials shall be purchased for or transferred to the Joint Property as may be required for immediate use and is reasonably practical and consistent with efficient and economical operations. The accumulation of surplus stocks shall be avoided.

In compliance to and support this contract provision of having the material ready for immediate use and preventing the accumulation of surplus stocks, this consignment fee has the vendor to agree to invoice for the full amounts of goods/ products shipped offshore for installation/consumption. Any items not used/ consumed/installed can be returned to vendor for credit. And the Joint Account will pay for items which are used in the well only.

The consignment fee is neither a warehouse nor storage fee. We as the operator do not own any of goods/ products or inventory at the vendor's facility. The contract provision described in Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreement (UOA)stated does not apply here. The credit is denied.

replies.text: Credit denied. Wash Water Injection is a technical requirement for Rydberg and has been part of the Wells Technology Development program and activities to study, develop, prove and provide required documentation to BSEE of this new technology to be utilized in the Rydberg wells. All Rydberg co-owners are aware and the topic has been discussed at various intervals. The key activity end of 2021 and in 2022 was required testing and proving for BSEE all of the parameters of WWI, which has been part of the BSEE (federal gov’t) requirements for Rydberg leases SOP approvals with BSEE. The Wells Technology and WWI scope has been covered via the IPT expenses since inception of the project (ECP has approved AFEs for initial and all subsequent IPT scope and cost). End of 2021 and into 2022, there was additional work scope required by BSEE. Rydberg is currently finishing up the entire program and the extensive validation with BSEE. This is new technology is not in use anywhere in our GOM portfolio, it was required and developed for production at Rydberg. Attached pls find: - Rydberg Co-Owner meeting, including Ecopetrol, whereby Wash Water Injection and Wells Technology Development was last discussed in detail. These slides were shared with Cesar Palagi [cesar.palagi@ecopetrol-america.com](mailto:cesar.palagi@ecopetrol-america.com) and [Bob.Kelsey@ecopetrol-america.com](mailto:Bob.Kelsey@ecopetrol-america.com) for further cascade in the ECP organization.
