The vendor agreement provided by the Operator indicates the services being provided was for testing and upgrades to the TSAT tool which would accommodate for various size and number of wash water injection lines. The MSA makes no reference to the Rydberg Well, which indicates this project was for the benefit of all future Shell Projects. If this service was to be exclusively used for the Rydberg asset the MSA would have indicated testing and tool upgrades for the specific design requirements of the Rydberg asset. Furthermore, this service benefits the Operators Dover asset which also utilizes wash water injection and is to be tied back to Appomattox. This type of service should be allocated to any asset which may receive benefit. Therefore, credit remains due to the Joint Account for this coding error in the amount of $884,242.45.

Credit denied. As stated in the initial Operator reply, "This is new technology not in use anywhere in our GOM portfolio, it was required and developed for production at Rydberg." These costs were required to derisk/enable Rydberg, that would have otherwise not have happened. This is the new tubing design software the Operator had to create to allow for the design of the control lines. No other software exists in the industry to model control lines. This was a crucial piece of work to mitigate the large control line interaction with the tubing and the design and testing of the connectors. The contract between Shell and Blade covers several work scopes and does not identify specifically the project(s) the services are provided for. As mentioned in the initial Operator reply, “Wash Water Injection is a technical requirement for Rydberg and has been part of the Wells Technology Development program and activities to study, develop, prove and provide required documentation to BSEE of this new technology to be utilized in the Rydberg wells”. Purchase Order #4513750193 copy provided in IR #03 identifies the work done was specifically for Rydberg. The PO settles to Network 30271091 – Rydberg Washwater Injection System (WBS P.US.RTD.EP.16.008.1106D – Rydberg Well Systems) as shown in screen shot below. The billed time all reference the line-item PPB TSAT (which is the program they developed for us) in full or part. Also attached is a copy of Purchase Order #4513516752, which also identifies the work done was specifically for Rydberg. The PO also settles to Network 30271091 – Rydberg Washwater Injection System (WBS P.US.RTD.EP.16.008.1106D – Rydberg Well Systems)

01.description: The Vito Joint Account was charged $192,859.95 for allocated boat and fuel costs on the above referenced invoices. A review of the boat logs revealed the Joint Account was charged in error. The boats served the Transocean Poseidon drillship from May 7,2018 through May 16, 2018. However, Poseidon did not start operations at the Joint Property until May 24 according to the Operator's records. The boat logs did remark that Mississippi Canyon 612 (Dover) and Walker Ridge 508 (Pontus) were served, consequently any dock time should have been charged to those properties. Information Request 23 was submitted to the Operator questioning the charges. The Operator responded that the charges were correct in that the vessels were bringing out equipment prior to the well starting. The logs did note casing and barite being loaded onto the M/V HOS Crockett at Fourchon. However, the vessel also backloaded cargo when it was at Dover and Pontus. In the case of the M/V Ipanema, the logs indicate the trips to D/W Poseidon were to retrieve backloaded cargo only, which should have been charged to Dover. The Operator is requested to review this again and supply the loadout and backload cargo manifests to support the charges. Exception stands until such time. The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $200,412.83 plus 2.5% development overhead for the boat and fuel costs charged to the Joint Account in error.. Amount Claimed: $205,423.15

16.description: The Operator charged $8,760,720.09 fixed fees on invoices from Shell Eastern Petroleum Ltd (SEPL) for the period of 2021. Information Request No. 8 was submitted requesting the Operator to provide service contract, personnel names, hours worked, job titles and services performed to support the charges. The Operator provided line item details and summary to show the actual costs incurred for the personnel working at the Singapore office. There are about 25 personnel provided services supporting both the Vito and Whale projects. The total costs were allocated between the two projects based on percentage of FTE headcounts on Vito and Whale projects. No hours worked or timesheets were provided to support the allocation. 1. The auditor comparted the allocation percentage used for the Vito invoices and the SELP FTE headcounts allocation percentage and noticed the discrepancies of the allocation percentages. A recalculation based on the FTE headcounts allocation percentage shows an over-charge of $237,632.70 to Vito due to the incorrect allocation percentage used. 2. A review of the 2021 SEPL costs pool shows that the Operator includes items such as Education costs and Singapore office allocation in the cost pool. 19.description: The Vito Joint Account was charged $27,893,762.03 P&T labor recorded in account A7393160 in 2021. The affiliate labor charges were manually adjusted from the SIEP invoices to replace the original invoice rates with the escalated affiliate rate of $363 or $366 per hour. The auditor identified the following 13 personnel are not on the consolidated P&T staff listing but on the contractor listing. Their services were billed at the affiliate flat rates instead of the actual cost as listed on the affiliate invoices. The total amount charged to the Joint Account from these personnel is $2,065,072.67 for 5,655 hours. The actual costs based on the invoices is $1,141,784.00, an overcharge of $923,288.67 at the higher flats. These personnel are contractors from various vendors including GATE, Cronus Technology, Riskbytes, SGS North America and Bureau Veritas North America. The Accounting Procedure, section 5. Services, allows “the cost of contract services, equipment, and utilities used in the conduct of Joint Operations” to be a direct cost. There is no place in the Unit Operating Agreement that allows a vendor’s employee to be up charged. Invoices billed to the Operator at $220 per hour for Brett Barousse cannot be billed to the Joint Account at $363. The flat rate was intended as a way for the Operator to easily recover its employee costs without the requirement to calculate and provide support for salary, benefit, and burden. It was not intended to circumvent vendor costs being billed at the actual cost paid by the Operator. In addition, charging vendor employees through the P&T labor also creates the risk of duplicate costs as identified in AE15 by directly charging the vendor invoice and also billing that employee on the monthly P&T Labor entry. The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account a total of $941,754.44 for over charge of contractor at the affiliate flat labor. Amount Claimed: $941,754.44

0003.short_description: CBOH - Offsite Tech - SIEP Affiliate Labor
0003.description:
The Operator charged the Great White Joint Account $47,365.25 for the affiliate labor services of a Mr. Kenneth Oyler (Lead Production Technologist). The identified offsite technical labor (OTL) does not qualify for direct chargeability under the Billing Standards settlement agreements between the parties, as they have not been adequately and properly documented by the Operator as activities required to comply with regulatory activities, and they have not been identified as Planners & Schedulers, maintenance and turnaround, rig administration whose job function was previously performed offshore/onsite but were relocated onshore. In addition, the identified Affiliates did not have a job title that enabled the auditor to conclude the personnel possessed special & specific engineering, geological, geophysical or operational skills absent proper documentation being provided by the Operator to support this labor classification.

The Operator is requested to credit the Great White Joint Account $47,365.25 ($46,210.00 plus overhead of $1,155.25) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
As demonstrated during the audit fieldwork in IR-24, the charges to the Great White Joint Accounts for Kenneth William Oyler were throughout 2022 and included only two days in October (the 19th and 20th) and zero days in November. This excludes the time period of October 31 - November 11, 2022 (as noted on the POB which was already provided) when he was briefly supporting at Olympus and the Proteus rig. Kenneth is the Lead Production Technologist and the Principal Technical Expert & Wells Technical Excellence for drilling and completion fluids. Confirmed that excluding these time periods he was supporting Great White. Hence the time writing charges of Kenneth William Oyler remain valid.

No credit is due.

This table is a time-based operational log for a drilling/completion operation at a depth of **12,250 ft**, covering activities from **0:00 to 6:00 hours**. It details sequential well operations including latching a locator (LSOTJ), rigging up a flowhead and power wire frame, pressure testing surface lines to **6,000 psi**, and landing/testing a tubing hanger (TH) with seal verification up to **10,000 psia**. replies.text:
The Material - Hardware SMIS Tie-In valued at $ 344,583.77 USD was originally generated from the document number #130160408 which was transferred from GWEB TRF (NW 30302270) to GA019 Tree end to CLB (NW 30330669). Please find the snippet below.

As per the Project Engineer, this cross over adaptor was moved from GWEB to CLB for the amount paid to the manufacturer for the component. However, after the transfer was completed the concept for CLB changed and the cross over adaptor was not able to be used. The purpose of the cross over adaptor is to allow two well jumpers to connect and thereby combine flow from two production wells into a single flow stream. There's a need for this component when there is only one manifold hub available for two adjacent wells.

Another project has just recently been identified for the use of this component. The receiving project is not yet at the stage where the transfer can be completed. We will continue to monitor the new project status and complete the transfer as soon as appropriate.

No credit is due.

Per the Accounting Procedure, Exhibit C.III (Overhead) "As compensation for administrative, supervision, office services and warehousing costs, Operator shall charge the Joint Account in accordance with Section III". COPAS MFI-21 (Overhead Principles) - Section II.B - further clarifies drafting is Operations Support and considered an indirect cost covered by the overhead rates.

Additionally, timesheets for Mr. Joshua Mills indicate the West Delta (not Perdido/GW) as receiving services on invoices 20150024-718798, 20150024-721039, and 20150024-721049.

This was the subject of Great White Information Request 53, which did not receive a response during fieldwork. There was no indication that these expenses were related to a Major Construction project, nor do they appear to be in compliance with the Billing Standards Section 3A, 3B or 3C.

For direct chargeability under the Billing Standards settlement agreements between the parties, as labor costs are to be adequately and properly documented by the Operator as activities required to comply with regulatory activities, and they have not been identified as Planners & Schedulers, maintenance and turnaround, rig administration whose job function was previously performed offshore/onsite but were relocated onshore. In addition, the identified personnel did not have a job title that enabled the auditor to conclude the personnel possessed special & specific engineering, geological, geophysical or operational skills absent proper documentation being provided by the Operator to support this labor classification.

The Operator is requested to provide source documents which confirm chargeable services, in accordance with the JOA and Billing Standards or credit the Great White Joint Account $146,910.98 ($130,009.72 plus overhead of $16,901.26) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
The invoice charges for Joshua Mills against the Perdido work order # 62197919, for the three invoices noted by the Auditor, were correctly charged to the Joint Accounts as confirmed through the Deployment Lead. Joshua also confirmed that when working on this project he correctly updated the work order but missed updating the reference from "West Delta" on the time sheet to "Perdido".

In addition, Joshua Mills was working offshore on Perdido for the laser scanning/survey of the Perdido BGC Deck compressors, then working with the ART team to utilize the new scan data and our PDMS model and load into Orbit. This regulatory work and the remaining invoices are direct billable as per the Settlement Agreement Billing Standards section 3.A Regulatory Activity - CFR §250.1916.

No credit is due.

table_references.summary: This table categorizes examples of computer applications used in two broad areas: **Field Operations** (direct charge) and **Administrative** (overhead). Field operations applications focus on hands-on operational tasks such as cathodic protection surveillance, meter calibration, production monitoring, well testing, and safety analysis. Administrative applications cover back-office functions including payroll, invoice processing, financial analysis, regulatory reporting, reservoir analysis, and personnel management.

replies.text:
As noted by the Auditor, the Operators response to IR # 51 but in full, was as follows " As per the RTOC Team Leader, the TDE ProNova system feeds information for operations, covering Drilling, Completion, and Well Intervention activities to the RTOC (real time operations centres) so that the Houston based RTOC receives real-time data from the rig, therefore these line items are direct chargeable."

As noted above, since the TDE ProNova system feeds real-time data from the rig to the RTOC from their performance analysis software and support, these charges are direct chargeable per the Settlement Agreement Billing Standards section 3.6.1 Scheduling & Maintenance Software Systems as management of the joint property under COPAS MFI #44 Field Computer and Communications Systems.

No credit is due.

0056.description:
The Great White Joint Account was charged $3,098,856.19 on multiple AFE's related the replacement of ESP (Electric Subsea Pump) which was billed at the Operating Overhead rate of 13.0% in lieu of the appropriate $595,910.05 Development Overhead rate of 2.5% as the AFE's indicate the replacements are not similar, but rather an upgrade with increased performance and output than what was originally installed.

Per the operating agreement Section III (Overhead), 2 (Application of Overhead- Percentage basis), a.5

- a. Development shall include all costs in connection with:
1. drilling, redrilling, plugging back or deepening of any or all wells
2. workover operations requiring a period of fifteen(15) consecutive work days or more on a well,
3. preliminary expenditures necessary in preparation for drilling,
4. expenditures incurred in abandoning when the well is not completed as a producer,
5. original construction or installation of fixed assets, expansion of fixed assets and any other project clearly discernible as a fixed asset, except Major Construction as defined in Paragraph 3 of Section Ill

The Operator is requested to credit the Great White Joint Account $2,502,946.14 with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
As per our regulatory SME (subject matter expert), ESP's are not classified as a well, as they have no API assigned to them. They are classified as production equipment thus are subject to the agreed upon appropriate Operating overhead rate. The replacement/maintenance of the ESP since inception (post first capitalization of first replacement) has always been billed as an operating expense and not an 'upgrade'. In addition, there is only one type of ESP on the market.

The section of the Operating Agreement Section III (Overhead), 2 (Application of Overhead - Percentage basis) quoted by the Auditor, is related to wells and is not applicable to an ESP (as noted above).

As per the Senior Finance Advisor, ESP installations are considered as Facility Maintenance activities as the ESPs have required changeouts every 1-3 years since Perdido startup. The only change was in Shell's internal accounting treatment in complying with IFRS16 lease interpretations that they are to be treated as a Right of Use Asset which sits on the balance sheet therefore requiring us to capitalize internally. There has been no change to overhead application or proposal through the COUA as a maintenance activity. This is the same consistent message that has been conveyed to Chevron Finance. If the Auditor requires further clarification, it may be best placed to seek resolution through the Finance and Commercial teams.

No credit is due.

A review of the marine voyage report and the boat logs showed approximately 13% of the allocation to the above WBS belongs to the Salsa asset. replies.text:
As per the Supply Chain Specialist, the travel time and dock time are not split evenly, as seems to be part of the Auditors calculations. Any standby time between voyages is considered VES (Pooled Time) and is charged to the Shell Stand by Code. The attached spreadsheet shows the appropriate split from the Final Cost Allocation XRPT. In addition, there is a further split provided by the rig for the Perdido amount of $187,765.36 for the percent of the voyage paid by Drilling (84%) and the percent of the voyage paid by Production (16%).

The total hours charged of the Harvey Liberty vessel was 206.75hrs for voyage 20211330, out of which 176.56hrs were charged to Perdido, 8.19hrs were charged to Salsa and 22.00hrs to the Shell stand by code (Pooled Time). Based on the voyage report, Salsa is only responsible for 4.43% of the 184.75hrs of the VES (Working Time).

No credit is due.

0065.description:
The Operator charged WBS P.US.GWH.WS.21.002.7241A (GA17 Coil Tubing-Xylene Stimulation-PLT-) $124,051.00 for Advanced Tool and Supply invoices 6674 and 6675. A review of the invoices showed they were for engineering & drawing services related to various equipment designs. The Accounting Procedure attached to the Unit Operating Agreement dated October 1, 2007 only allows charges for technical labor directly employed on or in the operation of the Joint Property. COPAS MFI-21 (Overhead Principles - Section II.B - also states that design and drafting is a function of Operations Support that are indirect costs covered by overhead. Additionally, the Billing Standards agreement between Chevron and Shell, effective January 1, 2019, does not allow for design and drafting costs to be directly billed.

The Operator is requested to credit the Great White Joint Account $127,152.28 ($124,051.00 plus overhead of $3,101.28) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
As per the Staff Wells Engineer, the Auditors comments that the invoices are for design and drafting is incorrect. The drawing numbers are references to the specific clamps that were designed and manufactured for sea fastening of the coiled tubing reel and tank (there were multiple types of clamps designed, which is why the drawing numbers are referenced to differentiate them). Additionally, there was analysis of the rig up conducted to ensure the weight of the equipment was spread properly to not overload the platform structure and not shift in the event of a storm.

No credit is due.

table_references.summary: This table tracks the operational history of drilling rig **H&P 205**, listing activities performed at various wells in the **Great White and Perdido fields** (AC 0857 OCS-G 17565) from late 2021 through early 2023. Events include drilling, well interventions, workovers, completions, abandonments, and idle/maintenance periods, with the rig spending notable time on the **GREAT WHITE GA-021** well (max drill depth of 21,925 units, up to ~200.9 days on location). The rig also experienced several significant idle and maintenance periods, including one lasting **113 days** (November 2021 – February 2022).

replies.text:
The 5 Year Rig Maintenance WBS was charged from H&P invoices for three separate periods of time when H&P 205 was idle:

* November 20, 2021 to February 25, 2022 - 98 consecutive days - warm stack rate
* May 8 to May 17, 2022 - 12 days - operating rate
* June 15 to 21, 2022 - 7 days - operating rate

The warm stack rate can only be used during consecutive days or uninterrupted days as noted above. Between February 25 and May 8, 2022 the rig was used to complete Perdido caissons. And between May 17 and June 15th, 2022 the rig was used for Great White intervention work at GA005 and GA017 (as noted in the rig schedule). The number of consecutive days will drive the use of the warm stack rate even if scope external to the 98 consecutive days was considered within the 5 year rig maintenance scope. Since these three periods of time are not consecutive the H&P invoices noted by the Auditor are correctly using the operating rate.

No credit is due.

0068.description:
The Operator charged WBS C.US.XOF.XG.21.006.0942A (GD-08 IEW) for the Transocean Pontus Unwind allocation for October 9-22, 2022. A review of the allocation showed the unwind costs were allocated based on a five (5) year contract from October 22, 2017, through October 22, 2022. The attached Transocean Fleet Report dated October 26, 2017, states the drill ships contracted with Shell were for a 10-year period.

Given the drill ships are not stationary or the 10-year drilling plans for one field, the Operator's decision to allocate the unwind costs to only the first five (5) years, put an undue burden on those wells drilled during the first half of the drilling programs. Additionally, it must be pointed out that had the Operator provided the full drilling contract, as requested during previous audits, this information would have been known to the Non-Operator parties at an earlier date. However, COPAS MFI-56 (Rig Related Costs) - Section XIX Adjustments - provides several options for adjusting the Joint Account allocations, with the fourth is the most equitable option for this scenario: 'Adjust all the charges from inception of the Rig Contract. If this includes periods outside the period allowed for adjustments under the terms of the accounting procedure, the Company should get approval of the Non-Operators to make the adjustments - unless the rate adjustment is the result of offsetting entries from another outside audit.'

For the audit period, the GD-08 is due a credit of $370,825.98 ($361,781.45 plus overhead of $9,044.54) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing. The exception will also remain open for a to be determined (TBD) amount awaiting the correction of the unwind allocations for all the Transocean drill ships.

The Operator's May 25, 2023, response stated the POB report and/or Helicopter Reservation Cost Code spreadsheet provided could be used to obtain the information needed. As previously stated, neither the POB report or Helicopter Reservation Cost Code spreadsheet provides rig crew titles or hours worked per shift. The attached example from a previous audit shows the Contractor uses IADC tour reports and has the relevant support needed for their additional crew charges.

The Operator is requested to provide the documentation to support the open request. Partners reserve the right to issue additional exceptions, if warranted, after reviewing the Operator's response.

replies.text:
The TOUR or IADC reports are not available and therefore not able to be shared with the Auditors. Chevron, as an Operator, also does not provide these reports during audits. As more Operators follow this practice (Chevron and Shell) there should not be an expectation that they will always be available.

In reviewing the amounts from the list of invoices submitted by the Auditor, there are three categories: additional labor; crew shortages; and 3rd party. The majority of the charges already had the name, titles and hours included in the invoice support (green highlighted amounts in the attached chart). In verifying the remaining lines (orange highlight), the applicable contract alteration contains the details for crew of the warm stack rate or operating rate.

No credit is due.

Great White Information Request 50 was submitted to the Operator inquiring as to why work continued into 2022, when AFE C.US.GWH.PD.09.008.1230 and its supplemental AFE was documented to be completed by end of 2012. No response was received before the close of the audit.

Pursuant to Article 6.2 Authorization for Expenditure, the identified costs are not chargeable as no support has been provided by the Operator to show a formal/informal communication to the partners for their approval of the current expenditures beyond the 2 years of the AFE end of life date.

The Operator is requested to provide supporting documentation or credit the Great White Joint Account $2,620,484.60 ($2,569,102.55 plus overhead of $51,382.05) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
As per the GOM Project Finance Advisor, the charges noted by the Auditor for 2022 relate to SURF installation for the GA018 opportunity, explicitly included in Phase 1, Stage 2 AFE scope with an estimated completion date of December 31, 2012 (the Operator was unable to locate any reference to an AFE end of life date). Within the AFE it was noted as installation of the remaining Stage 2 subsea tree systems (including well jumper fabrication and install) on the remaining wells, which included GA018. Therefore, the charges for the SURF installation were applied to these WBS's.

Please reach out to the Chevron Finance and Commerical representatives to understand the scope of work and the timeline of such work, as communications between Shell and Chevron would have been on-going.

No credit is due.

0083.description:
The Operator charged $2,711,717.54 to WBS C.US.GWH.PD.21.023.0941A (Spar Rig Mud Pumps Upgrade) for various Helmerich & Payne invoices. An additional $53,566.76 related to the mud pump upgrade were also identified as erroneously billed by Helmerich & Payne, for a total of $2,765,284.30 for the project.

The 'Alteration to Contract' #15 attached to Helmerich & Payne invoice 2022004626 showed the total install cost was not to exceed $2.5MM. Great White Information Request 39 was submitted to the Operator requesting an amendment to the contract between Shell and Helmerich & Payne for the additional $265,284.30 over the contract price. The information request remained open at the end of fieldwork.

The Operator is requested to provide supporting documentation or credit the Great White Joint Account $271,916.41 ($265,284.30 plus overhead of $6,632.11) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
The Alteration to Contract # 15 referenced by the Auditor includes the following wording:

" 2. H&P agrees to furnish the EQUIPMENT for US$1,200,000.00, plus all costs associated with transportation to and installation for a total install cost not to exceed $2,500,000.00 without prior written approval of the EQUIPMENT on H&P 205..."

Along with supporting invoice backup are written approvals for various costs. In addition, the same Alteration goes on to note the following:

" 3. In addition to providing the EQUIPMENT as described in sections 1 and 2 above, the PARTIES acknowledge that SHELL intends to utilize H&P personnel to assist SHELL in integrating some modifications to fit planned upgrades on SHELL's platform, including, without limitation, unitization on skids and developing logistics for the delivering and installation on the platform (collectively the "ADDITIONAL SERVICES")... "

As there are additional costs as described above, the amount charged by H&P would then potentially be above the amount referenced in section 2.

In addition, there was a Side Letter Agreement with accompanying AFE for this project, which was signed by both co-owners. It noted that the H&P Rig Mud Pump Upgrades included a percentage for estimated cost overage. Therefore, the costs on the Mud Pump WBS, noted by the Auditor, are direct billable to the Joint Account.

No credit is due.

0086.short_description: COUA - Project/OPEX Matrix - CBOH - Offsite Tech - CATS Labor
0086.description:
The Operator charged the Great White Joint Account $106,833.30 for CATS Payroll costs which appear to be coding errors. Upon review of Heli Logs and POBs, the employees were working at other locations.

This was the subject of Perdido Information Request 12, which the Operator responded, "The majority of the charges in this IR, show the Perdido CATS time-writing was at a different period of time as to when the employees traveled to other assets. Their time-writing was for regulatory work as shown by the CFR codes noted in column K or planners and schedulers. As per the Settlement Agreements, signed in 2021 and 2022 between Shell and Chevron / BP, and their applicable Exhibit for Agreed OTL Definition and Billing Standards, sections 3.A and 3.C show that both of these categories are direct chargeable. Thanks."

Upon review of the response spreadsheet provided by the Operator, there was no substantiation that the particular time charged was for the Joint Account and not for other properties as noted in the workpapers provided. According to the agreements regulatory work will be charged to the joint account provided such charges are pursuant to an approved AFE which the regulatory activities must be adequately and properly documented by the Operator, identifying the specific activity of the individuals and will reference specific program elements as described in the Federal Register. None of the AFE's being charged in this exception reflect this regulatory designation prescribed by the settlement agreement. In addition, no additional support was provided to reflect that the work being performed by the personnel identified as Planners & Schedulers as part of this exception was performing a function that was previously performed offshore.

The Operator is requested to credit the Great White Joint Account $106,833.30 ($95,247.25 plus overhead of $11,586.05) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
As was noted in the Audit Report regarding the employees working at other locations, the support doesn't seem to be attached to verify this comment for the time period it was charged to the Joint Account. However, according to the Settlement Agreement Billing Standards, and Exhibit C II of the Unit Operating Agreement the attached personnel are direct billable. The Operators response remains the same as was provided during the audit field work.

No credit is due.

0089.description: The Operator charged the Great White Joint Account $1,518,606.95 for SRA/PSP bonuses. This was the subject of Perdido Information Request 5 which was issued during the fieldwork. The Operator responded to the IR by providing a list of personnel who were charged, but no values associated with the personnel nor indication of which award was received (SRA/PSP/both). Personnel who were issued bonuses are either not chargeable to the Joint Account under the terms of the Settlement Agreement, did not work for the Joint Account, or were members of SIEP which charges an ALL-INCLUSIVE rate (see snip below from Perdido COUA Statement of Clarification and Intent).

replies.text:
## PRIVATE and CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION ATTACHED

The Auditor noted that there was no indication of which award was received for the individuals named. However, this was noted in the file and provided by the color coding on the pivot tab. SRA awards were noted in orange and blue, and PSP awards were noted in green and grey.

As noted during and after this audit, all 2022 amounts that recorded to the following feasex WBS's have been reversed. If the Auditor were to request a credit, this would mean the Joint Accounts would be credited twice. No further action is required.

## P.US.GWH.EP.19.005.1106A / P.US.GWH.EP.19.007.1106A / P.US.GWH.EP.19.008.1106A

The amounts received are not incentive and the rate and section of the agreement noted by the Auditor are not inclusive of recognition awards. These are service awards that everyone received or could receive, therefore the agreement section noted is not applicable.

There were two documents posting the SRA awards and there are no name duplications between the two lists. There are three documents posting the PSP awards and there may be duplication of names as there is the possibility the same person could get this award multiple years.

Please see attached for the PSP amounts per individual. As previously noted, the Operator cannot provide the amount per individual for SRA awards as this would breach the company and individuals privacy and confidentiality restrictions.

Since Joint Venture Audit is not the team to process these entries, we are waiting to receive further supporting documentation from the posting analyst.

No credit is due.

0006.short_description: COUA - Project - CBOH - Offsite Tech - HAZOP Actions Engineer Study (2020-2022)
0006.description:
On December 1 & 21, 2020, Chevron responded to the Operator that the costs associated with Perdido HAZOP Actions Engineer Study, while related to HAZOP, was for engineering and project management costs covered by overhead. Per the Perdido COUA referenced in the letter, overhead will cover any professional or contract services provided by technical personnel that are offsite. It remains Chevron's position that Shell cannot charge out any of these engineering and project management costs described in the AFE.

The AFE provided did not conform to the requirements described in the letter agreement dated October 13, 2021, that commenced for charges beginning January 1, 2019. In this agreement it states the following as it relates to OTL-Chargeable Activities (Attachment I, paragraph 3.A Regulatory Activity) "...OTL charges related to the above regulatory activities must be adequately and properly documented by the Operator, identifying the specific activity of the individual(s), and will reference specific program elements as described in the Federal Register. Following execution of this Settlement Agreement, this will be noted separately in the AFE document..."

The attached AFE is lacking documentation to the specific program elements as described in the Federal Register that the AFE is intending to remediate.

The Operator is requested to credit the Great White Joint Account $170,514.24 ($150,897.55 plus overhead of $19,616.69) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
The AFE sent in December 2020 was an 'information only AFE' as it was under the $300,000 threshold as noted in the Perdido COUA, Article 6, section 6.2 AFEs, '… the Operator will not make any single expenditure or undertake any activity or operation costing three Hundred Thousand Dollars ($300,000.00) or more, unless an AFE has been included in a proposal for an activity or operation … '. This Information Only AFE was total gross amount of $232,500 for the estimated costs associated with the Perdido HAZOP Actions Engineer Study and the Operator was furnishing written information describing the expenditure to each of the Participating Parties.

The AFE was provided in December of 2020 which was before the signing of the Settlement Agreements noted by the Auditor. The quote from the Settlement Agreement provided by the Auditor was not the full paragraph which is included here for ease of reference. ' OTL charges related to the above regulatory activities must be adequately and properly documented by the Operator, identifying the specific activity of the individual(s), and will reference specific program elements as described in the Federal Register. Following execution of this Settlement Agreement, this will be noted separately in the AFE document where applicable . '

The work performed by Keystone Engineering Inc was done to comply with HSSE control framework and OSHA 1910 regulatory requirements to address assigned HAZOP action items under CFR 250.1910 which is direct billable as per the Settlement Agreement Billing Standards, Exhibit C, 3.A Regulatory Activity.

No credit is due.

0011.description:
For each month of 2022, the Operator has manually transferred through a journal entry $2,100,000 at Mars, and $1,700,000 at Olympus as noted in the provided JADE lines. These journal entries transfer cost from Capex to Opex thereby capturing the additional 10.5% overhead differential. The Joint Account receives no benefit for this Overhead increase. Further, the boat captains are already correctly coding their time directly to the Capex and Opex projects served. The total amount transferred is $3,800,000, creating an overhead increase of $399,000.

The Operator was asked to explain the basis for this charge during 2021 in which they replied it was due to a " Concurrent Operating Agreement" which has never been signed, or agreed by BP.

The Non-Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $399,000 for these non-contractual overhead charges to which it did not agree or consent.

Credit Denied.

When a vessel travels to Joint Properties, besides carrying fuel, tool, equipment, and material for a project, it also carries supplies for the normal operation of the Joint properties as well. To simplify the vessel's billing, all the cost of the vessel including the marine logistic service and rig fuel for the normal operation are billed 100% to drilling project served.

In order to reflect the marine cost of drilling projects correctly, the Mars Concurrent Operation Cost Allocation Matrix established the reclassification of $175,000 from drilling project to production operation expense every month.

The purpose of this marine charge reclassification is to reflect cost properly between Drilling projects and normal production operation. No credit is due to the Joint Account.

replies.text:
Credit Denied.

Clarksons was the ship broker for the tender and flotel charter of the Harvey Subsea. The cost of this service is usually included in the Harvey Gulf vessel's day rate. However, Harvey Gulf had a disagreement with Clarksons midway through the tender, and all parties agreed to invoice this cost separately to the Operator.

According to Section 3 Billing Disputes Paragraph l of the BP-SOI Settlement Agreement dated December 2018, ancillary costs related to third-party project management that are charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services by such t hird party associated with a third party's provision of goods and services may be charged to the Joint Account as a component cost of the underlying goods and services. Clarksons' fee is a component cost of the underlying goods and services, and it do es not qualify as administrative costs covered under Overhead. OTL is chargeable to the Joint Account for planners, schedulers, and plan execution supporters working on facility maintenance, well maintenance, and turnaround activities.

0013.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $268,175.50 on various Tenaris invoices for Pipe Management Fees charges. This is a warehousing cost and is not a direct cost of the material; rather an additional fee to warehouse the material and ensure it is available when needed, similar to a vendor stocking program.

According to the Mars UOA Section IV. 1. the Operator shall charge the Joint Account as follows: "Material purchased shall be charged at the price paid by Operator [...]" The Pipe Management Fee is an additional cost beyond the cost of the material; it is not a cost of the pipe itself as noted in the aforementioned JOA section.

The Operator is requested to credit the joint account for $268,175.50 plus overhead of 2.5% for the fees which are covered by the Overhead rate.

Tenaris provides pipe management services, which include in-yard movement, inspection, tally, and preparation of pipes for running. They also provide technical services to reduce operational risk and optimize running times by ensuring the right practices are followed and products are installed at the rig site. The cost of the pipe management services is not an additional fee to warehouse the material.

According to Section 3 Billing Disputes Paragraph l of the BP-SOI Settlement Agreement dated December 2018, ancillary costs related to third-party project management that are charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services by such third party associated with a third party's provision of goods and services may be charged to the Joint Account as a component cost of the underlying goods and services. 0019.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $570,960.72 on various Sumitomo Corporation Of Americas invoices for SCM Fee Consignment charges. This is a warehousing fee and is not a direct cost of the material but an additional fee to house the material and ensure it is available when needed.

Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreement states: "As compensation for administrative, supervision, office services and warehousing costs, Operator shall charge the Joint Account in accordance with this Section III.'

Additionally, AG 19, Section IV.3.C states 'Actual costs may include costs of (I) Material, (2) making it suitable for use, and (3) transportation from the point of acquisition to the Joint Property including loading and unloading. Not included are storage or carrying costs." This was the subject of Information Request 034 which was raised during the audit field work.

The Operator is requested to reimburse joint account for $570,960.72 plus overhead of 2.5%.

replies.text:
Credit Denied. The Operator does not own any goods/ products or inventory at vendor's facility. Therefore, the contract provision described in Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreement (UOA) stated is for warehousing cost incurred for warehouse owned and operated by the Operator is not applicable to apply here.

The Sumitomo Corporation of Americas has been contracted to provide OCTG, Casing, tubing, well & Accessories for drilling and completion projects of KE Well KE002, Mars A24, MA04 ST1, MB-09 Yellow Smart, Olympus MB-20, MB10 Green Bice Well and Olympus MB10 Workover. The vendor ensures the material is ready for immediate use and prevent the accumulation of surplus stocks. The vendor invoices for goods/ products when the material is shipped offshore for installation or consumption and return and credit to the Joint Operation for any items not used/ consumed/installed.

This Sumitomo SCM fee is the Ancillary costs related to Sumitomo project management that is charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services.

According to BP-SOI February 2019 letter agreement, Attachment I, Section 3 Billing Disputes Paragraph l. Third-Party Project Management - Ancillary costs related to third party project management that are charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services by such third party associated with a third party's provision of goods and services may be charged to the Joint Account as a component cost of the underlying goods and services and shall not be qualified as OTL or as administrative costs covered under Overhead. Sumitomo SCM fee is a component cost of the underlying goods and services, and it does not qualify as OTL or administrative costs covered under Overhead.

replies.text:
Credit Denied.

Turnarounds are considered maintenance activities. Since this is a maintenance activity Operator applies the 13% Production Overhead rate as does the Non-Operator at the Nakika turnaround projects. The Operator utilizes the SAP amortization functionality to amortize turnaround expense during the years until the next turnaround event. In order to use this SAP functionality a "C" WBS is assigned to the turnaround projects. No credit is due to the Joint Account.

The Operator has not refuted the fact that the AFE says this is a C\_Capital project in the "C or P" field on the AFE header. The Non-Operator has approved the AFE on the basis of this being a Capital project, as stated on the AFE which would carry a 2.5% OH burden. The Non-Operator has not approved this AFE on the basis of this being an Opex/Expense project carrying the higher OH burden, and the Operator has never informed the Non-Operator to the contrary. If the Operator's AFE is mis-stating the overhead classification of this project, it should be revised and resubmitted to the Non-Operator to reflect the correct OH rate that the Non-Operator can expect.
Credit denied. The overhead rate is based on the nature and scope of the work performed, rather than on internal accounting treatment.

The Operator charged the Joint Account $928,805.72 for the following AFEs:

C.US.MR2.FI.22.004.1230A - Compr Flare/Vent 3Way Valve Replacement

C.US.MR2.FI.22.001.1230A - Olympus IAC Overhaul/Replacement Facilit

C.US.MR2.FI.21.004.1230A - Olympus Hot Water Heater Replacement

These maintenance costs are non routine in nature an consist of maintenance and integrity related items.

According to the PowerNap PHA section 5.1.2, these costs should be allocated to the Powernap Operator based on production:

replies.text:
Credit Denied.

The interpretation of section 5.1.2 of the Powernap PHA pertains to maintenance related activities aimed at keeping an asset functioning as intended. However, there is a distinction for the items listed below: while these activities qualify as non-routine or infrequent, they involve full replacements and enhancements. The Operator follows internal accounting guidelines and policies to classify costs, reviewing expenditures on assets after they have been placed in service. After an asset is in service the following guidelines apply:

·Costs included into the category of costs subject to section 5.1.2 are costs which are incurred to maintain the asset

- ·Costs incurred to provide a functional enhancement of an asset are considered facility improvement and are capitalized. These items improve the asset when compared to its original specifications.

o Criteria to determine whether a cost is an improvement to an asset include:

§Increase in operational performance

§Expenditures incurred to meet changed governmental or Shell requirements (excludes new requirements that are covered under 5.10)

§Decreases operating costs beyond a threshold

§Changes in the nature of use of the asset from its original use

§Where the primary intention of the expenditure is to significantly improve performance

·Section 5.10 only covers capital expenditures to remain compliant with future industry standards or government regulations Accordingly, the charges of $928,805.72 in question of three AFEs have been applied correctly and no credit is due to the Joint Account. Please see explanation shown below for details.

C.US.MR2.FI.22.004 Compressor 3-way valve replacement & supplement

Classification reason: Upon investigation and learning from an incident on another Shell operated asset, the 3-way valve replacement meets the criteria as a new operator standard. This is a safety enhancement and qualifies as a capitalized field improvement.

C.US.MR2.FI.22.001 Olympus IAC Overhaul/Replacement

Classification reason: this IAC overhaul/replacement changed the metallurgy, upgrading the structural frame metallurgy from carbon steel to stainless steel. This qualifies as a capitalized field improvement.

C.US.MR2.FI.21.004 Olympus Hot Water Heater Replacements Supplement

Classification reason: The hot water tank was leaking frequently and posed a safety risk as well as a possible deferment risk due to the potential to demobilize the crew if hot water tanks failed. This was a full replacement and upgrade to the hot water system and qualifies as a capitalized field improvement.

The Operator's statement that "Each AFE is a full replacement and enhancement, meeting the criteria for capitalized facility improvements." is irrelevant to the discussion.

The AFE's in question meet the financial threshold (500k+).

The AFE's in question are integrity related as the safe and compliant operation of the Joint Account assets would be compromised if the work in question was not performed.

As the AFEs meet the two pronged test per the PowerNap PHA section 5.1.2. the Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account as originally requested.

According to the WD 143 CIO Agreement, section 12.1 these facilities meet the definition of "Common Facilities" and therefore the costs for same should be shared among the parties utilizing space on WD143 in accordance with Exhibit "E" of the CIO.

Both AFEs are upgrades; therefore, control systems do not apply in this case. The AFE communication with the Non-Operator provided by the Commercial Team included the following explanations:

C.US.WD3.FI.21.002.1230A - Air Compressor Upgrade:

'This project will upgrade to slightly larger HP units which will come with an upgraded onboard control system to increase the reliability and to prevent potential downtime in the future. Under Article 2.5 of the CIO, modifications (upgrades) to the Common Facilities, such as this project, are to be funded by the Platform Owners and accordingly, the costs of this AFE will be allocated in that manner.'

## C.US.WD3.FI.21.003.1230A - Control System Upgrade:

'This project is not a like in kind replacement, instead we are upgrading the network communication system from coax to ethernet. Under Article 2.5 of the CIO, modifications (upgrades) to the Common Facilities, such as this project, are to be funded by the Platform Owners and accordingly, the costs of this AFE will be allocated in that manner.'

The Operator allocated $77,941.92 to the Joint Account through the attached allocating JADE lines.

Upon review the individuals were not located onsite.

In Information Request 18, the Operator was requested to provide a description of work performed by the individuals for the Joint Account and compliance with the Settlement Agreement, if any. On 10th July, the Operator responded as follows:

replies.text:
Refer to the attached file for Operator's response.

Suresh

The File provided by the Operator contained the following descriptions;

mycm The above nature of work is for asset optimization purposes, which is not in conformance with the February 2019 Letter Agreement, section 3.1., 3.2., or 3.3.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $77,941.92 plus 13% OH for these non chargeable OTL costs for a total credit due of $88,074.37.

mycm

Credit Denied.

The Non-Operator acknowledged the nature of work described is for asset optimization, which is in accordance with BSEE Subpart K, $250.1165 What must I do for enhanced recovery operations? It is in conformance with the February 2019 Letter Agreement, section 3.1. Regulatory Activities. Therefore, no credit is due to the Joint Account.

The Operator has misapplied the CFR statues. The CFR section cited (30 CFR 250.1165) contemplates enhanced recovery in terms of secondary and tertiary recovery. The work in question is not related to secondary recovery (gas injection/waterflood) or tertiary recovery (chemical flood). As the work in question does not meet BSEE requirements it is not chargeable per the February 2019 Letter Agreement and full credit remains due.

The Auditor asserts that the Operator 'misapplied the CFR statutes' by citing 30 CFR §250.1165 and concludes the work is not chargeable, yet provides no BSEE guidance, interpretive support, or technical rationale to substantiate this position. Under the February 2019 Letter Agreement, Attachment 1, Section 3, OTL is chargeable when incurred to comply with applicable BSEE regulations, including CFR obligations such as §250.1165. Therefore, the Operator disagrees with the assertion that the CFR was misapplied and maintains that no credit is due.

replies.text:
As stated previously, and not refuted by the Operator, asset optimization is not Enhanced Recovery Operations.

The below definition is used in 30 CFR 250.1165 (taken from 30 CFR 250.105) available in any law library:

## Enhanced recovery operations

nhs ry 'r rer re y rers sodro er e sry rer eciar recovery operations that alter the natural forces in a reservoir to increase the ultimate recovery of oil or gas.

Wax modelling is not an operation that alters the natural forces of the reservoir. It is only modeling and not an "operation".

Pipeline assurance (SPAIRS) does not alter the natural forces in the reservoir increasing ultimate recovery of oil or gas.

Process control support does not alter the natural forces of a reservoir and increase the ultimate recovery of oil or gas.

For the reasons listed above, the OTL contemplated herin is not in support of 30 CFR 250.1165 as it does not meet the definition of Enhanced Recovery Operations as defined in statute. Therefore the Operator is mis-applying the statue and should credit the Joint Account as originally requested.

Per the Operator's statement in the last reply, it has indicated that it is unable to account for Joint Account materials as they are not tracked in VPS or by the Wells team. Per MFI-38, the Operator is required to properly account for all Joint Account materials, regardless of whether they are considered controllable or non-controllable.

Appendix C lists materials classified as controllable. The materials listed are those materials that COPAS has classified as controllable as of the date of this publication. The classification of material as non-controllable does not, however, eliminate the operator's responsibility for properly accounting for material purchases, transfers and dispositions. Pursuant to the review of the Operator's rig fuel usage reports used for calculating the average price per gallon to be charged for boat and rig fuel for the applicable months, it was determined these Shell Trading invoices were not included in the diesel inventory amounts.

Also, there is the consideration that because diesel was inventory understated, the Operator may have over purchased diesel needed during 2022.

Finally, by the Operator not including these Shell Trading invoices in the diesel inventory, the Mars and Joint Account will never receive proper true-up and could ultimately be overcharged and never receive credit if credit is due. The Operator is requested to revise the fuel usagne and inventory calculations and include all of these Shell Trading invoices in those inventory totals and calculations. 0037.short_description: Shell Trading Diesel Invoices Priced With Markup Over Market
0037.description:
Various Shell Trading invoices charged the Mars and Olympus Joint Accounts for diesel using a market index price plus a mark-up rate of .15 per gallon.

Pursuant to COPAS MFI #18, an Operator may have Related Entities from which they purchase materials such as ... fuel , at prices which are higher than those paid by the Related Entity. The purpose of Labor, Materials and 'Equipment and facilities" provisions in the COPAS Accounting Procedure forms is to assure the Operator's employees, material purchased from outside sources and any equipment of facilities which are owned by the Operator and serve the Joint Property are charged to the Joint Account at actual cost, without mark-up .

The Related Entity must either historically or currently have conducted a substantial amount of its business with companies other than the Operator or other Related Entities. Therefore, unless the Related Entity is able to comply with the criteria of this preceding sentence, the material purchased for use on the Joint Property from the Related Entity shall be charged to the Joint Account at the price paid by the Related Entity to an independent third party.

Goods and services provided by the Related Entity should be priced on terms that do not exceed the lesser of (1) those offered by the Related Entity to its most favored customers or (2) those offered to or obtained by the Operator from unrelated entities providing such services or products in the geographical area.

Credit is requested for $431,442.34 (the $.15 cent per gallon mark-up charged by Shell Trading for diesel transfers to Mars and Olympus totaling $420,919.36 plus 2.5% overhead of $10,522.98). Note: If this mark-up was reversed, the Operator is requested to provide the specific transactions showing the reversal.

mycm

replies.text:
Credit Denied.

The price from Shell Trading quoted by the Non-Operator was not used as a basis to apply charges for diesel fuel consumed by the Joint Account.

As mentioned during the field audit for IR #27 and #97, when fuel is pumped into the rig from a vessel, the cost of the fuel will be charged to the project which is associated to the rig then. However, when the rig completes its activities with the project, Well Finance team will process a true up posting to the project. In the true up process, the team analyzes what is the total value of fuel consumed by the rig during the activity based on Rig fuel usage report produced by the rig cost desk with the cost charged to the Joint Account. If the cost charged to the Joint Account is higher, excess charge will be credited to the Joint Account and vice versa.

Therefore, after the true up posted for the WB05 Drilling project , 1,287,900 gallons of diesel consumed was charged at $2.81 per gallon for a total of $3,616,831.07 to the Joint Account. Please see the CJI3 worksheet in the attached file for details. The price of $2.81 is much lower than the price from Shell Trading invoice. No credit is due to the Joint Account.

The Operator has thus far not submitted agreement (i.e. contract) language obligating the Operator to pay the bonus. This was a discretionary bonus above and beyond contract language. If the Operator is unable to provide relevant agreement language, then it must credit the Joint Account in accordance with the February 2019 Letter Agreement

- i. Incentive Bonus— Incentive bonuses to vendors/contractors (excluding Affiliates) may be charged by the Operator to the Joint Account as a direct charge where the Operator's agreement(s)with such vendors/contractors contain contractual language obligating the Operator to pay the bonus, subject to the Operator providing documentation demonstrating that the contractor satisfied the contractual metrics or commitments triggering the bonus.

According to COPAS MFI-49 related to Awards, this scenario falls within the description of "discretionary and goodwill awards". As the awards is not an "integral part of the contract" (or amended contract) it is not chargeable here.

Discretionary and goodwill Awards are typically not an integral part of the contract or compensation arrangement with the contractor. Examples of discretionary Awards are those given for attainment of routine safety, environmental, or other general goals. Examples of goodwill Awards are those given in recognition of a long-term alliance between the Öperator and contractor or those offered only to managers or certain contractor representatives. Discretionary and goodwill Awards are viewed as a means of establishing or maintaining a good working relationship with the contractor, and as such, are viewed as providing future benefit to multiple properties rather than directly benefiting the property or properties previously served.

In addition to not being included in the base/amended contract, the Operator used such language as "has decided to issue" which is the very essence of Discretionary on the Part of the Operator which could have just as easily decided not to issue.

The Operator is again requested to credit the Joint Account for the bonus not chargeable

Credit denied. This was not a discretionary bonus. Communications issued to suppliers regarding the Mars Turnaround incentive program show the bonus was predetermined, tied to defined performance metrics, and communicated prior to execution. The documentation satisfies these conditions by demonstrating that the incentive was pre-established and based on objective turnaround completion criteria. Per COPAS MFI-49, the documentation as a written agreement or correspondence between the operator and contractor suffices as an agreement.

Per COPAS MFI-49:

IV. B:

"Discretionary or goodwill Awards are not chargeable, but the Operator is allowed to exercise its discretion in structuring the contractor's compensation to include Awards as a part of the cost of contract goods or services, within the guidelines described above, Refer to Exhibit 2 for a diagram of the decision criteria in determining the appropriate cost classification for a contractor Award. Also refer to Exhibit 3 for examples of Awards payments to contractors and the classification of the Awards as chargeable or not chargeable.

Upon a Non-Operator's request, the Operator should provide documentation that the Award constituted a component of the compensation due the contractor for goods provided or services rendered to the Joint Operation. This documentation may include a written agreement or correspondence between the Operator and contractor, Operator's procurement policies or guidelines, or Operator's internal correspondence."

III. E : "In order for the types of Awards discussed above to be chargeable to the Joint Account under the Services provision, the Award must be considered part of the 'cost of service.' An Award is considered part of the cost of service if it is an integral component of the compensation due the contractor, issued only if certain predetermined performance or operational metrics are met. The easiest way to establish the Award as an integral part of the compensation due the contractor is to include specifics of the metrics and potential Award into the contract with the vendor. In some instances, a contract may not exist between the Operator and contractor. In those situations, the Award may be chargeable as a 'cost of service' if the Operator can clearly document that the Award was predetermined and an integral part of the compensation, not discretionary, goodwill, or merely customary practice.'

The Operator charged the Joint Account in the amount of $32,000 for a Bluefin Turnaround Bonus according to the attached JADE line and invoice.

Per the Letter Agreement dated February 13, 2019, section I, "Incentive bonuses to vendor/contractors may be charged by the Operator to the Joint Account as a direct charge where the Operators agreements contain contractual language obligating the Operator to pay the bonus, subject to the Operator providing documentation demonstrating the contractor satisfied the contractual metrics"

Information request (IR071) submitted during fieldwork requested the vendor contract to include the contractual metrics. The Operator did not provide the vendor contract, including the contractual metrics.

Please credit the Joint Account $32,000.00 plus OH (13%) or provide the vendor contact.

table_references.summary: This table outlines a bonus structure based on project completion time. Workers receive a base bonus of **$2,000 per man** for on-time mechanical completion, with bonuses increasing by **$500 per man** for every additional 12 hours completed ahead of schedule. The maximum bonus reaches **$4,000 per man** for finishing 48 hours early.

replies.text:
The Operator has thus far not submitted agreement (i.e. contract) language obligating the Operator to pay the bonus. This was a discretionary bonus above and beyond contract language. If the Operator is unable to provide relevant agreement language, then it must credit the Joint Account in accordance with the February 2019 Letter Agreement.

- i. Incentive Bonus— Incentive bonuses to vendors/contractors (excluding Affiliates) may be charged by the Operator to the Joint Account as a direct charge where the Operator's agreement(s)with such vendors/contractorscontain contractual languageobligating the Operator to pay the bonus, subject to the Operator providing documentation demonstrating that the contractor satisfied the contractual metrics or commitments triggering the bonus.

According to COPAS MFI-49 related to Awards, this scenario falls within the description of "discretionary and goodwill awards". As the awards is not an "integral part of the contract" (or amended contract) it is not chargeable here.

Discretionary and goodwill Awards are typically not an integral part of the contract or compensation arrangement with the contractor. Examples of discretionary Awards are those given for attainment of routine safety, environmental, or other general goals. Examples of goodwill Awards are those given in recognition of a long-term alliance between the Operator and contractor or those offered only to managers or certain contractor representatives. Discretionary and goodwill Awards are viewed as a means of establishing or maintaining a good working relationship with the contractor, and as such, are viewed as providing future benefit to multiple properties rather than directly benefiting the property or properties previously served.

In addition to not being included in the base/amended contract, the Operator used such language as "intend" which is the very essence of Discretionary on the part of the Operator which could have just as easily decided not to issue. Further, evidence of the goodwill nature of this bonus is the vendor's acknowledgement " Great News! " This is prima facie evidence of the goodwill created by the bonus, as it was not anticipated by the vendor. This is contrary to an expected outcome based on a negotiated contract.

The Operator is again requested to credit the Joint Account for the bonus not chargeable.

replies.text:
Credit denied. This was not a discretionary bonus. Communications issued to suppliers regarding the Mars Turnaround

incentive program show the bonus was predetermined, tied to defined performance metrics, and communicated prior to execution. The documentation satisfies these conditions by demonstrating that the incentive was pre-established and based on objective turnaround completion criteria. Per COPAS MFI-49, the documentation as a written agreement or correspondence between the operator and contractor suffices as an agreement.

Per COPAS MFI-49:

IV. B

"Discretionary or goodwill Awards are not chargeable, but the Operator is allowed to exercise its discretion in structuring the contractor's compensation to include Awards as a part of the cost of contract goods or services, within the guidelines described above, Refer to Exhibit 2 for a diagram of the decision criteria in determining the appropriate cost classification for a contractor Award. Also refer to Exhibit 3 for examples of Awards payments to contractors and the classification of the Awards as chargeable or not chargeable.

Upon a NonOperator's request, the Operator should provide documentation that the Award constituted a component of the compensation due the contractor for goods provided or services rendered to the Joint Operation. This documentation may include a written agreement or correspondence between the Operator and contractor, Operator's procurement policies or guidelines, or Operator's internal correspondence."

## III. E :

"In order for the types of Awards discussed above to be chargeable to the Joint Account under the Services provision, the Award must be considered part of the 'cost of service.' An Award is considered part of the cost of service if it is an integral component of the compensation due the contractor, issued only if certain predetermined performance or operational metrics are met. The easiest way to establish the Award as an integral part of the compensation due the contractor is to include specifics of the metrics and potential Award into the contract with the vendor. In some instances, a contract may not exist between the Operator and contractor. In those situations, the Award may be chargeable as a 'cost of service' if the Operator can clearly document that the Award was predetermined and an integral part of the compensation, not discretionary, goodwill, or merely

customary practice.'

The Operator has thus far not submitted agreement (i.e. contract) language obligating the Operator to pay the bonus. This was a discretionary bonus above and beyond contract language. If the Operator is unable to provide relevant agreement language, then it must credit the Joint Account in accordance with the February 2019 Letter Agreement.

- i. Incentive Bonus— Incentive bonuses to vendors/contractors (excluding Affiliatcs) may be charged by the Operator to the Joint Account as a direct charge where the Operator's agreement(s)with such vendors/contractorscontain contractual language obligating the Operator to pay the bonus, subject to the Operator providing documentation demonstrating that the contractor satisfied the contractual metrics or commitments triggering the bonus.

According to COPAS MFI-49 related to Awards, this scenario falls within the description of "discretionary and goodwill awards". As the awards is not an "integral part of the contract" (or amended contract) it is not chargeable here.

Discretionary and goodwill Awards are typically not an integral part of the contract or compensation arrangement with the contractor. Examples of discretionary Awards are those given for attainment of routine safety, environmental, or other general goals. Examples of goodwill Awards are those given in recognition of a long-term alliance between the Öperator and contractor or those offered only to managers or certain contractor representatives. Discretionary and goodwill Awards are viewed as a means of establishing or maintaining a good working relationship with the contractor, and as such, are viewed as providing future benefit to multiple properties rather than directly benefiting the property or properties previously served.

In addition to not being included in the base/amended contract, the Operator used such language as "intend" which is the very essence of Discretionary on the part of the Operator which could have just as easily decided not to issue.

The Operator is again requested to credit the Joint Account for the bonus not chargeable

Credit denied. This was not a discretionary bonus. Communications issued to suppliers regarding the Mars Turnaround incentive program show the bonus was predetermined, tied to defined performance metrics, and communicated prior to execution. The documentation satisfies these conditions by demonstrating that the incentive was pre-established and based on objective turnaround completion criteria. Per COPAS MFI-49, the documentation as a written agreement or correspondence between the operator and contractor suffices as an agreement.

Per COPAS MFI-49:

IV. B

"Discretionary or goodwill Awards are not chargeable, but the Operator is allowed to exercise its discretion in structuring the contractor's compensation to include Awards as a part of the cost of contract goods or services, within the guidelines described above, Refer to Exhibit 2 for a diagram of the decision criteria in determining the appropriate cost classification for a contractor Award. Also refer to Exhibit 3 for examples of Awards payments to contractors and the classification of the Awards as chargeable or not chargeable.

Upon a Non-Operator's request, the Operator should provide documentation that the Award constituted a component of the compensation due the contractor for goods provided or services rendered to the Joint Operation. This documentation may include a written agreement or correspondence between the Operator and contractor, Operator's procurement policies or guidelines, or Operator's internal correspondence."

III. E :

"In order for the types of Awards discussed above to be chargeable to the Joint Account under the Services provision, the Award must be considered part of the 'cost of service.' An Award is considered part of the cost of service if it is an integral component of the compensation due the contractor, issued only if certain predetermined performance or operational metrics are met. The easiest way to establish the Award as an integral part of the compensation due the contractor is to include specifics of the metrics and potential Award into the contract with the vendor. In some instances, a contract may not exist between the Operator and contractor. In those situations, the Award may be chargeable as a 'cost of service' if the Operator can clearly document that the Award was predetermined and an integral part of the compensation, not discretionary, goodwill, or merely customary practice.'

Credit Denied.

The Operator has thus far not submitted agreement (i.e. contract) language obligating the Operator to pay the bonus. This was a discretionary bonus above and beyond contract language. If the Operator is unable to provide relevant agreement language, then it must credit the Joint Account in accordance with the February 2019 Letter Agreement.

- i. Incentive Bonus— Incentive bonuses to vendors/contractors (excluding Affiliates) may be charged by the Operator to the Joint Account as a direct charge where the Operator's agreement(s)with such vendors/contractorscontain contractual languageobligating the Operator to pay the bonus, subject to the Operator providing documentation demonstrating that the contractor satisfied the contractual metrics or commitments triggering the bonus.

According to COPAS MFI-49 related to Awards, this scenario falls within the description of "discretionary and goodwill awards". As the awards is not an "integral part of the contract" (or amended contract) it is not chargeable here.

Discretionary and goodwill Awards are typically not an integral part of the contract or compensation arrangement with the contractor. Examples of discretionary Awards are those given for attainment of routine safety, environmental, or other general goals. Examples of goodwill Awards are those given in recognition of a long-term alliance between the Operator and contractor or those offered only to managers or certain contractor representatives. Discretionary and goodwill Awards are viewed as a means of establishing or maintaining a good working relationship with the contractor, and as such, are viewed as providing future benefit to multiple properties rather than directly benefiting the property or properties previously served.

In addition to not being included in the base/amended contract, the Operator used such language as "intend" which is the very essence of Discretionary on the part of the Operator which could have just as easily decided not to issue.

The Operator is again requested to credit the Joint Account for the bonus not chargeable.
replies.source_file: 2023/Mars et al/Rebuttal 2/Auditor Report/Audit Report - Final Mars [2023-102].pdf

replies.text:
Credit denied. This was not a discretionary bonus. Communications issued to suppliers regarding the Mars Turnaround incentive program show the bonus was predetermined, tied to defined performance metrics, and communicated prior to execution. The documentation satisfies these conditions by demonstrating that the incentive was pre-established and based onobjective turnaround completion criteria. Per COPAS MFI-49, the documentation as a written agreement or correspondence between the operator and contractor suffices as an agreement.

Per COPAS MFI-49:

IV. B

"Discretionary or goodwill Awards are not chargeable, but the Operator is allowed to exercise its discretion in structuring the contractor's compensation to include Awards as a part of the cost of contract goods or services, within the guidelines described above, Refer to Exhibit 2 for a diagram of the decision criteria in determining the appropriate cost classification for a contractor Award. Also refer to Exhibit 3 for examples of Awards payments to contractors and the classification of the Awards as chargeable or not chargeable.

Upon a NonOperator's request, the Operator should provide documentation that the Award constituted a component of the compensation due the contractor for goods provided or services rendered to the Joint Operation. This documentation may include a written agreement or correspondence between the Operator and contractor, Operator's procurement policies or guidelines, or Operator's internal correspondence."

## III. E :

"In order for the types of Awards discussed above to be chargeable to the Joint Account under the Services provision, the Award must be considered part of the 'cost of service.' An Award is considered part of the cost of service if it is an integral component of the compensation due the contractor, issued only if certain predetermined performance or operational metrics are met. The easiest way to establish the Award as an integral part of the compensation due the contractor is to include specifics of the metrics and potential Award into the contract with the vendor. In some instances, a contract may not exist between the Operator and contractor. In those situations, the Award may be chargeable as a 'cost of service' if the Operator can clearly document that the Award was predetermined and an integral part of the compensation, not discretionary, goodwill, or merely customary practice.'
