026.short_description: Shell Trading Diesel Invoice Priced With Markup Over Market
026.description:
Shell Trading Company invoice no. 11297086, dated March 4, 2022 totaling $1,262,244.06, charged the Europa Joint Accounts for diesel using a market index price plus a mark-up rate of .15 per gallon.

Pursuant to COPAS MFI #18, an Operator may have Related Entities from which they purchase materials such as ... fuel , at prices which are higher than those paid by the Related Entity. The purpose of Labor, Materials and 'Equipment and facilities" provisions in the COPAS Accounting Procedure forms is to assure the Operator's employees, material purchased from outside sources and any equipment of facilities which are owned by the Operator and serve the Joint Property are charged to the Joint Account at actual cost, without mark-up .

The Related Entity must either historically or currently have conducted a substantial amount of its business with companies other than the Operator or other Related Entities. Therefore, unless the Related Entity is able to comply with the criteria of this preceding sentence, the material purchased for use on the Joint Property from the Related Entity shall be charged to the Joint Account at the price paid by the Related Entity to an independent third party.

Goods and services provided by the Related Entity should be priced on terms that do not exceed the lesser of (1) those offered by the Related Entity to its most favored customers or (2) those offered to or obtained by the Operator from unrelated entities providing such services or products in the geographical area.

Credit is requested for $65,343.44 (the $.15 cent per gallon mark-up charged by Shell Trading for the diesel transfer to Europa totaling $63,749.70 plus 2.5% overhead of $1,593.74).

replies.text:
Credit Denied.

The price from Shell Trading quoted by the non-operator was not used as a basis to apply charges for diesel fuel consumed by the Joint Account.

When fuel is pumped into the rig from a vessel, the cost of the fuel will be charged to the project which is associated to the rig at that time. However, when the rig completes its activities with the project, the Wells Finance team will process a true up posting to the project. In the true up process, the team analyzes the total value of fuel consumed by the rig during the activity period, based on the rig fuel usage report that is produced by the rig cost desk with the costs charged to the Joint Account. If the cost charged to the joint account is higher, the excess charge will be credited to the Joint Account and vice versa if the cost charged to the joint account is lower.

Therefore, after the true up posted for the EA3ST2 LLEDrill project…648,741 gallons of diesel consumed was charged at $2.33 per gallon for a total of $1,514,392.11 to the Joint Account. Please see the attached worksheet with the JADE and CJI3 details. No credit is due to the Joint Account.

Mandatory OTL regulatory requirements for drilling, completion, and intervention activities will be chargeable to the joint account as designated within the BSEE Certified Federal Register.

0062.description:
The Operator charged the Great White Joint Account $583,466.00 for FMC invoice 92836603 dated 12/28/22, $404,255.05 for FMC invoice 92945471 dated 9/12/2023, and $188,119.00 for FMC invoice 92863639 dated 2/28/2023.

Upon review, these invoices are for additional costs caused by the delay of GD009 operations, which was caused by the Operator utilizing the drillship to work on Vito wells between the GD008 and GD009 tophole sections. As the Joint Property was not the cause of, and received no benefit from these delay costs, they should be credited to the Joint Account and charged to the Vito project which drove the need for this incremental cost.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $1,205,236.05 ($1,175,840.05 plus 2.5% OH of $29,396.00) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing for these coding errors.

replies.text:
The auditor did not provide any contractual or COPAS reference why charges are not billable. The exception was written as a coding error but the exception is the auditor's opinion rather than non-compliance with the contract.

The example is not a normal coding error where the vendor invoice is for another asset and the wrong charge code is used by mistake. The operator made a decision as allowed under Article 5 Rights and Duties of Operator of the Great White UOA and the decision was communicated to co-owners in rig sequence updates during co-owner meetings at which the co-owners had the opportunity to discuss. In this case, the auditor might not like that the operator's decision resulted in more cost, but the operators decision doesn't make the cost non-billable.

The credit is denied and exception considered closed.

However, a review of this project revealed that the total expenditure (2020-2023) was $313,408.07 (excluding overhead) which exceeded the $300,000.00 threshold as stated by the Operator. Since Chevron disputed the costs related to the Perdido HAZOP Actions Engineer Study in 2020 and no AFE was authorized, Auditor maintains position that these charges should be credited to the Joint Account.

The Operator is requested to credit the Great White Joint Account $290,403.90 ($256,994.60 plus overhead of $33,409.30) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

0093.description:
The Great White Joint Account was charged $13,772,373.80 (excluding overhead) on multiple AFE's related to the replacement of ESP (Electric Subsea Pumps) which was billed at the Operating Overhead rate of 13.0% in lieu of the appropriate $344,309.35 Development Overhead rate of 2.5%. The AFE descriptions include phrases such as " This AFE is to proactively pull and replace Perdido ESP with the upgraded 880 Motor ESP. The upgrade will provide immediate production uplift to Perdido..."

It remains BP's position that the upgraded motors and increased production uplift meet the definition of " expansion of fixed assets" as contemplated in the operating agreement Section III (Overhead), 2 (Application of Overhead - Percentage basis), a.5

- a. Development shall include all costs in connection with:
1. drilling, redrilling, plugging back or deepening of any or all wells
2. workover operations requiring a period of fifteen(15) consecutive work days or more on a well,
3. preliminary expenditures necessary in preparation for drilling,
4. expenditures incurred in abandoning when the well is not completed as a producer,
5. original construction or installation of fixed assets, expansion of fixed assets and any other project clearly discernible as a fixed asset, except Major Construction as defined in Paragraph 3 of Section III.

The Operator is requested to credit the Great White Joint Account $1,446,392.52 for the incorrectly charged overhead with a reference to the audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
As per our regulatory SME (subject matter expert), ESP's are not classified as a well, as they have no API assigned to them. They are classified as production equipment thus are subject to the agreed upon appropriate Operating overhead rate. The replacement/maintenance of the ESP since inception (post first capitalization of first replacement) has always been billed as an operating expense and not an 'upgrade'. In addition, there is only one type of ESP on the market.

The section of the Operating Agreement Section III (Overhead), 2 (Application of Overhead - Percentage basis) quoted by the Auditor, is related to wells and is not applicable to an ESP (as noted above).

As per the Senior Finance Advisor, ESP installations are considered as Facility Maintenance activities as the ESPs have required changeouts every 1-3 years since Perdido startup. The only change was in Shell's internal accounting treatment in complying with IFRS16 lease interpretations that they are to be treated as a Right of Use Asset which sits on the balance sheet therefore requiring us to capitalize internally. There has been no change to overhead application or proposal through the COUA as a maintenance activity. This is the same consistent message that has been conveyed to Chevron Finance. If the Auditor requires further clarification, it may be best placed to seek resolution through the Finance and Commercial teams.

No Credit is due.

Additionally, per the BP-SOI Settlement Agreement effective 1st February 2022, Section 3 of Billing Standards, paragraph 3.12 states that Third Party Project Management - Ancillary costs related to third-party project management that are charged as part of the overall cost for the provision of goods and services provided by a third party associated with a third party's provision of goods and services may be charged to the Joint Account as a component cost of the underlying goods and services and shall not be qualified as OTL or as administrative costs covered under Overhead.

According to MFI-19, Section IV, interpretative section, carrying costs are not chargeable. This SCM Fee is a form of carrying cost and therefore considered covered by Overhead (not allowed to be charged) as stated in MFI-19:

## C. Chargeable Costs

Actual costs may include costs of (I) Material, (2) making it suitable for use, and (3) transportation from the point of acquisition to the Joint Property including loading and unloading. Not included are storage or carrying costs.

Therefore, the Operator is requested to grant credit for this exception as originally written. Full credit remains due.

MFI-19 Section IV, issued in 1987, is an interpretative guideline-not a governing agreement-and predates the BP-SOI Settlement Agreement, which took effect in February 2022. The more recent agreement provides more clarity on the billing practices and explicitly allows ancillary third-party project management costs to be charged as part of the overall cost of goods and services. Additionally, the MFI-19 provision applies only to materials owned by the Operator, which is not the case here. The inventory is held at a vendor facility and not owned by the Operator, so the SCM Fee does not qualify as a carrying cost or fall under Overhead. This fee ensures materials are available when needed, allows invoicing only upon shipment for installation, and enables the return of unused items without a 15% restocking fee-helping to avoid surplus and reduce costs for the Joint Operation.

No credit is due.

Sumitomo is a manufacturer, importer, and supplier of oil country tubular goods (among other tangible property) and not a management nor consultancy firm. As they do not provide project management services, the "Ancillary" provisions as contemplated in the February 2019 Letter Agreement are inapplicable here.

The Operator has stated that the SCM fee is for "the vendor to ensure the material is ready for immediate use and the prevention of accumulation of surplus stocks". According to the statement by the Operator, this SCM fee therefore represents the vendor's cost of warehousing and storage for the materials in question.

As with other types of costs, warehousing and storage cost does not become chargeable by virtue of being outsourced. The costs incurred will always be overhead in nature, and covered by the overhead rate, regardless of whether they are incurred by a vendor or the Operator directly. Full credit remains due.

The operator maintains its position that the SCM fee is chargeable in accordance with the BP-SOI Settlement Agreement, effective February 1, 2022, and Section 3, paragraph 3.12 of the Billing Standards. Following the face-to-face meeting in February 2025 with SOI\_BP, both parties agreed to escalate this issue to the commercial departments of both companies. The operator's position remains unchanged.

As outlined in the Settlement Agreement (SA) between BP and Shell with effective date of December 1, 2019, the Amortization Period for the SA, section 2.1.d.i (Calculation of Accumulator Account for Transocean Rigs), for BP is extended through the end of December 31, 2023 for the Transocean Rigs, including Pontus. The Operator is adhering to and fulfilling the attached sections of the agreement.

In its response, the Operator shows that the adjustment is calculated as the no. of hours on particular Transocean invoices multiplied by a "new day rate for bp" multiplied by 33.33%. Thus, the auditors cannot determine the nature of this "new day rate for bp". Please provide an explanation as to what this new day rate/accumulator is for and provide documentation of the calculation for the new day rate as requested on the original IR.

We were able to verify the # of hours used to calculate this charge and have attached the invoices to this exception, except for the hours related to Transocean invoice #756B. Credit of $1,169,243 plus 2.5% overhead is due to bp unless the requested documentation above is received and verified.

The Operator allocated $459,602.35 in SAP Master Data Management and other administrative IT costs per the attached allocation lines and JADE lines.

The charges in question are from Greg Como and FIN Systems, which are providers of administrative data management services, supporting SAP (Blueprint - Shell Financial Accounting System). According to documentation provided by the Operator, the charges were previously classified as overhead costs, and should continue to remain so as they are not chargeable to the Joint Account due to being administrative and managerial in nature because they are for management and administrative systems.

The PO from Greg Como was reviewed, and it includes such tasks as "Consulting support for Total Reliability Process throughout SEPCo to implement Total Reliability Management, including but not limited to:[...] ", " Implement Equipment Strategy Optimization (ESO) to proactively, systematically, and holistically seek out opportunities to reduce equipment Total Cost of Ownership. ", " Implementing Performance Management - to support and assure measures are aligned with Global minimum reporting requirements " The above systems and implementations are administrative and managerial in nature and therefore are reimbursed to the Operator in the Overhead Rate.

The PO from FinSystems was reviewed and it is for " Development of AH (Asset Hierarchy) and MRP (Maintenance Reference Plans) for SAP upload for Upstream Americas - Onshore U.S. " . This is for the creation of master data not specifically related to the Mars asset, and not for the management of the Mars asset and is therefore also not chargeable to the Joint Account as the cost is already included in the Overhead Rate.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $459,602.35 plus 13% OH for a total credit due of $519,350.66 for the administrative system data management and master data management costs.

replies.text: Credit has been consistently denied. GCC Solutions LLC, based in Kingwood, Texas, is a consulting firm specializing in maintenance and reliability. Their expertise lies in benchmarking and implementing process improvements across maintenance, turnaround, and project (MTAP) activities. Finn Systems and Gregory Como provide services utilizing the NRX AssetHub software, which supports maintenance operations by enabling the analysis, visualization, creation, editing, organization, approval, and management of high-quality asset and maintenance data. This software is specifically designed for Maintenance and Integrity execution activities within the Joint Account. It is not intended for accounting functions within the SAP system, which appears to be the source of confusion for the co-owner. According to COPAS Document MFI-35 (Charging of Training Costs to the Joint Account), COPAS Model Form Interpretation 44 regarding Field Computer and Communication Systems, and the CFR# requirements in SEMS, as well as the February 13, 2019 letter agreement—specifically sections 1d (Data Repository Systems) and 1ei (Scheduling and Maintenance Software Systems)—the charges in question are directly chargeable to the Joint Account.

The Operator charged the Joint Account $8,490,737.72 for the following AFEs:

C.US.MR2.FI.22.004.1230A - Compr Flare/Vent 3Way Valve Replacement

C.US.MR2.FI.22.001.1230A - Olympus IAC Overhaul/Replacement Facilit

C.US.MR2.FI.21.004.1230A - Olympus Hot Water Heater Replacement

C.US.MR2.FI.23.001.1230A - HVAC Control System Upgrade Field Improv

These maintenance costs are non routine in nature and consist of maintenance and integrity related items.

According to the PowerNap PHA section 5.1.2, these costs should be allocated to the Powernap Operator based on production:

replies.text: The Operator's response has not changed since giving it as a response to Information Request 11. The interpretation of section 5.1.2 of the Powernap PHA pertains to maintenance related activities aimed at keeping an asset functioning as intended. However, there's a distinction for the items listed below: while these activities qualify as non-routine or infrequent, they involve full replacements and enhancements. Shell follows internal accounting guidelines and policies to classify costs, reviewing expenditures on assets after they have been placed in service. After an asset is in service the following guidelines apply: ·Costs included into the category of costs subject to section 5.1.2 are costs which are incurred to maintain the asset ·Costs incurred to provide a functional enhancement of an asset are considered facility improvement and are capitalized. These items improve the asset when compared to its original specifications. o Criteria to determine whether a cost is an improvement to an asset include: §Increase in operational performance §Expenditures incurred to meet changed governmental or Shell requirements (excludes new requirements that are covered under 5.10) §Decreases operating costs beyond a threshold §Changes in the nature of use of the asset from its original use §Where the primary intention of the expenditure is to significantly improve performance ·Section 5.10 only covers capital expenditures to remain compliant with future industry standards or government regulations Accordingly, the charges of $8,490,737.72 in question of three AFEs have been applied correctly and no credit is due to the Joint Account. Please see explanation shown below for detail. C.US.MR2.FI.22.004 Compressor 3-way valve replacement & supplement Classification reason: Upon investigation and learning from an incident on another Shell operated asset, the 3-way valve replacement meets the criteria as a new operator standard. This is a safety enhancement and qualifies as a capitalized field improvement. C.US.MR2.FI.22.001 Olympus IAC Overhaul/Replacement Classification reason: this IAC overhaul/replacement changed the metallurgy, upgrading the structural frame metallurgy from carbon steel to stainless steel. This qualifies as a capitalized field improvement. C.US.MR2.FI.21.004 Olympus Hot Water Heater Replacements Supplement Classification reason: The hot water tank was leaking frequently and posed a safety risk as well as a possible deferment risk due to the potential to demobilize the crew if hot water tanks failed. This was a full replacement and upgrade to the hot water system and qualifies as a capitalized field improvement. C.US.MR2.FI.23.001 Mars HVAC Control System Upgrade Classification reason: The HVAC controls system is obsolete and pose a threat with potential of platform shutdown. Upgrading to ensure system integrity. This qualifies as a capitalized field improvement.

replies.text: The Operator is incorrectly co-mingling its internal accounting policy with the requirements of the Powernap PHA. The PHA section 5.1.2 does not make mention of any requirement for any particular cost to be classified as capital or expense. Rather, there are other specific criteria mentioned that invoke 5.1.2. For example, exceeding $500k, refurbishment, maintenance, integrity related items all invoke the provisions of 5.1.2. Addressing the items individually: C.US.MR2.FI.22.004 - Compressor 3-way valve replacement & supplement: A safety valve is an integrity related item. Without a properly functioning safety valve, pressure vessels, compressors, and other high pressure equipment will not maintain structural integrity which will cause significant damage. As noted above, integrity related items fall distinctly within 5.1.2. C.US.MR2.FI.22.001 Olympus IAC Overhaul/replacement: Per section 5.1.2., whether an item is considered a capitalized (or expensed) is irrelevant. As an Overhaul or Replacement, this would be considered both refurbishment and/or maintenance which is squarely within the verbiage of 5.1.2. C.US.MR2.FI.21.004 Olympus Hot Water Heater Replacement Replacement of the hot water tank is considered a "refurbishment and maintenance" of the hot water system. Again, this falls squarely within 5.1.2. Alternatively as mentioned by the Operator if there is an aspect of safety risk here, then this item would be considered integrity related within the provisions of 5.1.2. C.US.MR2.FI.23.001 Mars HVAC Control System Upgrade As noted by the Operator in its own response, this was "upgraded to ensure system integrity". As cited in 5.1.2., " *integrity related items"* are included in said provisions. Full credit remains due as originally written.

In information request 12, the Operator was requested to explain why these costs were charged direct, to which they replied: " The interpretation of section 5.1.2 of the Powernap PHA pertains to maintenance related activities aimed at keeping an asset functioning as intended. g. Third Party Staging, Warehousc Facilities - For approved projects, the labor and facilities costs directly incurred for preservation, maintenance, and staging for jointly owned equipment or materials for Joint Operations may be charged by the Operator to the Joint Account as a direct charge consistent with COPAS Model Form Interpretation #21. The chargeable amounts are limited to periods of six (6) months or less occurring prior to execution of the project. 0010.short_description: Operating OH charged should be Development
0010.description:
The Operator charged 13% Operating overhead for the 7 AFEs in the attached list. Upon review, the AFEs in question qualified for development overhead at 2.5% as they included 5 or more consecutive workdays as required by the JOA to quality for 2.5%. Full documentation is provided in the attached file.

This was the subject of Information Request 008 issued during the fieldwork. The Operator provided comments in the response, to which the Non-Operator adds the following:

P.US.MAR.WS.22.005.7241A - the Operator did not address the 22 days of vessel dayrate utilized to perform this job according to Page 2 of Baker invoice 913207306 which was furnished with the IR and this exception.

- P.US.MAR.WS.22.006.7241A - the Operator only provided a screenshot from their system and did not address the 12 days of vessel dayrate utilized to perform the job according to Baker invoice 913251678 which was furnished with the IR and this exception.
- P.US.MR2.WS.23.001.7241A - the Operator is relying solely on the Baker Hughes invoice mentioned to support the position that the wellwork was less than 5 consecutive days. It does not address that the well supervisor, Johnny Clark was onsite, performing work specifically for this job, greater than 5 days.
- P.US.MR2.WS.23.002.7241A - the Operator is relying solely on the Baker Hughes invoice mentioned to support the position that the wellwork was less than 5 consecutive days. It does not address that the well supervisor, Michael Crochet was onsite, performing work specifically for this job, greater than 5 days.
- P.US.MR2.WS.23.006.7241A - the Operator contends that the job was less than 5 work days due to loading and standby time. However, the Joint Account still pays for these days, and the crew is required to work these days to load, unload, and prepare operations. Thus these days are also considered work days as the crew is performing work, and count towards the consecutive workday requirement.
- P.US.MR2.WS.23.003.741A - the Operator is relying on the Halliburton timesheets, without addressing the fact that the wellsite supervisor, Richard Villanueva, was offshore at Mars specifically for this job, for a time period exceeding 5 days.
- P.US.MR2.WS.23.004.7241A - the Operator contends that the standby time from the Supreme Service invoice does not contribute towards the 5 consecutive workday requirement, however the Joint Account is still required to pay this standby time and the Operator did not offer any evidence to support that standby time is excluded from the 5 consecutive workday requirement as stated below in the Mars UOA.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $1,186,788.88 for the excess overhead charged.

replies.text: Please find the attached file along with the Operator's comments regarding the seven AFEs in question, which qualify for operational overhead at 13%. According to COPAS MFI-48 on the Application and Calculation of Drilling Overhead, the count of the five (5) consecutive workdays or more for any remedial operations starts in the Date workover operations, with rig or other units used in workover, commence and stop on the date the rig or other unit released. The concerns raised by the non-operator do not factor into the determination of five or more consecutive workdays as required by the JOA to qualify for 2.5%. P.US.MAR.WS.22.005.7241A - According to COPAS MFI-48 regarding the Application and Calculation of Drilling Overhead, the count for five (5) consecutive workdays or more for any remedial operations begins on the date that workover operations commence with the rig or other units. This count concludes on the date the rig or unit is released. It’s important to note that the 22 days of vessel day rate are not included in determining these five consecutive workdays. As a result, the credit claim of $524,079.93 has been denied. P.US.MAR.WS.22.006.7241A - According to COPAS MFI-48 regarding the Application and Calculation of Drilling Overhead, the count for the five (5) consecutive workdays for any remedial operations begins on the date workover operations commence with the rig or other units and ends on the date the rig or unit is released. The 12 days of vessel day rates utilized do not factor into the determination of these five consecutive workdays. Therefore, the credit claim of $300,338.65 is denied. P.US.MR2.WS.23.001.7241A - According to COPAS MFI-48 on the Application and Calculation of Drilling Overhead, the count for five (5) consecutive workdays for any remedial operations begins on the date workover operations commence with the rig or other units and concludes on the date the rig or unit is released. The duration of the well supervisor's stay on the Joint Property does not factor into this calculation. Johnny Clark, the well supervisor, was responsible for operations on the Joint Property and was engaged in multiple tasks, which naturally resulted in him staying for more than five consecutive workdays. Therefore, the credit claim of $96,470.43 is denied. P.US.MR2.WS.23.002.7241A - According to COPAS MFI-48 on the Application and Calculation of Drilling Overhead, the count for five (5) consecutive workdays for any remedial operations begins on the date workover operations commence with the rig or other units and concludes on the date the rig or unit is released. The duration of the well supervisor's stay on the Joint Property does not factor into this calculation. Michael Crochet, the well supervisor, was responsible for operations on the Joint Property and was engaged in multiple tasks, which naturally resulted in him staying for more than five consecutive workdays. Therefore, the credit claim of $ 116,231.21 is denied. P.US.MR2.WS.23.006.7241A - According to COPAS MFI-48 regarding the Application and Calculation of Drilling Overhead, the count for the five (5) consecutive workdays for any remedial operations begins on the date workover operations commence with the rig or other units and ends on the date the rig or unit is released. The days of load, unload, and prepare operations by crew do not factor into the determination of these five consecutive workdays. Therefore, the credit claim of $ 81,641.79 P.US.MR2.WS.23.003.741A - According to COPAS MFI-48 on the Application and Calculation of Drilling Overhead, the count for five (5) consecutive workdays for any remedial operations begins on the date workover operations commence with the rig or other units and concludes on the date the rig or unit is released. The duration of the well supervisor's stay on the Joint Property does not factor into this calculation. Richard Villanueva, the well supervisor, was responsible for operations on the Joint Property and was engaged in multiple tasks, which naturally resulted in him staying for more than five consecutive workdays. Therefore, the credit claim of $45,828.97 is denied. P.US.MR2.WS.23.004.7241A - According to COPAS MFI-48 regarding the Application and Calculation of Drilling Overhead, the count for the five (5) consecutive workdays for any remedial operations begins on the date workover operations commence with the rig or other units and ends on the date the rig or unit is released. The standby time do not factor into the determination of these five consecutive workdays. Therefore, the credit claim of $ 22,197.89 is denied.

0012.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $143,398.10 in TRACK LABOR from Waldemar S Nelson. Upon review of the track report provided, the charges are for a GOM Senior Designer 2E Joshua Mills.

According to the Statement of Clarification and Intent, Engineering, Design and Drafting is only chargeable for Major Construction Projects. The costs here are not charged to Major Construction as noted in the attached JADE lines. This was the subject of Information Request 46 issued during the fieldwork, to which the Operator responded:

Josh Mills is a 3-dimensional modeler & coordinator plus laser scan survey organizer & director.

The 3D model is key not only to major maintenance & projects work execution but is a critical part of the Safety and Environmental Management System (SEMS) Mechanical Integrity. Mechanical Integrity §250.1916 Any work associated with inspections, inspection programs, LOD's of programs, AIPSM and MTO meetings (Assurance of Quality and Mechanical Integrity of Equipment).

Per the February 2019 Letter Agreement, a Technical Employee must have "...special and specific engineering, geological, geophysical, technical or operational skills...". This definition does not include design, drafting, or modeling skills which are considered overhead. As this modeler does not meet the definition of OTL due to not being a Technical Employee, his work is not chargeable under Section 3.1., 3.2., or 3.3. of the February Letter Agreement.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $143,398.10 plus OH of $9,132.80 for a total credit of $152,530.90.

mycm

replies.text: The term "Technical Employees," as defined in the February 2019 Letter Agreement, refers to employees, affiliates, and contractors who possess specialized engineering, geological, geophysical, or operational skills. This includes roles such as planners, schedulers, and those providing execution support for facility maintenance, well maintenance, and turnaround activities. Their primary function in Joint Operations, as outlined in the relevant Applicable Operating Agreement, is to deliver services that benefit the Joint Property. It is important to clarify that Technical Employees do not encompass roles related to procurement, administration, accounting, auditing, pipeline nominations and scheduling, human resources, management, or legal services. Additionally, first-level supervision of operational staff is billable but excluded from this definition. While design, drafting, or modeling skills are not explicitly mentioned in the February 2019 Letter Agreement, individuals with these technical or operational skills are still considered to be providing services for the Joint Property and fall outside the excluded categories. Mr. Jordon, Josh Mills, serves as a 3D modeler, coordinator, and director of laser scan surveys. He has contributed to inspection programs, LODs, AIPSM, and MTO meetings, all aimed at benefiting Joint Property. His involvement has been crucial in supporting the Safety and Environmental Management System (SEMS) Mechanical Integrity, specifically under Mechanical Integrity §250.1916 for the project. Consequently, the Joint Account is not entitled to a credit of $143,398.10 plus overhead.

Material This fee enables Joint operation to have the material ready for immediate use, be invoiced by the vendor for goods/ products when they have been shipped for installation. Any material not used/ consumed/installed can be returned and credit to the Joint Operation without restocking charges (15%). It prevents the accumulation of surplus stocks and eliminate the restocking fee. According to the BP-SOI Settlement Agreement, dated December 2018, Section 3 Billing Disputes Paragraph l, third-party project management costs that are charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services by such third party associated with a third party’s provision of goods and services may be charged to the Joint Account as a component cost of the underlying goods and services. These costs shall not be qualified as OTL or as administrative costs covered under Overhead. The Sumitomo SCM fee is a component cost of the underlying goods and services, and it does not qualify as OTL or administrative costs covered under Overhead. The Sumitomo SCM fee is not storage or carrying cost covered under Overhead. No credit is due to the Joint Account.

The Operation of Mars and Olympus has a maintenance team led by Justin Trussell, who is responsible for maintenance and has an oversight of the contractor service provided by Allied Reliability. Based on the maintenance team lead confirmation " Lionel Guidry was filling the Work Prep Technician role and Jason Hynson was filling the Offshore General Planner role during this window of time. Both of these roles primarily focus on building work packages and ordering materials for maintenance activities. The WPT role also executes the majority of the job walk downs in the field and stages materials for the jobs once they are delivered to the platform, again this is primarily for maintenance tasks. 0023.short_description: Tenaris Rig Direct Pipe Management Service Fee
0023.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $472,275.51 on various Tenaris invoices for Rig Direct/Pipe Management/Service Fee. This fee is inclusive of supply chain management and administrative aspects from call-out to delivery to invoicing (per vendor).

Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreement states: "As compensation for administrative, supervision, office services and warehousing costs, Operator shall charge the Joint Account in accordance with this Section III.'

Additionally, AG 19, Section IV.3.C states 'Actual costs may include costs of (I) Material, (2) making it suitable for use, and (3) transportation from the point of acquisition to the Joint Property including loading and unloading. Not included are storage or carrying costs."

This was the subject of IR048 submitted during fieldwork.

The Operator is requested to reimburse joint account for $472,275.51 plus overhead of 2.5%.

mycm

replies.text: Credit denied. Tenaris provides pipe management services, which include in-yard movement, inspection, tally, and preparation of pipes for running. They also provide technical services to reduce operational risk and optimize running times by ensuring the right practices are followed and products are installed at the rig site. According to Section 3 Billing Disputes Paragraph l of the BP-SOI Settlement Agreement dated December 2018, Ancillary costs related to third-party project management that are charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services by such third party associated with a third party’s provision of goods and services may be charged to the Joint Account as a component cost of the underlying goods and services. Tenaris’s fee is a component cost of the underlying goods and services, and it does not qualify as administrative costs covered under Overhead.

0034.description:
The Joint Account was charged $768,748.00 of P&T-- Non-Labor per the attached JADE line.

The attached SIEP invoice contains no additional detail regarding these 3rd party expenses except that it is related to the Mars 4D OBN (Ocean Bottom node) Project and that it was for "HPC Allocation West--1Q". On IR-78, we requested that the Operator provide further documentation regarding the charge.

| 3rd Party Vendor Costs (pass thru) Total: 768,748.00 | 3rd Party Vendor Costs (pass thru) Total: 768,748.00 | 3rd Party Vendor Costs (pass thru) Total: 768,748.00 | 3rd Party Vendor Costs (pass thru) Total: 768,748.00 | 3rd Party Vendor Costs (pass thru) Total: 768,748.00 | 3rd Party Vendor Costs (pass thru) Total: 768,748.00 | 3rd Party Vendor Costs (pass thru) Total: 768,748.00 | 3rd Party Vendor Costs (pass thru) Total: 768,748.00 |

In its response, the Operator provided an email that shows this charge as part of an "HPC cost reallocation to billable projects" and the following explanation:

The costs are indeed costs for the internal processing of 'Mars 2022 Ocean Bottom Node Seismic Acquisition and Processing Agreement'. The charges in question are for the HPC (High Performance Computing) charges that are calculated based on the cost of the leased HPC hardware in the Shell MegaCenter, support staff, Power, real estate lease, etc. The services are provided by SIEP, IT Service & Operations and not provided by the 3rd party vendor. Therefore, no vendor invoices are available.

HPC charges are calculated based on various factors, including the cost of leased HPC hardware, support staff, power, and real estate lease. It is recovered on a project-by-project basis according to the seismic processing projects objectives and compute needs. Seismic processing costs are divided in staff and HPC based on project objectives, technologies requirement to address the Geophysical problems presented by the asset and previous analogue projects. The total staff and HPC cost for a seismic processing project are agreed upon with the asset before the project is started. Depending on the total time for the project completion, the total HPC budget is divided equally between quarters.

These charges are only a portion of the full charges for the project. The letter agreement between Shell and BP is attached for your information.

Please provide documentation of the allocation calculation that shows:

mycm

- a. The costs which comprise the pool of HPC costs being allocated, substantiated by third party invoices, time writing, or other relevant explanation and details to support the costs charged.
- b. The basis of allocation to the various billable projects.

If the Operator is unable to provide the requests above, please credit the Joint Account $768,748.00 plus 2.5% overhead.

The Operator charged the Joint Account $218,585.38 for Houma Distribution Center costs according to the attached JADE lines. These were the subject of Information Request 36 where the Operator explained that these costs were charged in accordance with the Mars UOA Section 7.B. which allows the Operator to charge company owned facilities and equipment at market rate less 20%.

The Operator did not provide sufficient analysis of the market. These costs are therefore not chargeable in accordance with Section 7.B. of the Mars UOA and should be credited to the Joint Account. Additionally, According to the 2018 Settlement Agreement section 9.a., the Settlement Documents supersede all previous communications, etc. COPAS MFI-46 was not a referenced Settlement Document in the Settlement Agreement. Therefore, any argument using MFI 46 is not in accordance with the Settlement Agreement. Full credit remains due as requested until the Operator determines which charging methodology it wishes to use.

The SAP document number 0132691047 reflects a credit of $60,477.22 for Mars, and SAP document number 0132691048 reflects a credit of $335,994.64 for Olympus. The credit for the year of 2022 and 2023 is at $157,213.45. For details on these adjustments, please refer to exception number 75 of 2021 Mars audit for detail.

0039.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $910,323.31 plus 2.5% OH for costs which appear to be for Shell's Houma Distribution Center according to the provided JADE lines. This was the subject of Information Request 38.

Upon review, these costs appear to be the costs of Ownership and Operation which are in accordance with the Mars UOA Section 7.A. The Operator is, however, also charging costs in accordance with Section 7.B. While either method is allowable, they are not allowable together and the Operator must select only one for recovery. Additionally, according to the 2018 Settlement Agreement section 9.a., the Settlement Documents supersede all previous communications, etc. COPAS MFI-46 was not a referenced Settlement Document in the Settlement Agreement. Therefore, any argument using MFI 46 is not in accordance with the Settlement Agreement. Full credit remains due as requested until the Operator determines which charging methodology it wishes to use.

replies.text: During the face-to-face meeting in February 2025 with SOI\_BP, the Operator presented the Houma DC corrections, adjustments, new processes, and the new Houma Cost Recovery Calculation sheet. The adjustment for the correction/true-up from April 2020 to March 2024 was posted in SAP in March 2025. The SAP document number 0132691047 reflects a credit of $60,477.22 for Mars, and SAP document number 0132691048 reflects a credit of $335,994.64 for Olympus. For details on these adjustments, please refer to exception no. 75 of 2021 Mars audit. The expense captured in exception 39 pertains to the operating cost of the Houma Distribution Center, which is directly chargeable to the Joint Account. No credit is granted.

0044.description:
The Joint Account was charged $817,005.32 of Core Contractor Labor costs per the attached JADE lines. We compared the list of contractor labor names noted on the JADE against the "Contractor Listing-- IQN" file provided by the Operator and against the POB.

On IR-73 which was submitted during the fieldwork, the auditors noted the following:

- a. Malbrough, Anthony: We noted that Anthony Malbrough was on Mars/Olympus on July, August, and November 2023 but on other properties the rest of the year. Please explain why he was charged to Mars during months other than July, August and November. Please also provide his job title and what he was doing for the Joint Property as we cannot find him on the Contractor Listing provided.
- b. Stein, David: We noted that David Stein was on Mars/Olympus from Aug- Dec 2023 but was on Auger the rest of the year. Please explain why he was charged to Mars on Jan-July while he was on Auger. Please also provide his job title and what he was doing for the Joint Property as we cannot find him on the Contractor Listing provided.
- c. Vaclavik, Jason: Jason Vaclavik was noted as being on Pontus during 2023. Please explain why he was charged to Mars. Please also provide his job title and what he was doing for the Joint Property as we cannot find him on the Contractor Listing provided.
- d. Vollrath, Nathan: Nathan Vollrath was noted as being on the Pontus only per the POB. Please explain why he was charged to Mars. Please also provide his job title and what he was doing for the Joint Property as we cannot find him on the Contractor Listing provided.
- e. Hippler, Chris: Chris Hippler was found on the POB as being on Globetrotter 2 during most of 2023. However, GT2 was servicing Mars during January, 2023 only. Please explain why Chris Hippler's costs were charged to the Joint Account when he was in GT2 while GT2 was not servicing Mars.
- f. Poche, Michael: Mike Poche was on Pontus in Nov and Dec of 2023 and not found on the POB in June 2023. Please explain why he was charged to the Joint Account for these months. Please also provide his job title and what he was doing for the Joint Property as we cannot find him on the Contractor Listing provided.
- g. Dennis, Duncan: We did not find Duncan Dennis on the POB or the Contractor Listing. Please explain why he was charged to Mars. Please also provide his job title and what he was doing for the Joint Property as we cannot find him on the Contractor Listing provided.

Please provide explanations and documentations pertaining to the above 7 contractors or credit the Joint account $516,877.79 plus 2.5% overhead. (see file "exception 44 value", "pivot" tab for calculation of exception value)

0065.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $47,400.86 for storage labor according to the attached JADE lines. Upon review, these charges were made to Operations WBS elements such as Well/Facil operations. According to the February 2019 Letter Agreement, labor and facilities costs for storage must be " For approved projects". At the end of fieldwork, the Operator was unable to provide Non-Operator approval for the following WBS elements and therefore is requested to issue the Joint Account a credit of $47,400 plus 13% OH for the storage labor for unapproved projects.

O.US.MR2.OLY.001.71300 O.US.175.DEI.762.71300

O.US.175.KOS.764.71300

g: Third Party Staging, Warehousc Facilities – For approved projects, the labor and facilities costs directly incurred for preservation, maintenance, and staging for jointly owned equipment or materials for Joint Operations may be charged by the Operator to the Joint Account as a direct charge consistent with COPAS Model Form Interpretation #21. The chargeable amounts are limited to periods of six (6) months or less occurring prior to execution of the project. After use of the material or equipment for the Joint Operation is completed, the equipment or material storage costs will no longer be charged to the Joint Account unless the Parties have agreed in writing that the material or cquipment is a critical spare.

mycm

replies.text: Credit denied. As acknowledged by the co-owner, the charges for storage labor were allocated to the following Operations WBS elements. O.US.MR2.OLY.001.71300 - Olympus Routine O&M (Surf Base) - BI O.US.175.DEI.762.71300 - Perform Well and Facility Ope-3248963C00 O.US.175.KOS.764.71300 - MC 764 King Well/Facil Oper These WBS elements pertain to the regular operation and maintenance of Joint Properties and are not designated for "projects" or related to the storage issues addressed in the February 2019 Letter Agreement. Additionally, contractors from Danos LLC, including Anthony Keys, Austen Daliet, Christopher John Landy, Jason Denton, and Richard Randall, have been regularly identified on the helicopter reservation table, indicating their offshore work on the joint properties. During the fieldwork, the auditor was requested to provide a list of Danos’s employees but was unable to do so by the end of the audit. Therefore, the credit claim of $47,400 plus 13% overhead for the storage labor has been denied.

0070.description:
The Operator allocated $426,240.00 to Olympus and $376,094.00 to Mars in 2021 and 2022 for CBCM IT cost recovery for 2021 and 2022 according to the attached allocation and JADE lines. The Journal Entry (SAP doc 131642193 - attached) was reviewed, and it showed the costs originating from WBS O.US.GLB.CBC.011.DW242. A CJI3 was run on this WBS element for the audit period, and that showed the costs were re-classed from the original WBS of O.US.GLB.CBC.016.OU242. When the supporting details of the Journal Entry itself were reviewed, it showed that these costs were allocated based on current PC Count. No details were given around the applications charged, cost per user, past PC count, etc.

The JADE lines from 2022 and 2021 were reviewed and showed that the Joint Account was paying for IT Costs on an ongoing, as-used basis. When examined, these Journal Entries show the allocation of costs which appears to be based on rig days. For example, the file titled '2021 CBCM 130107957.xlsx' is one of the supporting files for the 2021 JADE lines. From this file, in the 'Supporting' tab, is a zip file which contains the key source file, 'Billing Report Reference Q4 2020.xlsb'. This is the file that contains the source costs for the CBCM charge outs to the assets. By filtering on Column 'AM', using filter 'O.US.GLB.CBC.016.OU242' it can be seen that these ongoing Journal Entries also include costs from this WBS same element which is why current charges appear to be duplicated.

The Journal Entries (either current or previous) do not make it clear which specific IT applications, products or services are being provided or utilized by the Joint Account. Rather, they just allocate a portion of the overall IT Cost. The current Journal Entries, therefore, either appear to duplicate a portion of the previous billing, or increase the allocation for the previous billing based on a new metric. Insufficient details and documentation was provided in order for the auditor to determine whether the billings are for one application vs. another, a change in allocation methodology, or a true duplication of billing based on oversight during review.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $802,334 plus 13% overhead for the IT costs that were previously billed.

mycm

replies.text: Credit has been denied. Upon review by the Operator, the file titled “2021 CBCM 130107957.xlsx” provided by the co-owner pertains to the charge for IT & COMM SV, WELLVANTAGE ROC SUPPORT. The allocation of these charges is based on rig hours. The 2021 and 2022 JADE lines provided by the auditor also relate to charges for IT & COMM SV, WELLVANTAGE ROC SUPPORT. They are not the same charges of $426,240.00 to Olympus and $376,094.00 to Mars for CBCM IT cost recovery for 2021 and 2022. The charges in question are to recover applications and IT support for preventive maintenance, production control/monitoring, and well service tracking of field operations, as outlined in the CBCM GOM - Cost Sharing Process Overview document. There is no duplication of charges. Co-owner did not provide any analysis that is comparing prior years' charges against the entry made in 2023. The credit claim of $802,334 plus 13% overhead for the IT costs has been denied.

On December 1 & 21, 2020, Chevron responded to the Operator that the costs associated with Perdido HAZOP Actions Engineer Study, while related to HAZOP, was for engineering and project management costs covered by overhead. Per the Perdido COUA referenced in the letter, overhead will cover any professional or contract services provided by technical personnel that are offsite. It remains Chevron's position that Shell cannot charge out any of these engineering and project management costs described in the AFE.

This issue was raised in the prior year audit to which the Operator responded that "The AFE sent in December 2020 was an information only AFE as it was under the $300,000 threshold as noted in the Perdido COUA, Article 6, section 6.2 AFEs, … the Operator will not make any single expenditure or undertake any activity or operation costing three Hundred Thousand Dollars ($300,000.00) or more, unless an AFE has been included in a proposal for an activity or operation … This Information Only AFE was total gross amount of $232,500 for the estimated costs associated with the Perdido HAZOP Actions Engineer Study and the Operator was furnishing written information describing the expenditure to each of the Participating Parties."

However, a review of this project revealed that the total expenditure (2020-2023) was $313,408.07 (excluding overhead) which exceeded the $300,000.00 threshold as stated by the Operator. Since Chevron disputed the costs related to the Perdido HAZOP Actions Engineer Study in 2020 and no AFE was authorized, Auditor maintains position that these charges should be credited to the Joint Account.

The Operator is requested to credit the Silvertip Joint Account $52,652.53 ($47,011.19 plus overhead of $5,641.34) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

On December 1 & 21, 2020, Chevron responded to the Operator that the costs associated with Perdido HAZOP Actions Engineer Study, while related to HAZOP, was for engineering and project management costs covered by overhead. Per the Perdido COUA referenced in the letter, overhead will cover any professional or contract services provided by technical personnel that are offsite. It remains Chevron's position that Shell cannot charge out any of these engineering and project management costs described in the AFE.

This issue was raised in the prior year audit to which the Operator responded that "The AFE sent in December 2020 was an information only AFE as it was under the $300,000 threshold as noted in the Perdido COUA, Article 6, section 6.2 AFEs, … the Operator will not make any single expenditure or undertake any activity or operation costing three Hundred Thousand Dollars ($300,000.00) or more, unless an AFE has been included in a proposal for an activity or operation … This Information Only AFE was total gross amount of $232,500 for the estimated costs associated with the Perdido HAZOP Actions Engineer Study and the Operator was furnishing written information describing the expenditure to each of the Participating Parties."

However, a review of this project revealed that the total expenditure (2020-2023) was $313,408.07 (excluding overhead) which exceeded the $300,000.00 threshold as stated by the Operator. Since Chevron disputed the costs related to the Perdido HAZOP Actions Engineer Study in 2020 and no AFE was authorized, Auditor maintains position that these charges should be credited to the Joint Account.

The Operator is requested to credit the Tobago Joint Account $10,530.55 ($9,402.28 plus overhead of $1,128.27) with a reference to Chevron's audit number and exception number on the Joint Interest Billing.

replies.text:
Charges related to Perdido HAZOP Actions Engineering Study are currently being reviewed by the Commerical Advisor. Operator will provide more information when available.

No credit is due.

001.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $41,675.90 on various Sumitomo Corporation Of Americas invoices for SCM Fee Consignment charges. This is a warehousing fee and is not a direct cost of the material but an additional fee to house the material and ensure it is available when needed.

Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreement states: "As compensation for administrative, supervision, office services and warehousing costs, Operator shall charge the Joint Account in accordance with this Section III.'

Additionally, AG 19, Section IV.3.C states 'Actual costs may include costs of (I) Material, (2) making it suitable for use, a nd (3) transportation from the point of acquisition to the Joint Property including loading and unloading. Not included are storage or carrying costs."

The Operator is requested to reimburse joint account for $41,675.90 plus overhead of 2.5% for a total credit due of $42,717.80.

replies.text:
Credit denied.

The Sumitomo Corporation of Americas has been contracted to provide OCTG, casing, tubing, well, and accessories for drilling and completion projects. The Operator does not own any goods/ products or inventory at the vendor's facility and is not charged for the material until is ready for immediate use and shipped out for installation (thus avoiding an accumulation of surplus stock), or for any items not used or returned.

Sumitomo SCM fee is a component cost related to Sumitomo project management that is charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services, and it does not qualify as administrative, or procurement costs covered under Overhead.

Therefore, the contract provision described in Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreement (UOA) stated is for warehousing costs incurred for warehouses owned and operated by the Operator is not applicable here.

According to BP-SOI February 2019 letter agreement, Attachment I, Section 3 Billing Disputes Paragraph l. Third-Party Project Management - Ancillary costs related to third party project management that are charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services by such third party associated with a third party's provision of goods and services may be charged to the Joint Account as a component cost of the underlying goods and services and shall not be qualified as OTL or as administrative costs covered under Overhead.

replies.text:
Credit denied.

The Sumitomo Corporation of Americas has been contracted to provide OCTG, casing, tubing, well, and accessories for drilling and completion projects. The Operator does not own any goods/ products or inventory at the vendor's facility and is not charged for the material until is ready for immediate use and shipped out for installation (thus avoiding an accumulation of surplus stock), or for any items not used or returned.

Sumitomo SCM fee is a component cost related to Sumitomo project management that is charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services, and it does not qualify as administrative, or procurement costs covered under Overhead.

Therefore, the contract provision described in Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreement (UOA) stated is for warehousing costs incurred for warehouses owned and operated by the Operator is not applicable here.

According to BP-SOI February 2019 letter agreement, Attachment I, Section 3 Billing Disputes Paragraph l. Third-Party Project Management - Ancillary costs related to third party project management that are charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services by such third party associated with a third party's provision of goods and services may be charged to the Joint Account as a component cost of the underlying goods and services and shall not be qualified as OTL or as administrative costs covered under Overhead.

In its response, the Operator states that the Sumitomo Corporation of America has been contracted to provide materials and that "the Operator does not own any goods/ products or inventory at the vendor's facility and is not charged for the material until is ready for immediate use and shipped out for installation (thus avoiding an accumulation of surplus stock), or for any items not used or returned". The Operator contends that the SCM fee is a component cost related to Sumitomo project management that is charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services, and it does not qualify as administrative, or procurement costs covered under Overhead.

Per the above, the SCM fee ensures that the material is ready for immediate use and prevents an accumulation of surplus stocks. Thus, this SCM fee represents the vendor's cost of warehousing, and storage for materials on behalf of the Operator until the use of the material. As with other types of costs, warehousing and storage cost does not become chargeable by virtue of being outsourced. The costs incurred will always be overhead in nature, and covered by the overhead rate, regardless of whether they are incurred by a vendor or the Operator directly.

Furthermore, the Operator cited provision from the Feb 2019 Letter Agreement covering 3rd party project management costs. Sumitomo is a manufacturer, importer, and supplier of tubular and other tangible materials. It is not a management nor consultancy firm and do not provide project management services. Therefore, the fees here are not 3rd party project management costs but are material storage costs and consignment fees. These are not ancillary costs and are not allowable under the Feb 2019 Letter Agreement or the UOA.

Full credit remains due.

022.short_description: Boats - May 2022 OSV Standby Allocation Error
022.description:
The auditor noted in IR53 several discrepancies with the way Voyage Standby Allocations are being calculated, specifically with regards to hours for voyages without standby time not being excluded from the allocation base in 2022. In May 2022, the Operator included a total of 554.06 hours in the allocation base from Ursa orders 61466737 and 62165854 for voyages that did not have applicable standby time. These hours should have been left out of the allocation base, along with hours for voyages without standby time applicable to all other assets. The auditor has recalculated the OSV Standby time for May 2022 (please refer to tab "OSV Marine data") by removing hours for all vessels for which standby time did not apply. Doing so changes the allocation base from 5,773.62 to 3,103.75 hours, and Ursa's portion from 555.34 to 1.28 hours.

The majority of the impact is due to 390 hours from Harvey Intervention voyages that did not contribute standby costs but also should have been left out of the allocation base as it did not service any other assets in May or June 2022 and appears to have b een dedicated to Ursa during this time frame in support of the 2022 TAR. Per the Operator's Vessel Allocation Procedures, on Dedicated Spot Hires, the asset/project would receive all the charges, including standby time, but the working hours for this vessel would not count in the monthly standby allocation, as this asset is already paying all the costs.

The difference between the charge and the auditor's calculation for what should have been charged to Ursa is $241,020.70.

$11,476.58 was originally charged to WBS O.US.342.342.342.713000. The allocated charges were received through O.US.REV.RC1.016.321277 and O.US.REV.RC1.016.324261. Additionally, $230,581.97 was charged through order 61466737 (WBS P.US.URS.EW.20.07.7240A) and received through C.US.URS.FI.20.003.1230A.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $172,699.86 ($152,830.25 plus $19,869.61 overhead). See calculations on JADE file.

The procedure adhered to the COPAS standards outlined in MFI 45 for offshore marine and aircraft allocation. The Flexible Pool Method allocates offshore transportation costs to locations based on the actual services utilized during the month. It is particularly effective when multiple locations are involved, ensuring that only those receiving the service are charged.

业

## 2. Flexible Pool Method

The Flexible Pool Method allocates the cost of offshore transportation to locations based upon actual service received during the month. This allocation method is appropriate in cases where offshore transportation service is provided to more than one location and the desired outcome is to charge only those properties that actually use the service during the month. The locations serviced form a flexible pool that may expand during the allocation period as operational needs dictate. This approach is preferred where the establishment of a fixed allocation pool may not be suitable or equitable because locations are not receiving consistent service each month.

The Flexible Pool Method can be applied in various ways. Below are three versions, which illustrate its use:

- Standby to All Locations
- Standby to Selected Locations
- Selected Standby to Selected Locations

The Operator's response does not address the issue at hand, which is: Why are voyages, such as the Harvey Intervention, included in the base when they specifically service URSA during the time period?

MFI-45 notes that "Consideration should be given to the particular reason why a vessel or aircraft is on standby" and depending on the circumstances surrounding the vessel's inactivity, segregate the job specific from the non-job specific standby time. In this exception, we noted that the exception stems from the inclusion of the Harvey Intervention into the standby allocation pool. Given that the Harvey Intervention only served URSA, it is job-specific and should be excluded from the pool.

Furthermore, MFI-45 notes that the Flexible Pool Method is appropriate "in cases where offshore transportation service is provided to more than one location and the desired outcome is to charge only those properties that actually use the service during the month". Again, note that the Harvey Intervention only served URSA and therefore should not be part of the pool. By including the Harvey Intervention and other voyages that were job specific in the standby allocation pool, the properties which had paid for dedicated boat services are unfairly burdened by the standby costs of boats/voyages which they did not benefit from.

Lastly, the allocation methodology used here did not adhere to the Operator's Vessel Allocation Procedures, which notes that on Dedicated Spot Hires, the asset/project would receive all the charges, including standby time, but the working hours for this vessel would not count in the monthly standby allocation, as this asset is already paying all the costs.

The exception remains open and credit remains due.

035.short_description: Boats - June 2022 OSV Standby Allocation Error
035.description:
The auditor noted in IR53 several discrepancies with the way Voyage Standby Allocations are being calculated, specifically with regards to hours for voyages without standby time not being excluded from the allocation base in 2022. The auditor has recalculated the OSV Standby time for June 2022 by removing hours for all vessels for which standby time did not apply.

The auditor also found that $56,718.75 ( 24.75 hours) in standby costs for Harvey Intervention Voyage 20220658 was included in the allocation (see BW Clean tab). The allocation base also includes 437.67 in working hours for this vessel, causing a disproportionate amount of total standby time to be allocated the Ursa asset. This vessel did not service any other assets in May or June 2022 and appears to have been dedicated to Ursa during this time frame in support of the 2022 TAR. Per the Operator's Vessel Al location Procedures, on Dedicated Spot Hires, the asset/project would receive all the charges, including standby time, but the working hours for this vessel would not count in the monthly standby allocation, as this asset is already paying all the costs.

The auditor has removed the cost from the allocated amount and has also excluded the working hours from the allocation and requests that the $56,718.75 standby cost be charged directly to the Ursa asset.

Additionally, $387,644.55 was charged through order 61466737 (WBS P.US.URS.EW.20.07.7240A) and received through C.US.URS.FI.20.003.1230A.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $210,733.04 ($186,489.25 plus $24,243.25 overhead). The requested credit is net of the credit due to the recalculated amount ($250,380.47) plus a debit of $39,647.43 allocated from the $56,718.75 standby cost associated with Voyage 20220658. The procedure complied with COPAS standards as specified in MFI 45 for offshore marine and aircraft allocation. Additionally, the Flexible Pool Method distributes offshore transportation costs to locations based on actual services utilized during the month, ensuring fair allocation when multiple locations are involved.

业

## 2. Flexible Pool Method

The Flexible Pool Method allocates the cost of offshore transportation to locations based upon actual service received during the month. This allocation method is appropriate in cases where offshore transportation service is provided to more than one location and the desired outcome is to charge only those properties that actually use the service during the month. The locations serviced form a flexible pool that may expand during the allocation period as operational needs dictate. This approach is preferred where the establishment of a fixed allocation pool may not be suitable or equitable because locations are not receiving consistent service each month.

The Flexible Pool Method can be applied in various ways. Below are three versions, which illustrate its use:

- Standby to All Locations
- Standby to Selected Locations

By including the Harvey Intervention and other voyages that were job specific in the standby allocation pool, the properties which had paid for dedicated boat services are unfairly burdened by the standby costs of boats/voyages which they did not benefit from.

Lastly, the allocation methodology used here did not adhere to the Operator's Vessel Allocation Procedures, which notes that on Dedicated Spot Hires, the asset/project would receive all the charges, including standby time, but the working hours for this vessel would not count in the monthly standby allocation, as this asset is already paying all the costs.

036.short_description: Boats - May and June Marine Terminal Allocation Errors
036.description:
The auditor noted in IR54 a change in the way the Marine Terminal allocations were calculated beginning in April 2023. The Operator had been including OSV and FSV Voyage Standby Allocation charges in the allocation base. The Operator had also been calculating the OSV and FSV Voyage Standby Allocation charges incorrectly by including hours in the allocation base for voyages that did not have applicable standby time. Significant impacts were noted in May 2022 and June 2022 as hours for Harvey Intervention, a vessel that was only serving Ursa at the time in support of the 2022 TAR, were also included in the allocation base. These charges were included in exceptions 22 and 35. Because the inflated OSV and FSV Voyage Standby Allocation charges from May and June 2022 were included in the base of the May and June 2022 Marine Terminal allocations, the auditor has recalculated the Marine Terminal allocations for these months to exclude OSV and FSV Voyage Standby Allocation amounts for all assets.

The auditor has not recalculated the Marine Terminal allocations for January through April 2022 or July 2022 through March 2023, other months in which the vendor included OSV and FSV Voyage Standby Allocation charges in the allocation base. It is expected that May and June 2022 had the most significant impact due to the inclusion of hours for the Harvey Intervention vessel.

For the Operator to claim that the individuals in question are Technical Employees and therefore chargeable, shows a misunderstanding of the provision.

Full credit, including the credit granted which had not yet been verified, remains due.

049.short_description: Reclassification of Shared Expenses related to replacements
049.description:
At the end of 2021, bp and Shell reached an agreement (attached) regarding the handling of bp short payments for Ursa and Crosby. As part of the close out of this matter, Shell has agreed to make accounting adjustments to AFEs noted on Table 1 for projects classified as "replacements". These adjustments are to allocate historical and future costs related to these AFE's as "Ursa TLP Shared Expenses". Final accounting adjustments were to be made no later than the January 2022 accounting month.

053.short_description: OTL Incorrectly charged to 2022 Direct Staff Labor
053.description:
On IR-12, the auditor noted that the following Offsite Technical Staff was erroneously charged to the Joint Account:

- Michael Crochet-- Lead Wellsite Supervisor (Organization: Platform Well Interventions)-- Mr. Crochet was not found on the POB for the time that he was charged to the Joint Account.

The Operator claims that he was working on a "Project Study" and therefore was chargeable per the Agreed OTL Definitions and Billing Standards as agreed with the partners.

We noted that Mr. Crochet was working on A3 Wireline Intervention project and that this project has a 13% overhead and therefore was an Operating AFE and not associated with "field improvement or facility improvements or feasibility studies undertaken to progress future projects".

In its follow-up response, the Operator contends:

Well interventions are crucial for maintaining well productivity and ensuring efficient operation, used for various tasks such as milling, debris removal, plug setting, fishing, etc., staff coordinated for the intervention activities providing the inputs and activity descriptions. Hence has time written to the A3 well is deemed to be a project study.

Based on the above follow-up response, it is clear that the project was undertaken to maintain well productivity and ensure efficient operations. The work is not deemed to be field or facility improvement nor a feasibility study.

Thus, please credit the Joint account $6420.96 plus 64.781% burden and 13% overhead for a total of $11,955.99.

replies.text:
Claim Declined,

Michael Crochet-- Lead Wellsite Supervisor, as the Job title denotes his role is Technical in nature and is Direct chargeable as per the OTL agreement. He had performed Pre-work inspection related to A3 Well Intervention project from remote site. Hence the claim of Staff not in POB is declined.

Claim Declined.

Michael Crochet-- Lead Wellsite Supervisor, as the Job title denotes his role is Technical in nature and is Direct chargeable as per the OTL agreement. He had performed Pre-work inspection related to A3 Well Intervention project from remote site.

Hence the claim of Staff not in POB is declined.

We do not disagree that Mr. Crochet is a technical employee. However, not all offsite technical labor (OTL) is chargeable per the 2018 settlement agreement. Only OTL who fall under the following categories are chargeable.

- a. Regulatory Activity
- b. Feasibility and Project Studies
- c. Planners, Schedulers, maintenance and TAR, rig administration

During fieldwork, in its response to our IR, the Operator had claimed that Mr. Crochet falls under the 2nd category above (Feasibility and Project Studies), but we note that since the project he was charged to was operational in nature (with a 13% overhead), then he wasn't working on a feasibility or project study.

In its latest response, the Operator's claims that since Mr. Crochet is OTL, therefore he is chargeable. This line of reasoning is not in accordance with the 2018 agreement. We again request the Operator to explain why it believes (based on their IR response) that Mr. Crochet is chargeable under Feasibility and Project Studies when he was working on an Operational project.

Credit remains due.

In its response, the Operator contends that since these employees were charged to the URSA home cost center and that they are technical labor, they are allowed to be direct charged to the Joint Account.

Regardless of which cost center an employee is charged, his work is chargeable only if it benefitted the Joint Property. An employee's "home" cost center is not proof that his work benefitted the Joint Property. We looked for this benefit when we examined the POB and since we did not find them onsite during the period for which they were charged, we requested additional information to make a determination of chargeability.

The Operator's claim that these technical employees were supporting the Joint Property remotely overlooks the 2018 Settlement Agreement requirement that Offsite Technical Labor is only chargeable when performing regulatory work, feasibility or project studies, or planning and scheduling for maintenance, TAR, or rig administration.

The Operator's response did not provide additional information as to the nature of these employees' work and how they are chargeable. Therefore exception remains open until we acquire additional information on the 11 employees in question.

061.short_description: Insufficient backup for Partner Direct charges
061.description:
BP was charged a total of $544,698.23 net on its partner direct JADE. The backup attached to the journal entry shows that a total of $1,310,919 was charged to bp, XOM, and CoP in proportion to their working interests. It appears that this is a reclassification of 2021, 2022, and 2023 non-billable labor and its corresponding burden and overhead to billable labor/burden/overhead. However, the attached backup does not show which employees are being reclassified from nonbillable to billable. On IR-10, we requested the Operator to provide backup that identifies the employees being charged and how they benefitted the Joint Property.

In its response, the Operator provided a workbook showing the calculation of the partner direct charges. Per the Operator, these represent the billing out of unbilled staff costs related to the URSA Staff Home cost center (101045). The Operator also provided a list of staff who were tagged to URSA Staff home cost center on the same workbook.

We compared the list of employees provided on the workbook with direct labor charges and the PoB and noted the following (see notes on blue tabs on the file called "L&B workings 21-23 with EPS comments"):

- a. There are several employees who had already been charged as Direct Labor to the Joint Account.
- b. Several employees were only on the Joint Property during parts of the year and/or were on locations other than the Joint Property during parts of the year.
- c. A few employees were not found on the POB for the entire year.

Thus, we are unable to confirm that these partner direct charges relate to employees' work for the Joint Property.

We requested the Operator to provide details regarding which employees these partner direct charges are specifically for and for which time period so that we can ascertain that these charges benefitted Ursa. This follow-up request has not been fulfilled at the end of fieldwork.

Furthermore, we also requested the Operator to explain why its system of charging Labor over/under would not have already charged any employees' time which had not been timewritten. Per the description provided to us in the Audit Manual, it appears that if hours timewritten do not match actual hours worked or the tariff charged do not match the actual labor rate, then the system would have already automatically charged these out in Labor over/under, making a manual entry charging any unbilled labor costs unnecessary. We have not received an explanation for this query as of the end of fieldwork.
