However, the following are unclear to us:

- a. It appears that certain costs are allocated from O.US.175.MAR.GEN.724FP, O.US.175.MAR.GEN.71300, and O.US.175.MAR.PLF.71300. But these WBS include costs other than just Hoist and Lifting Equipment. Please explain why costs from these WBS are being allocated as Mars Crane Allocation.
- b. Please explain how the remaining costs in the 3 WBS's noted above are being allocated.
- c. It appears that in general, 80% of the costs identified to be allocated were allocated to Mars. Please explain the basis of allocation.

In response, the Operator provided an email from an accountant that notes that per the Mars COA ( Concurrent Operating Cost Allocation Matrix) crane expenses are to be allocated 80% to drilling codes and 20% are to be retained in Operations.

- a. Please explain what the COA is? Is this a Shell internal cost allocation matrix?

b. It appears that certain line items, including labor costs, are pegged to Mars based on their "functional locations". Please explain how functional location is determined for cost items since this information does not appear to be available in the cost report of the originating WBS. (we have attached the cost report for O.US.175.MAR.GEN.724FP to show that we were unable to find the "functional location which appears to be the key to identifying Mars related crane expenses). The below snippet was attached to the SAP documentation.

The Operator is requested to provide the information requested in follow-up questions a. and b. or credit the Joint Account $1,152,971.53 plus 2.5% overhead for the unsupported charges.

replies.text:
a. The COA (Concurrent Operating Cost Allocation Matrix) is cost allocation methodology used to allocate shared operating costs across concurrent activities such as drilling, production, and construction. For crane costs, charges are initially booked to Operations (Opex) and then allocated based on the COA, under which crane expenses related to drilling activities are allocated 80% to drilling (Capex) and 20% retained in Operations.

b. Mars crane charges are initially booked to Operations using O-type (Opex) WBS elements. Mars-related crane costs are identified using established functional codes associated with the Mars asset, which are captured in the PB7 report. Functional location is not available in standard SAP line-item cost reports. As noted in the email from Balaji that the auditor attached, they maintain the list of crane functional locations and will run the PB7 report using the parameters 'C.US.MAR.FI.23.004.1230A' and 'PM: Funct. Location Des'. The functional-location list provided in that prior email is the list being used for the crane allocation. The identified Mars crane costs are then allocated from Opex to Capex in accordance with the standard 80/20 allocation methodology.

0041.short_description: Coding Error - JE - Flowline PSVs - PowerNap/Olympus
0041.description:
The Joint Account was charged $198,341.98 per the attached JADE. Based on the supporting documentation, this was a transfer from C.US.PNP.FI.23.002.1230A (Powernap Well Flowline PSVs) to C.US.MR2.FI.23.004.1230A (Olympus Well Flowline PSVs Field improvement).

There was no further documentation attached to explain why Powernap expenses were transferred to Olympus.

In IR 73 issued during fieldwork, the Operator was requested to provide documentation to substantiate that the Joint Property benefitted from these expenditures.

In its response, the Operator claimed that the flowline PSVs that were delivered and installed during the original build of OLY were made of the wrong material and therefore did not meet the process safety basic requirement for cold metal brittle fracture. Thus, it had to be replaced from a Design Integrity point of view. The Operator replaced these as part of the 2023 TAR but claimed that these were erroneously charged to Powernap. However, the Operator did not include any further documentation to corroborate this claim.

The Operator is requested to provide evidence that the flowlines which were replaced were for Olympus and not Powernap. Evidence may include documentation of discovery and subsequent replacement in Olympus.

If the Operator is unable to provide evidence that these costs are for Olympus it is requested to credit the Joint Account $198,341.98 plus Overhead.

replies.text:
Credit Denied. Below is the confirmation from the Operations manager (Igor) and attached Fit4 documentation demonstrating that the flowlines which were replaced were for Olympus and not Powernap.

## Re: Reclass from Opex to CAPEX

From Kochberger, Igor SEPCO-IUD/P/C <Igor.Kochberger@shell.com>

Date Wed 9/27/2023 7:53 PM

To Benedict, Gary SEPCO-FIU/DGM <Gary.Benedict@shell.com>

Cc KV, Sivakaamu SSSCCH-FO/RUG <Sivakaamu.KV@shell.com>

Hi Gary,

Happy to provide context. Sometime in 2022 (could even have been late 2021) we found out that the flowline PSVs that were delivered and installed during the original build of OLY were made of the wrong material. This meant that they did not meet the process safety basic requirement for cold metal brittle fracture (I believe PSBR8) and had to be replaced from an Design Integrity point of view. Not meeting a PSBR is deemed a significant risk which had to be signed off by Colette while we were awaiting the change out to PSVs with the correct material specs.

We then went ahead and replaced these as part of the 2023 TAR and in my mind we should've always carried them as CAPEX given the flowchart and the above.

Hoping this suffices but happy to provide more details if needed.

Thanks, Igor

In Information Request 46, issued during the fieldwork, the Operator was requested to provide the asset utilization report for all assets for the entire audit period (i.e. all 2024) so the auditors could determine that the allocation of costs was fair and correct, and that the allocation was not over 100%.

The Operator was unable to provide the requested asset utilization report by the end of fieldwork. Accordingly, the Operator is requested to provide the complete asset utilization report for all assets for all months under audit, or credit the Joint Account $154,157.09 for the unsupported storage costs.

0046.description:
The Joint Account was charged costs from Partner object O.US.175.MAR.GEN.724FP per the JADE lines noted on "IR 53 JADE", tab "receiving JADE". The auditors ran the cost object report for O.US.175.MAR.GEN.724FP and noted that 100% of the cost from this partner object were charged to Mars. Information Request 53 was issued during the fieldwork, requesting the Operator provide additional details. On the tabs of the "IR 53 JADE" file, the auditors noted the invoices that were tested, and which are the subject of IR53.

Testing revealed issues with 3 vendors:

- a. Bilfinger-- The Operator did not address questions with the vendor Bilfinger regarding the invoices related to TRACK numbers 6996052, 7040972, and 6995948. As noted in the IR, these invoices do not show any indication that these charges were incurred for Mars. The Operator was not able to provide additional evidence to prove that these expenditures are for Mars by the end of fieldwork. Credit due $85,862.94 including 13% OH
- b. Can USA-- Per the report provided by the Operator, TRACK numbers 6853015, 6411026,6872718, 6411035,6411836 pertain to "Equipment". The Operator is requested to provide actual invoices to substantiate that these equipment items were used for the Joint Property. The line items in question are marked up in yellow and green on the file called "CAN USA IR#53 response". Credit due $134,744.18 including 13% OH
- c. GIS-- Track numbers 6407510, 6407516, 6418299, 6407513, 6407518, 6418301, 6418300, 6407520, 6407498 pertain to labor charges for the individuals listed on tab "Alloc JADE--GIS" on the file called "IR#53 JADE updated". All of these individuals, except for Jeff Oglee were not on the Joint Property for the time period charged. (late Dec 2023). Please explain why these labor costs are chargeable per the Mars UOP and/or the 2019 Letter Agreement. Credit due $32,061.40 including 13% OH

The Operator is requested to provide supporting invoices and other documentation/explanation as outlined above or credit the Joint Account $252,668.52 including 13% OH for the unsupported charges. Please see accompanying file "Exc 46 Allocated Charges final.xlsx"

The Operator is requested to provide third party documentation or support such as invoices for the remainder of the charges in question, or credit the Joint Account $115,520.73 plus 13% OH for the unsupported charges.

0051.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $154,157.09 for Houma DC storage costs according to the attached JADE lines.

These charges were based on the Operator's calculation of depreciation, taxes and other costs, multiplied by the occupied sq.ft. as noted/requested in Exception 46 of this report. While the aforementioned costs are allowed per the JOA, there is an upper limit established by Section 7.A. of the JOA which states that " ...shall not exceed average commercial rates currently prevailing in the immediate area of the Joint Property".

7. Equipment and Facilities Furnished by Operator

This upper limit of rates was established by the table below, taken from the current audit.

Explanation of this table was provided in previous audits, namely 2022 Mars (2022SOV\_E104) Information Request 30 where the Operator explained that these were the market rates for space at facilities equivalent to the Houma DC. See below Operator response from same:

These rates establish the "average commercial rates currently prevailing in the immediate area of the Joint Property" as contemplated by the JOA.

As the Operator has not provided the square footage utilization reports in response to Exception 46 at the time of writing, the Non-Operator is unable to determine the correct charges, and importantly, the upper limit thereto.

At this time, the Non-Operator takes exception to all charges ($154,157.09 plus 2.5% OH) for the Houma DC pending the Operator providing the asset utilization reports requested in Exception 46 so that the correct upper limit can be calculated and compared against the actual charges to the Joint Account.

replies.text:
The Operator notes that the Houma DC costs charged to the Mars Joint Account were allocated using the same methodology previously discussed during the 2022 Mars audit (Exception 6). Under that audit, the Operator explained that Houma DC costs are allocated based on occupied square footage applied to market-based commercial rates for comparable facilities, consistent with Section 7.A of the Joint Operating Agreement, which limits charges to 'average commercial rates currently prevailing in the immediate area of the Joint Property.'

The Operator further notes that this allocation methodology was reviewed with BP during the February 2025 face-to-face meeting between the parties. At that meeting, the Operator outlined the continued use of market-based rates and square footage utilization as the basis for allocating Houma DC costs to the Mars Joint Account. No objection to the methodology was raised at that time, and no alternative allocation basis was proposed.

Accordingly, the Houma DC costs reflected in the current audit period were allocated using the same methodology previously discussed with BP and consistent with prior audit explanations. The Operator has provided one month of square footage utilization information to support verification of the charges, as the asset utilization each month does not swing significantly, these reports involve information for other assets, the Operator considers that these reports do not add additional value for Mars, the allocation methodology applied to be consistent with the JOA and prior audit discussions.

08/12/2025:

The costs in the question are directly related to the technical expertise which includes

-  The Underwater Inspections/In Service Inspection Plan for the asset
-  Post hurricane damage assessments

The technical labor is critical in properly carrying out these tasks. These are not related to administrative costs.

The Operator did not provide a name or job title of any individual performing these activities, nor did it address that "Project Services" is not technical in nature, and therefore this is not technical labor.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $67,998.01 plus 13% OH for the administrative labor covered by Overhead

Credit Denied. Gibson Applied Technology and Engineering (GATE) provides specialized technical labor that directly drives subsea integrity and inspection decision-making. GATE's personnel apply expert judgment based on extensive experience with subsea construction, installation, and offshore component performance to assess observed conditions, identify potential failure modes, and determine whether repair, cleaning, or enhanced inspection is required. Their work involves evaluating structural, corrosion, and protection risks in complex subsea environments and adjusting inspection scope based on technical findings. These activities are essential technical deliverables that materially contribute to the safety, integrity, and long-term operability of the Mars production system. Per BP-SOI Settlement Agreement, Section 3, Paragraph l, 'Third-Party Project Management - Ancillary costs related to third party project management that are charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services by such third party associated with a third party's provision of goods and services may be charged to the Joint Account as a component cost of the underlying goods and services and shall not be qualified as OTL or as administrative costs covered under Overhead.' The project management component is part of the cost of the technical services delivered and is therefore chargeable to the Joint Account.

In addition, the 67,998.01 USD in JADE already represents the totals (60,175.23 USD subtotal + 7,822.78 USD at 13% OH), and the auditor's calculation adds Overhead a second time, inflating it to 76,837.75 USD

0003.short_description: Tenaris Rig Direct Charges Covered by Overhead
0003.description:
The Operator charged the Joint Account $328,445.95 in Rig Direct Surcharge fees (marked as "price surcharge of 6.5%") on multiple Tenaris invoices per the attached JADE. In IR 13, the Operator was requested to provide a copy of the contract relating to these fees. According to the vendor contract snippet provided below, these fees cover "Demand Sync, Logistics to Patterson, Storage + Maint. + WK, and Pipe Management Services".

- 3.2 Rig Direct Rate: is defined as percentage of Product Price and applicable to take out quantities, to be included in the PO prior to dispatch to the well.

*Ownership of Damaged Pipes after Rig Return CONTRACTOR

L

x

Included

Not included

Excluded from rate but accounted in credit note based on Rig Return quantities

The Tenaris website noted that "Demand Sync" is a process where "The production and management of pipes and accessories are scheduled according to customer drilling needs to minimize inventories and waste". This function is a form of supply chain integration and is administrative and management in nature. "Storage + Maint. + WK" are various warehousing and inventory carrying costs, as is "Pipe Management Fee". All of these "rig direct" fees are covered by the Overhead rate reimbursed to the Operator and not directly changeable to the Joint Account.

Exhibit 'C' Section III Overhead of the Unit Operating Agreement states: "As compensation for administrative, supervision, office services and warehousing costs, Operator shall charge the Joint Account in accordance with this Section III.'

Additionally, MFI 19, Section IV.3.C states 'Actual costs may include costs of (I) Material, (2) making it suitable for use, and (3) transportation from the point of acquisition to the Joint Property including loading and unloading. Not included are storage or carrying costs."

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account for $328,445.95 plus overhead of 2.5%. for the fee which is not directly chargeable.

replies.text:
Credit denied.

Tenaris provides rig direct / pipe management services, which include in-yard movement, inspection, tally, and preparation of pipes for running. They also provide technical services to reduce operational risk and optimize running times by ensuring the right practices are followed and products are installed at the rig site.

According to Section 3 Billing Disputes Paragraph l of the BP-SOI Settlement Agreement dated December 2018, Ancillary costs related to third-party project management that are charged as part of the overall cost for provision of goods and services by such third party associated with a third party's provision of goods and services may be charged to the Joint Account as a component cost of the underlying goods and services. Tenaris's fee is a component cost of the underlying goods and services, and it does not qualify as administrative costs covered under Overhead.

In its response, the Operator contends that:

Generally, team leads are not recognized as second-level supervisors if their role is primarily technical advisory rather than administrative, as typically performed by a manager. Therefore, claims are accepted only for individuals who supervise at least two levels of staff contributing time to projects."

As a result of their interpretation of the Accounting Procedure, the Operator has granted $76,871 of the total $126,098 exception.

The Accounting Procedure of the JOA does not in any way qualify that only 2nd level supervisors who "oversee two or more tiers of staff whose time is directly charged to a project" are non-chargeable. It simply states that 2nd level supervisors are not chargeable. Thus, all 2nd level supervisors are non-chargeable and a full credit of $126,098.14 plus burden and overhead or $ 217,126.55 as calculated on the attached file "IR-19 exception value".

0008.description:
Per the attached JADE lines and the attached Transocean invoices, the Joint Account was charged $882,945.00 for a Tax Cuts & Jobs Act (TCJA) Tax Rebill in 2024.

This Act reduced the top corporate income tax rate from 35 to 21 percent and increased investment incentives by making equipment investment fully tax-deductible.

The Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT) was introduced as part of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017. Its purpose is to discourage large multinational corporations from stripping earnings out of the United States into lower-tax jurisdictions by targeting deductible payments made to foreign affiliates.

BEAT functions as a corporate minimum tax. A company calculates its regular tax liability and then performs a separate BEAT calculation. If the BEAT liability is higher, the company must pay the difference as an additional tax. This system ensures that corporations with significant payments to foreign related parties pay a minimum level of U.S. tax.

By adding back certain deductible payments made to foreign affiliates when calculating this alternative tax, the provision neutralizes the tax benefit of shifting profits offshore. The BEAT applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2017.

When questioned about the "TCJA Tax Rebill" costs being billed on the Transocean invoices attached and their chargeability to the URSA Joint Account, the Operator replied as follows:

Transocean completed an organizational restructuring in 2019 and an associated amendment was signed at that time related to Transocean's difference in tax liability. The restructuring was related to the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) enacted in 2017. A calculation is performed to compare the estimated tax liability for the Proteus in the prior org. structure (bare boat charter - BBC structure) and the current org structure of the owner-operated model. If the tax liability is estimated to be higher in the current structure, then a variation is issued for a monthly incremental cost due to this tax impact.

The Shell-Transocean contract, signed in 2012, contains a change in law clause as we previously shared, and reproduced below for convenience:

- 16.8 Notwithstanding any other provision of the CONTRACT, if there is any change in the interpretation or application or enforcement of existing tax law or subsequent enactment of any new tax law in the COUNTRY OF OPERATION after the 31st July 2012 which, during the CONTRACT DURATION, results in a significant increase or decrease in the cost to CONTRACTOR of performing the WORK, then COMPANY shall, in consultation with CONTRACTOR and upon an open book basis, reimburse

CONTRACTOR for any increase or recover from CONTRACTOR any decrease in the cost to CONTRACTOR of performing the WORK by means of a VARIATION.

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act enacted on December 22, 2017, introduced a Base Erosion anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT), and effectively applied a 5-12.5% tax on any lease payments to foreign affiliates (which would include the day rates payable to Transocean). Transocean notified Shell that the rig rates had to be adjusted to reflect the impact of the BEAT under the change in law clause - specifically, because of the changes in the Federal tax law that came about as the result of the 2018 tax bill, there will be an increas e in CONTRACTOR'S costs due to said change in tax law, to be reimbursed by Shell (and therefore it's co -owners) pursuant to Article 16.8. The subsequent restructuring undertaken by Transocean was to mitigate the expected cost increases due to BEAT. Had Transocean not taken these steps, the costs borne by the co-owners would have been greater, as the cost of mitigating the BEAT are less than the underlying Transocean BEAT exposure, leaving Shell and its co-owners in a better position.

As such, the cost incurred to reimburse Transocean for the BEAT is incurred under the terms and conditions of the contract. The subject operating agreement under this audit (including industry practice and COPAS accounting guidance) allow for Shell to pass on to its co-owners these costs, whether they are either (i) the Transocean BEAT or (ii) costs associated with mitigating the Transocean BEAT. Furthermore, the Operator is entitled to pass on costs as they are incurred and billed to Shell. The dates of the law enactment and subsequent restructuring are immaterial, rather the date when Transocean receives a tax-related invoice that can be passed to Shell under the contract as first time charges that were not previously received are determinative. Accordingly, Shell billed these costs to the co-owners as it was incurred by Shell.

We disagree with the Operators interpretation that these BEAT costs, applicable to income taxes, are billable to the URSA Joint Account. There is nothing in any of the COPAS Model Form Interpretations (MFIs) that allows income taxes by themselves, or additional costs incurred to reduce income taxes of a vendor as being chargeable. In addition, this is not industry practice since this is the first time we have seen any Operator pass on this type of costs to the Joint Account. Even though Shell may have an agreement between Transocean and themselves that makes these costs chargeable to themselves, there is nothing in the Accounting Procedure that makes these taxes chargeable to the URSA Joint Account.

Please credit the Joint Account $882,945 plus 2.5% overhead or a total of $905,018.63.

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) represent a cost imposed on the operator, and Section 10 has a broad scope that encompasses such taxes. These taxes are necessarily incurred by the operator to source and maintain rig operations and therefore are appropriately chargeable.

The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act enacted on December 22, 2017, introduced a Base Erosion anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT), and effectively applied a 5-12.5% tax on any lease payments to foreign affiliates (which would include the day rates payable to Transocean). 0027.short_description: Shell Trading Diesel Invoices Priced With Markup Over Market & Coding Error
0027.description:
1. Various Shell Trading Company invoices totaling $8,300,321.42, were charged to the Ursa Joint Accounts for fuel oil using a market index price plus a mark-up (differential) rate of $.15 to $.35 per gallon depending on the time period and property. On the attached file called "Exception 27 JADE", a schedule is provided calculating this differential amount to be $720,714.10

Pursuant to the four attached invoices charging fuel oil (Shell Trading Invoices 15104770, 15492229, 15492230, 15741130) for the drill ships, the URSA Joint Account is being charged a differential of $.15 to $.35 per barrel for fuel oil plus a market index (i.e. PLT\_USGC\_ULSD\_WB\_15ppm/PLATTS-Mid). Please provide support from Shell Trading Company that this is the actual cost without mark-up for these purchases or proof that this is a competitive market price for the area. The Operator is also requested to explain what the differential is for and why it is added to the market index for pricing.

Pursuant to COPAS MFI #18, Interpretation, "The purpose of Labor, Materials and 'Equipment and facilities" provisions in the COPAS Accounting Procedure forms is to assure the Operator's employees, material purchased from outside sources and any equipment of facilities which are owned by the Operator and serve the Joint Property are charged to the Joint Account at actual cost, without mark-up ."

2. In addition, pursuant to Shell Trading Invoice 15104770, the Joint Account was charged $855,283.33 for bunker freight applicable to M/V HOS RUNNING BUCK delivered to the Globetrotter II. In the Operator's response to IR-30, the Operator said the following:

There were two delivery attempts for this fuel bunkering. The rig had concerns with the fuel quality with the first delivery, even though testing confirmed it met specifications.

Although testing confirmed the fuel met specifications, STUSCO agreed to use the fuel at a different rig and deliver another load of fuel to the rig, Globetrotter 2.

Pursuant to support provided (file called "Contract snippet and Calculation") by the Operator for the calculation of the $855,283.33 bunker freight charge mentioned above, it was indicated that $746,833.33 was delivered to another rig. Therefore, an additional $746,833.33 is due the URSA Joint Account for this coding error.

Finally, again reference is made to IR-030, where it was requested that the Operator provide support for the bunker freight charge on Shell Trading Invoice 15104770 totaling $855,283.33 that would show the actual cost for M/V HOS RUNNING BUCK billed by Hornbeck Offshore to Shell Trading. Please note that this support was not provided by the Operator as of the end of audit fieldwork.

Credit is requested for the price differential portion of this exception totaling $720,714.10 plus the $746,833.33 coding error for a cumulative total of $1,467,547.43 plus 2.5% overhead.

replies.text:
Credit denied.

The auditor characterizes the differential of $0.15-$0.35 per gallon as an impermissible mark-up. This characterization is incorrect.

The pricing applied by Shell Trading (STUSCO) reflects a market index (PLATTS) plus commercially necessary components. The $0.15 -$0.35 per gallon differential is not a markup but a necessary cost to meet the required fuel specifications for MODU operations. The index price reflects Colonial 62 grade diesel, which does not meet MODU standards specifically, flash point (125.8°F vs. 140°F minimum) and viscosity (1.9 cSt @ 40°C vs. 2 cSt @ 40°C).

Under the Accounting Procedure and COPAS MFI-18, the requirement is that materials be charged at actual cost incurred, not that all components must equal a single observable index price. The PLATTS index represents a benchmark price, not the delivered transaction cost. The differential reflects real, incurred commercial costs necessary to procure and deliver fuel to offshore operations, and therefore forms part of the actual cost to the Operator.

With respect to Shell Trading Invoice 15104770 ($855,283.33), there were two delivery attempts. During the initial attempt to Globetrotter II (NGT2), the fuel was rejected by the rig due to quality concerns.

The bunker freight associated with this first delivery attempt amounted to $746,833.33. Following the rejection, the vessel returned to Port Fourchon, and the fuel was subsequently redirected to another rig. As such, the $746,833.33 represents costs incurred in attempting delivery to NGT2 and is therefore a valid charge.

It is further noted that the URSA Joint Account was not charged the full $746K. Charges were applied only in proportion to the volume consumed by the asset. Out of the total purchased quantity of 646,077 gallons per the STUSCO invoice, only 398,427 gallons were consumed by URSA.

Please refer to the supporting details provided in the 'Rig Fuel Workings' file submitted under IR-30.

0028.error_type: 06 Costs Included in Administrative Overhead Fee O.US.342.342.342.71300/Perform Well and Facility Ope-3003423A30
0028.description:
Pursuant to Corporate Events & Occasions invoice no. 4266 dated July 2, 2024 the URSA Joint Account was charged a total of $154,925.26 for a URSA Family Day 2024 in Gulf Shore Alabama. Pursuant to IR-058 the following questions were asked and were still outstanding at the end of audit fieldwork:

1. What Shell meeting took place at the event and how did they benefit all of the URSA Partners?
2. What percent of the event was actually spent in meetings?
3. Who attended this event?
4. Please provide an itemized copy of all the expenses charged on this invoice.
5. This invoice was for an estimated amount and not for the actual expenses. Please provide a copy of these actual expenditures.

As a result, this Open IR-058 has been written as an audit exception for the following reasons:

Pursuant to MFI-21, specifically Section II- B.3 Direct vs Indirect Costs- Personal Expenses states in regard to reimbursable travel, meal and lodging, Operator's employees whose salary and wages are directly chargeable to the Joint Account may, in the course of performing their assigned duties, incur personal "out of pocket" expenses that are chargeable.

Operators' employees whose salary and wages are directly chargeable to the Joint Account may, in the course of performing their assigned duties, incur personal "out of pocket" expenses. Such costs normally are Direct Charges to the Joint Account and should be allocated consistent with the salary and wages of the employee who incurs them.

Since this event included employees' spouses and children and was not primarily performed in regard to the employee's assigned duties, it is not chargeable to the URSA Joint Account and covered by the overhead charge.

In addition, MFI-19 states, specifically Section II.3 Direct Charges-Employee Benefits, Costs which primarily beneficial to the Operator should be excluded from employee benefits and treated as overhead. Such costs to be borne by the Operator would include safety awards, service awards, social functions and dinners and programs for retirements.

Costs which are primarily beneficial to the Operator should be excluded from employee benefits an treated as overhead, for which the Operator is compensated under the provisions of Section III. This event is a social function and primarily benefited the Operator and is therefore not chargeable.

Therefore, credit is requested for this $154,925.26 charge plus 2.5% overhead of $3,873.13 for a total of $158,798.39.

0032.short_description: Noble Globetrotter II Inspection and Repair Expenditures Prior to Use
0032.description:
Per the attached JADE lines, the URSA Joint Account was charged a total of $13,965,823.95 for various expenditures applicable to BOP repairs and UWILD-5-year maintenance performed on the Globetrotter II from December 23, 2023 to January 20, 2024 prior to the drilling of the URSA UI5 well. We examined the AFE C.US.URS.PD.22.007.0942A for URSA UI5 Yellow Drilling and there was no specific mention of /authorization for a 5-year UWILD or major maintenance needed for the rig. Thus, we requested the Operator to explain why such major maintenance costs for the Globetrotter II, performed prior to drilling, were being charged to the Joint Account.

In its response, the Operator indicated that a majority of these repairs were needed for the SSBOP Maintenance which is normal maintenance for the NGT2 between wells because the rig only has one SSBOP which requires maintenance between wells before it is ready to deploy on the next well. So, this is normal maintenance and there was no specific event or incident that caused this maintenance to be required. In addition, the Operator indicated the critical path operation on the rig was the SSBOP In Between Well Maintenance (IBWM), which is required before the rig can start well work. The Operator noted that UWILD was performed as a concurrent operation to the IBWM, and that the Noble invoice doesn't include any additional costs associated with the UWILD.

It is the URSA Non-Operator Partner's position that these expenditures were primarily for the 5-year UWILD (Underwater Inspection in Lieu of Dry-Docking) and not the normal BOP maintenance between wells, and the Noble daywork invoices do apply to the 5-year UWILD. Please see the Daily Drilling Reports for the UI5 well, and the invoice support behind Noble invoices II9700067 and II9700058. The normal maintenance on the BOP between wells would not have taken 28 days by itself. This UWILD is required for the vessel to remain compliant with Coast Guard and/or ABC Certification.

In addition, reference is made to Technip Invoice 93001233, where the URSA Joint Account was charged $64,658.00 for ROV service for a BOP changeout. BOP changeout would not be normal BOP maintenance. The combination of the BOP changeout as well as a 5-year UWILD makes these expenditures major rig maintenance that normally would be, according to industry practice, amortized to all future wells used by the rig.

We had requested for the lease term of the Noble GT2 in IR #5. In response, the Operator provided us with this snippet:

In the above snippet, a reference was made to a contract dated June 25, 2010, between Shell EP Wells and assigned to Shell Offshore on July 25, 2019. Furthermore, the Operator highlights in yellow what it claims to be the commencement date of the contract as starting on September 10, 2013, and ending May 2, 2024.

It is not equitable to charge the URSA Joint Account for the entire cost of the 5-year UWILD or for the BOP changeout. Even if the end date of the GT2 contract was May 2, 2024, URSA should not be penalized for being the last well drilled before demobilization of the NGT2 and charged for 100% of these expenditures. If the Operator approves the use of the GT2 on URSA knowing that there is significant maintenance necessary that will benefit future use after URSA, then they had made this decision as a company and not as an Operator, as agreeing to pay for these major maintenance will preclude Noble from including the costs of such major repairs in their rig rates.

In addition to the rig costs shown on the JADE, we have collected and documented other costs related to the performance of the UWILD which were charged to the Joint Account. These are documented on the file called PE32 JADE and invoices are attached accordingly. Furthermore, we have segregated the costs related to the UWILD vs routine bop maintenance and shown these on the same file. Based on our calculations, a credit of $10,408,288.32 is due to the Joint Account plus overhead.

table_references.summary:
## Summary

This table contains operational log entries from a marine drilling/maintenance operation recorded at two time intervals (12:00 and 18:00), each spanning 6-hour periods with **RMI/RMN crew designations**. The 12:00 entry documents telescopic joint maintenance, a successful subsea pump pressure test (500 psi/15 mins), and notes diving operations were suspended due to unfavorable sea conditions (5 ft waves, 18-knot NNW winds). The 18:00 entry covers continued mechanical work including TJ packer torquing, kelly hose installation, and high-pressure testing (15,000 psi/5 mins), while reporting completion progress on key maintenance milestones: **BOP maintenance at 86%** (est. completion 1/17/2024), rig floor IBWM at **95%** (est. 1/16/2024), and UVMILD at **83%** (est. 1/18/2024).

replies.text:
Credit denied.

The Operator rejects the proposed reclassification. The costs in question were necessary, operationally driven expenditures incurred to ensure the rig and BOP system were fit-for-purpose for the URSA UI005 well and are therefore properly chargeable to the Joint Account.

Based on discussions with the BOP engineers and a review of the daily operations report, three activities occurred during the Ursa UI005 drilling period: In Between Well Maintenance (IBWM), BOP maintenance and testing, and UWILD inspection. These activities were conducted as part of standard rig readiness operations and were extended to 28 days due to weather delays, as evidenced in the daily operations reports.

Please see the snippet from the daily operations report dated January 15, 2024 as an example.

[table 1]

The costs meet the governing standard of direct attribution to the operation, the work performed was required to restore and verify BOP system integrity, complete required testing and readiness activities and ensure safe commencement of URSA UI005.

The Auditor's assertion that the work constitutes "major maintenance" requiring amortization is unsupported. Because the activities were not undertaken as part of a planned lifecycle upgrade or fleet-level recertification program. The scope was limited to restoration and verification of operability, not enhancement or extension of asset capability. All work was executed immediately prior to and in direct support of a specific well. The presence of UWILD does not alter this conclusion. UWILD was performed concurrently with IBWM activities and did not represent an independent, cost-driving event.

The rig schedule confirms that no wells were drilled after UI005 and NGT-2 rig was released from contract immediately thereafter. The work did not generate a multi-period or campaign-level benefit. There is no reasonable basis for amortization across future operations. The Operator acted within its role to ensure safe and compliant execution of the well, not as a company incurring costs for independent commercial benefit.

Accordingly, the costs are properly chargeable to the URSA Joint Account, and the requested credit is denied in full.

0034.short_description: Globetrotter II Rig Fuel FIFO Pricing Adjustments
0034.description:
Pursuant to Shell journal entry 131895199 dated May 31, 2024, the Joint Account has been charged $912,120.91 for a rig fuel pricing adjustment as a result of a change in policy as to the way the rig fuel is priced and charged out to all of their operated properties. The Operator's explanation for the change in policy was to ensure that the fuel expenses are recorded based on the real prices paid at the time of purchase, rather than relying on an averaged figure calculated over a period of time. This approach will provide a more precise and transparent reflection of the fuel costs.

The Operator has the right to change policies, going forward, as long as the change is consistent and equitable. However, the intent of the twenty-four month allowable adjustment period within the JOA is to correct errors or mistakes, not changes in policy. Pricing fuel inventory using a weighted average price versus a FIFO price is a change in methodology and not a correction of an error or mistake.

Furthermore, it is not industry practice to retroactively adjust rig fuel pricing policies over a two-year period unless the original pricing was demonstrably incorrect or deviated from the agreed contractual terms.

During audit fieldwork and per IR-33, the Operator was requested to provide a copy of Shell's accounting policy that says that their FIFO change in rig fuel pricing is to be applied retroactively for 2 years instead of just prospectively. No policy was provided nor response received from the Operator by end of field work.

Per the reasons noted above, credit is requested for $934,923.93 ($912,120.91 plus 2.5% overhead of $22,803.02) for this improper charge.

replies.text:
Credit denied.

The Operator disagrees with the auditor's position. The change from a weighted-average inventory costing method to FIFO represents a change in accounting policy/accounting principle, not an unsupported or discretionary adjustment. Under both IFRS (IAS 8) and US GAAP (ASC 250), changes in accounting principle are generally required to be applied retrospectively unless retrospective application is impracticable. In this case, the necessary historical information was available for the relevant twoyear period, and retrospective application was practical and supportable. FIFO also provides a more reliable and relevant basis for inventory valuation because it better aligns the accounting cost flow assumption with the physical flow of materials. Accordingly, the adjustment was properly applied within the available two-year period and is consistent with the COPAS 24month adjustment principle. No credit is warranted.

0042.description:
At the end of 2021, bp and Shell reached an agreement (attached) regarding the handling of bp short payments for Ursa and Crosby. As part of the close out of this matter, Shell has agreed to make accounting adjustments to AFEs noted on Table 1 for projects classified as "replacements". These adjustments are to allocate to Kaikias, historical and future costs related to these "replacements" AFE's. These adjustments are shown on the JADE as "Ursa FIMP Replacement Shared Costs".

The agreement also notes that this methodology is to be used to categorize costs on a go-forward basis. In consultation with our Commercial team, we noted the following AFEs which are replacement in nature and therefore should have costs allocated to Kaikias as shared expenses. In examining the journal entry backups (attached) for the credits related to the cost allocation of replacement AFEs, we did not locate any adjustments made for the following AFEs:

- C.US.URS.FI.23.004.1230A VRU Bridge Crane Field Improvement
- C.US.URS.FI.24.003.1237A Ursa Yokogawa PC Upgrade Field improvement
- C.US.URS.FI.24.004.1237A Ursa FCS 102/103 Upgrade
- C.US.URS.FI.24.001.1230A URSA 45Hz ADCP Field improvement
- C.US.URS.FI.23.017.1230A Ursa Obsolete ASD Upgrades Field improvement

Furthermore, we noted that the costs being shared with Kaikias for several AFEs did not align with the costs being charged to the Joint Account in 2024. These include costs for the following AFEs:

- C.US.URS.FI.22.003.1237A Ursa HVAC Obsolescence & Rel Field improvement
- C.US.URS.FI.22.002.1237A Solar Controls Upgrade Ph3 - ZAN's Field improvement
- C.US.URS.FI.22.006.1230A Ursa Firewater Pump Replacement Field improvement
- C.US.URS.FI.23.015.1230A High end Collaboration Improvements
- C.US.URS.FI.23.012.1230A Life Extension-BSEE Submittal Field improvement
- C.US.URS.FI.23.016.1230A Inspect Tendon Top Flex Element Field improvement
- C.US.URS.FI.23.007.1230A Ursa VRU spare compressor Field improvement
- C.US.URS.FI.21.002.1230A Ursa RO Unit Upgrade LLE

Based on the calculations made on tab "replacements only" on the file called "JADE lines--shared cost credits revised", the Joint Account should be credited an additional $1,612,251.78 for cost sharing with Kaikias for the above mentioned projects.

As of the end of fieldwork, the Operator has not responded to this IR. Thus, we request the Operator to provide an explanation as to why cost sharing adjustments were not correctly made for the above AFE's or credit the Joint Account $1,612,251.78 plus 2% overhead.

Please also note that we reserve the right to ascertain the monthly Barrel Equivalent Quantity (BEQ) used to allocate the costs between URSA and Kaikias during the URSA revenue audit.

replies.text:
The matters raised in this exception relate to distinct issues. To ensure clarity, the Operator will address these items separately rather than collectively, as presented in the referenced file.

## Improvement AFEs - Credit Denied. $351,792

The characterization of these activities must be based on the nature of the work performed and the definitions set out under the Kaikias PHA. Upgrades are distinct from replacements, as they enhance functionality, capacity, or performance beyond the original design, rather than restoring an asset to its prior condition. The scope of work associated with these AFEs reflects improvements to existing assets, indicating an upgrade in nature rather than a like-for-like replacement. Accordingly, these AFEs are properly classified as upgrades under the PHA framework.

- 

C.US.URS.FI.23.004.1230A - VRU Bridge Crane Field Improvement





## Life Extension - Partial Credit Accepted. $810,980

Life Extension sharing was missed in the Q1-Q3 runs and was rectified in this quarter (Q2 2026). Amount shared with Kaikias: $810,980

Since this entry is being completed by the asset team, we will send the SAP separately once it has been posted.

## Incorrect Calculation - Credit Denied. $ 449,301

The auditors calculated the difference by taking 'Charges to Joint Account by WBS,' subtracting 'Amounts Shared with Kaikias per JE documentation,' and multiplying the result by BEQ; however, this approach overlooks the actual 'Amount shared to Kaikias (credited to Joint Account)' line included in the JE. 0043.description:
The Joint Account was allocated Marine costs from WBS O.US.342.342.342.71300 per the attached JADE lines.

We noted that there was a total of $665,752.27 (net value allocated) which pertain to "Marine reclass" per the lines shown on the 2nd tab of the JADE file.

We examined the attached "Marine Allocation" files attached for these journal entries and noted the following:

- a. There is a tab called "input" listing various line items, which are then summarized in the "Summary" sheet. However, it is unclear what these costs are for and why it is necessary to charge them to O.US.342.342.342.71300. Please explain the nature of these costs and why they are being allocated.

b. On the summary tab of the documentation, we noted that the costs from the "input" tab are then being aggregated with a monthly cost/amount of $170,000 labelled as "COA": The sum of these 2 numbers is the amount being charged to O.US.342.342.342.71300 and subsequently allocated to the Joint Account. However, it is not clear what "COA" is, where the $170k value comes from, and why it is being added to the costs from the input sheet and eventually charged to the Joint Account.

The Operator was requested to explain what these costs represent and why they are being charged to WBS O.US.342.342.342.71300 and subsequently the Joint Account.

The Operator's initial reply was as follows:

The marine cost allocation as per COA happens to standing order 62841034 which settles to WBS - O.US.342.342.342.71300.

COA stands for Concurrent operating agreement. When we have TLP rigs in platform, COA stands operative, and as per COA marine cost should be $170K.

In this case, marine cost reclassifications are made when there are no costs recorded under Production Operations, as most marine allocations have been charged to rigs. These reclasses are performed to transfer the relevant costs from rigs to operations.

This initial response of the Operator does not adequately answer our questions nor explain the process. It did not explain what the costs on the "input" listing were and why they are being allocated. The response also refers to the COA or "Concurrent Operating Agreement". But this agreement was not provided to us.

Below is the Operator's response to our follow-up questions:

- a. The input tab includes Marine-related expenses for the specified month, sourced from SAP. According to the COA, a fixed monthly amount of $170,000 is allocated as Producing Operation's share of Marine costs.
- b. Please find the below screenshot of details from COA.

Best Practice: The fixed monthly amount will be $170,000, which represents Producing Operation's share of Marine Logistics and associated terminal fees. The estimate is based standard COA allocation across Mars corridor.

The Operator's last response did not provide assurance that the charges benefitted the Joint Property:

- a. In its first response, the Operator noted that Marine costs are reclassed from rigs to Operations. How does it know which costs to transfer and to which property to transfer it to? Please provide evidence that the costs being transferred in this case to WBS O.US.342.342.342.71300 should be allocated to the Joint Account.
- b. The added-on cost of $170,000 per month of COA Marine Logistics and terminal fees appears to be an arbitrary amount that is charged to WBS O.US.342.342.342.71300 and eventually charged to the Joint Account via allocations. It appears to be a cost that is not based on actual expenditures but on a "standard" benchmark cost. We also inquired of bp's Commercial team and they are not aware of the "Concurrent Operating Agreement" (COA). Thus, it appears that the COA is not an amount agreed upon with the partners. Please provide more context and explanation regarding this process.

The Operator is requested to answer the above questions or credit the Joint Account $665,752.27 plus 13% overhead.

replies.text:
The Operator response stands same with the IR response.

In accordance with the COA, the Marine cost allocation is processed through standing order 62841034, which is subsequently settled to WBS element O.US.342.342.342.71300.

COA stands for Concurrent operating agreement. When we have TLP rigs in platform, COA stands operative, and as per COA marine cost should be $170K.

In this case, marine cost reclassifications are made when there are no costs recorded under Production Operations, as most marine allocations have been charged to rigs. These reclasses are performed to transfer the relevant costs from rigs to operations.

The Input tab captures all Marine-related expenses incurred during the relevant reporting month. These expenses are directly extracted from SAP to ensure accuracy and completeness.

As outlined in the (COA), a fixed allocation of USD 170,000 per month is assigned to Producing Operations share of Marine costs.

This is also the same COA marine reclass from Rigs to Prod Ops. As per COA we need to record $170K each month until the TLP Rig is operative and the Oct-Dec reclass is nothing, but the cost charged from A12 WBS to Prod ops.

This is legitimate cost and we see credits in Capex for this cost charge in Prod ops so no credit should be granted for BP. Hope this helps.

replies.text:
The Operator response stands same with the IR response.

We had TLP Rigs in platform (Ursa A12 activity) COA stands operative and as per COA agreement we need to charge $170K to Ops cost crediting Rig. In this case there will be no impact to BP as cost moved from Rig (Capex) to Ops cost (Opex).

COA stands for Concurrent operating agreement. When we have TLP rigs in platform, COA stands operative, and as per COA marine cost should be $170K. Below is the screenshot of details from COA for your reference.

Best Practice: The fixed monthly amount will be $170,000, which represents Producing Operation's share of Marine Logistics and associated terminal fees. The estimate is based standard COA allocatlon across Mars corridor.

0045.description:
The Joint Account was charged with $607,908.43 of direct labor for individuals who were not working on the Joint Account for the time in which they were charged, per the attached JADE lines. Their onsite locations during the time for which they charged the Joint Account are shown on column BF on the tab called "JADE lines." On a separate tab called "POB locations", we attach the documentation from the POB supporting our claim.

Please explain why these individuals were charged to the Joint Account when they were onsite another property; or credit the Joint Account $607,908.43 plus burden and overhead for a total of $1,060,319.13.

In its response, the Operator provided a workbook and noted: " we have conducted a comparison of the total monthly hours, calculated at 8 hours per day, against the hours spent at the other location. Any discrepancies or excess hours have been reviewed, and we are accepting any overcharged hours accordingly. " Based on this calculation, the Operator granted $ 67,636.92 of credits BEFORE burden and overhead.

We examined the logic of their calculations and do not agree that the credit granted is adequate. For example, taking the first person on the list: Michael Ables-- The POB shows he was at VITO whenever he is shown on the POB (snippet below).

The Operator explains their calculation of the credit (as related to January 2024 charges) for Michael Ables as such:

Ables, Michael

Based on POB, Michael was assigned to VITO from 01/10/2024 13:53 CST to 01/26/2024 13:12 CST, accounting for 17 days in January. This leaves 14 days available for allocation across other assets, including URSA. However, the total hours charged to URSA for January stand at 210 hours, which equates to approximately 26 days (assuming 8 hours/day). This results in an overlap of 12 days (~98 hours) beyond the available allocation. Accordingly, a credit of 98 hours is acknowledged and accepted for URSA. (Note by auditor-- actual credit granted was only 42 hours since the calculations used a 12 hour day instead of an 8 hour day.-- but we understand the logic being presented).

The operator does not assert that all periods during which staff were not in any specific platform are charged to URSA. The personnel in question belong to a shared resource pool, primarily from the MTAC (Maintenance, Turnaround, and Constructions) team. This team operates on a flexible assignment model, wherein staff are allocated to various projects based on operational requirements. When assigned to a specific project, their costs are directly charged to that project.

For activities supporting multiple assets, time is allocated based on individual timesheets submitted by the staff. The MTAC group records time against orders that reference CFR codes in the description field, as reflected in the Posting Object WBS/CC/OR field within JADE. These CFR codes fall under the scope of the OTA agreements.

The process of rationalizing overlapping hours is undertaken to identify the time spent on specific platforms or locations. This ensures that such time is directly charged to the respective location, rather than being distributed according to generalized percentage allocations provided by the teams.

This methodology is not flawed; rather, it represents a fair and logical approach to distinguishing total time from time spent on individual locations, in alignment with the POB.

It is incorrect to assume that any of the 210 hours charged for Michael Ables benefitted Ursa as that assumes that when he was not at VITO, that he would be working on URSA, as the calculation provided by the Operator implies. For the time charged in January or March, he was either on VITO, thus erroneously charged; or he was not onsite, thus, the Operator should explain why he is chargeable in accordance with the UOA or the 2018 letter agreement. The Operator noted in its response above that ' The MTAC group records time against orders that reference CFR codes in the description field, as reflected in the Posting Object WBS/CC/OR field within JADE. These CFR codes fall under the scope of the OTA agreements." However, an examination of the JADE lines show that there were not CFR references shown on the column Posting Object WBS/CC/OR. Furthermore, even if the group was supporting multiple assets, it appears that Mr. Ables was supporting Vito throughout the year. Thus, it is unlikely that an allocation of 14 days of his time ((210 hours less 42 hours credit granted)/12 hours per day) in January to URSA is "equitable" given that there was no evidence that he worked on URSA at all.

In its response, the Operator also provided a second example:

Bergeron, Bryan-- January charges

Bryan was assigned to MARS from 01/31/2024 08:51 CST to 02/14/2024 09:08 CST, which includes only 1 day in January. The remaining 30 days were available for allocation across multiple assets. In this case, 40 hours (5 days) were charged to URSA, which falls well within the available allocation.

Therefore, no credit is due for Bryan's January URSA charges.

This approach has been uniformly applied across all staff to identify overlapping days and validate URSA charges. It provides an unambiguous and efficient alternative to manually reviewing extensive timesheet entries, ensuring credibility and fairness in determining overcharged hours.

Again, we take issue with the logic of the calculation. The Joint Account was charged 40 hours but there is no evidence that Mr. Bergeron was working onsite the Joint Property. Thus, the Operator needs to either provide explanation as to what offsite work the employee is doing or credit the Joint Account. Simply implying that there are enough hours left in a particular month where the employee "may be working on URSA" is not enough evidence for chargeability.

In conclusion, we again assert that the employees brought forth here were not found onsite the Joint Property during the periods for which they were charged. Thus, we request the Operator to explain what work they were performing, how the work benefitted the Joint Property and if performed offsite, how their work is chargeable based on the provisions of the UOA or the 2018 Settlement Agreement.

While the Operator has already granted $ 67,636.92 BEFORE burden and overhead, unless the questions above are answered, we request a full credit of $1,060,319.13 ($607,908.43 plus burden and overhead, as calculated on JADE lines tab).

replies.text:
Claim Partly accepted for Overlapping hours,

for the details related to the Job Description, required details supporting the employee's offsite work and chargeability have been provided in the Excel workbook.

SAP doc number 133345077

replies.text:
The $1.011 million exception balance primarily relates to manual journal entries (MJEs) recorded to align costs with the appropriate WBS elements and accounting treatment prior to the Whale asset reaching First Oil. The most significant balances are reclassification entries across multiple WBS elements, including:

C.US.WHL.PD.21.004.1230J - $1.800 million

C.US.WHL.PD.21.002.1230F - ($1.290 million)

O.US.WHL.772.001.724FP - ($1.028 million)

C.US.WHL.PD.21.004.1230J - $0.930 million

During fieldwork, auditors had access to both the sending and receiving WBS elements, enabling review of the underlying transactions supporting these reclassifications. To further support the current rebuttal, employee-level detail has been provided for time-writing reclassifications, and the top balance components for the remaining reclassifications have been included where invoice-level detail is not readily available.

The remaining ($1.1 million) balance on C.US.WHL.PD.21.002.1230B relates to the transfer of materials from Whale to Sparta. These materials were originally procured as part of the long-lead equipment package, with a contracted value of approximately $1.58 million, and were transferred in accordance with COPAS Condition B. 0042.description:
The Operator allocated the Whale Joint Ventures $418,902.62 for Transocean Thalassa HP Shear Upgrade covering the periods of August 2023 through February 2024. The total allocation amount was $1,806,848.18 for a rate of $10,266.18/day, using 176 days from August 14, 2023, through February 5, 2024.

Information Request 23 was submitted to the Operator requesting information regarding the start date as well as the end date of the allocation. The Operator's response stated the allocation was based on an internal 12-month assignment period between SEPWES (Shell EP Wells Equipment Services) and SOI (Shell Offshore Inc).

COPAS MFI-56 (Rig-Related Costs) defines a Rig Contract as 'an agreement between a Company and a drilling contractor to provide a Rig to drill one or more wells, or perform other downhole operations.' The document also defines a Company as 'an individual entity hiring a Rig, acting on its own behalf.' It also addresses acting Company versus Operator Roles in Section II (Background) of the document. An internal assignment within Shell does not equate to a Rig Contract or extension of a Rig Contract, but rather an internal Company decision as to the location and use of the Rig during its contract term. Rather the contract term for the Rig Contract is the 10-year period from February 2016, through February 2026, as supported by the attached Transocean Fleet Report dated February 11, 2016.

COPAS MFI-56 - Section VI (Rig Modifications) states that the ultimate goal of any allocation methodology is to share the costs based on the benefit derived, which would be all the wells for the remainder of the contract term. Therefore, the exception has been calculated using the correct contract end date of February 28, 2026, for a total of 929 days at a rate of $1,944.94/day. Please also note that not every well on the Whale asset carries the same working interest, making a proper allocation imperative. replies.text:
Credit denied.

The Auditor's inquiry references Exhibit C, Section IV.3 (Premium Prices) of the Crosby UOA. That provision applies only when material is 'not readily obtainable at published or listed prices' due to specified unusual causes, in which case the Operator may charge actual cost provided written notice is furnished prior to billing and the Non-Operator is given ten (10) days to elect to furnish its share in kind.

The Auditor's position improperly conflates a vendor-imposed pricing component with a Premium Price transaction under Exhibit C, Section IV.3. Baker Hughes supplied the material through normal commercial channels at a quoted market price that expressly included an Estimated Material Surcharge. The surcharge was a component of the vendor's sales price and constituted actual third-party cost incurred by the Operator in acquiring the material.

Here, the procurement documentation reflects that the material was obtainable via normal procurement at a vendor-quoted price. Proposal 2457548 explicitly includes an 'Estimated Material Surcharge' line item in the amount of $38,619.38 as part of the quoted commercial pricing. Attached the proposal document for your reference.

Accordingly, the IV.3 condition precedent ('not readily obtainable at published or listed prices') is not met on these facts, and IV.3's written notice / in-kind election mechanism is not triggered.

0013.description:
This was the subject of Information Request 024 which was issued during the fieldwork.

The Operator charged the Joint Account $447,387.01 for additional fuel costs per the attached JADE lines. Upon review, the charges are to increase the price of diesel charged to the Joint Account from $2.39/gal to $3.46/gal.

The diesel being supplied is from the Operator's own inventory, and therefore considered a Material Transfer per the JOA. It should be priced at the current new price per the excerpt below:

- (3) Other Material shall be priced at the currenr new price, in effect at date of movement, as listed by a reliable supply store nearesr the Joint Property, or point of manufacture, plus transportation costs, if applicable, to the raiway receiving poinr nearest the Joint Property.

The current new price is established by the below snipped STUSCO invoice, which prices at $2.74/gal. While not a pure arms-length transaction, the below invoice is believed to be substantially similar to the price available to any other party on the open market.

Shell Trading (US) Company 1000 MAIN ST LEVEL 12, HOUSTON, TX, UNITED STATES, 77002-6336 Tax ID: 76-0580508

Invoice

replies.text:
11/21/2025

Credit denied.

Although the Crosby UOA does not provide specific guidance on fuel oil, it is classified as a consumable and should be treated consistently with other similar inventories for pricing, cost, and volume tracking purposes. Therefore, the reference to 'the current new price' in Crosby UOA Accounting Procedure IV.2.(3) does not apply in this context. The most widely accepted accounting method for inventory valuation is FIFO, which is reflected in the $3.xx price shown in the supporting file. FIFO is preferred because it offers simplicity and aligns with the natural flow of inventory, making it a standard practice across the industry. This approach is further supported by BP's 20-F footnote disclosure on inventory. - Niya

Consumables, as a category are covered by the UOA Materials section. For example, small sundry items like office supplies, toiletries (used on-site), etc. are permitted charges under the Materials section. Diesel fuel consumed for drilling, likewise, falls under this section of the UOA. In the same way it would be impermissible for the Operator to mark up the price of ink pens pulled from inventory and charged to the Joint Account, the same is true here for fuel.

A recalculation of the price increase charged to the Joint Account, shows that the Joint Account should have been charged only an additional $45,107.02 to adjust the too-low inventory price of $2.39/gal to the current market price of $2.74. The difference between the $45,107.02 and $447,387.01 reveals an overcharge of $432,279.99 for the fuel.

See calculation from included file "Exc 13 Rig Fuel Cost Adjusted.xlsx, Fuel Cost Adjusted tab" which details out the below calculation. This file is attached to this Exception in the Operator's MyCM system.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account $432,279.99 plus 2.5% OH for diesel transferred from inventory at a price in excess of the then-current market price, supported by 3rd party invoice.

The credit is denied.

The diesel fuel charged to the Joint Account was properly valued in accordance with the Crosby UOA Accounting Procedure and standard inventory accounting principles.

The diesel fuel is a consumable material, not equipment nor a third-party resale transaction. The inventory value charged to the Joint Account reflects the actual carrying cost of inventory, determined using the FIFO inventory valuation method. FIFO is a widely accepted and industry-standard accounting method for inventory valuation and is consistently applied across the Operator's inventory accounting.

No markup, profit, or margin was applied to the fuel transferred to the Joint Account. STUSCo invoices and differential were clearly explained in other IRs during fieldwork.

The auditor's calculation assumes that the Joint Account must be priced at a single external invoice price, despite the fuel being sourced from multi-lot inventory accumulated over time. The auditor also ignored the actual historical acquisition costs embedded in inventory under FIFO. The FIFO inventory method was implemented precisely to improve transparency, strengthen reconciliation between physical fuel and financial reporting, and prevent selective repricing of fuel after consumption.

The diesel fuel was charged to the Crosby Joint Account at actual inventory cost determined under FIFO, without markup or profit, in accordance with standard accounting practice, and The Crosby UOA Materials provisions.

Accordingly, the requested credit of $432,279.99 plus 2.5% overhead is not supported and the exception is denied in full.

Although Team Lead positions may have direct reports and supervisory responsibilities, they are considered First Level Supervisors because their primary role is providing technical support, operational guidance, and subject matter expertise to their teams. Their responsibilities remain closely aligned with the day-to-day execution of technical and operational activities.

Positions with a Manager title are generally classified as Above First Level Supervisors due to the broader administrative and management responsibilities associated with the role. These positions typically focus on workforce management, business planning, resource allocation, performance management, and other organizational leadership functions, rather than direct technical oversight and expertise.

Accordingly, the costs are first recorded on the Ursa platform (P type WBS) and then redistributed to the respective fields (C type WBS) during month close to ensure that each field bears its proportionate share of the expenditure. Regarding the Overhead question:

$15,423.81 - Credit Denied.

The costs in question do not represent the Operator's internal warehousing or administrative expenses contemplated under Section III Overhead. Rather, they are third-party charges incurred for the storage, maintenance, inspection, testing, fabrication, and preservation of jointly owned materials and critical spare equipment.

The charges in question fall under Section III Materials Pricing. As described in MFI 38 (Warehouse Operation), warehouse operation, storage fees, and maintenance expenses represent the cost of storing and handling material that (1) may not be readily available in current market conditions for immediate use, (2) is frequently used, or (3) is otherwise held as surplus. These costs are incurred through third-party services for storage, maintenance, and preparation activities, including inspection, fabrication, and testing. The material is jointly owned, not readily available off the shelf, often has long lead times, and in many cases constitutes critical spares that require routine maintenance to ensure readiness for deployment. Accordingly, these thirdparty charges are directly chargeable to the Joint Account under Section III Materials Pricing and are not intended to be borne solely by the Operator.

001.description:
The Operator is charging contract services for engineering project support from the vendor Worley Group Inc. A review of the invoices finds administrative functions, including management, supervision and office services are being charged by the vendor. These types of services are covered by overhead and should not be charged directly to the Joint Account.

Section III, Overhead of Exhibit C, the Accounting Procedure (attached to the Prospect Appomattox Joint Operating Agreement dated effective April 1, 2009) provides that all compensation for supervision and office services, the Operator should charge the Joint Account in accordance with Section III.

Additionally, the Offsite Technical Labor Letter Agreement, dated October 1, 2025 (OTL Agreement), states "For the avoidance of doubt, Technical Services do not include Overhead functions, whether provided by the Operator, Non-Operator, Affiliate or third parties such as ...administration ... management, Supervision (excluding first-level supervision of operational staff, which is billable) ...." Section 4.

The Operator is requested to credit the Joint Account for the costs associated with the contract labor services that are for administrative office and supervisory services that are being charged directly to the Joint Account as detailed in the supporting workpapers provided in the amount of $22,290.89 plus the 2% Major Construction Overhead for these costs covered by overhead.

003.description:
Workpapers provided to the Operator detailed charges during the audit period to various Rydberg WBS from Ryder Carrier Management for ground freight charges. The auditor's review of the Ryder invoices support documentation indicated that management and administrative expenses were included in the invoice amounts charged to the Joint Account.

The management and administrative expenses charged by Ryder Carrier are covered by overhead as defined in the Accounting Procedure, Exhibit C of the Rydberg Joint Operating Agreement and Exhibit E of the Settlement Agreement of 10/01/2025.

replies.text:
## Credit Denied.

Ryder Carrier transports materials to shore base locations that are then shipped offshore to the appropriate production asset. The materials could not be transported if there were no administration systems present such as the safety systems and processes, as well as information on equipment being transported and destination. The Ryder invoices are separated by Asset and Line of Business where each asset being serviced by Ryder incurs their share of the management fees which are site-specific to field operations (identifiable on the JADE Venture/Cost Object descriptions and field invoices including the location name) and allocated based on volumes trucked by location during that specific period of time. These are the necessary and the ancillary costs of the overall trucking service provided by Ryder.

006.short_description: Open IR No 11 - The Reynolds Company
006.description:
Multiple invoices from the Reynolds Company charged a total of $127,976.45 to WBS C.US.RYD.PD.22.001.1233J, Rydberg Topsides, for offshore labor, parts, and equipment. Upon review of each invoice, the auditor observed there was no documentation supporting the Appomattox Platform or for the benefit of the Joint Account. Information Request (IR) No 11 was submitted asking for such documentation or an explanation supporting why the charges were billed to the Joint Account and why sales taxes were charged for parts, and equipment used offshore.

The Operator did not respond to IR No. 11 by November 19, which was the agreed-upon date the auditor would accept responses to open IRs from the Operator. Scheduled fieldwork ended November 14.

The Operator is requested to provide the requested support documentation or credit $127,976.45 to WBS C.US. RYD.PD.22.001.1233J, plus 2.0% Major Construction Overhead for these unsupported charges.

replies.text:
Credit denied.

The Operator confirms that the Reynolds Company charges were incurred in support of the Rydberg project and the work was performed on the Appomattox Platform. The invoices were charged to WBS C.US.RYD.PD.22.001.1233J (Rydberg Topsides) as costs benefiting the Joint Account. References to Dover on certain invoices do not indicate a separate benefiting asset.

Accordingly, these costs were properly charged to the Joint Account and no credit is due.

009.short_description: Open IR No 18 - Subsea and Facility WBS TBD
009.description:
Fi document 013256096 charged $102,039.52 to WBS P.US.RTD.EP.16.008.1106C, Rydberg Subsea and Facility. The entry was an allocation from WBS P.US.ITL.ES.23.028.BM241. Information Request (IR) No 18 was submitted requesting the Operator provide additional documentation and responses to questions regarding the allocation of the costs to the Rydberg WBS.

The Operator did not respond to IR No 18 by November 19, which was the agreed-upon date the auditor would accept responses to open IRs from the Operator. Scheduled fieldwork ended November 14.

The Operator is requested to provide the explanations with supporting documentation in order to justify the charge to the Joint Account. It should be noted that additional exceptions may be issued depending upon the Operator's response to the IR.

replies.text:
Please refer to the responses provided for the questions in IR 18 for which this exception has been raised, corresponding to the relevant question numbers.

1. Please refer Zip attachment for the relevant supporting invoices requesting in the IR -18 CJI3 tab.
2. WBS P.US.ITL.ES.23.028.BM241 (Application Support Brownfield Topsides) - This WBS is the cost code for all of Brownfield Topsides IM charges. This is the document management of Rydberg's over 2,500 deliverables. Managing where these files came from, when to, and the IFR/IFA process of every revision of every file. Rydberg was a Type 1 (Large BFP project).
3. Basis of the allocation - Allocation for each Brownfield Topsides project is based on the number of deliverables the Brownfield Topsides IM team processes for that project during that month. Some projects had more deliverables processed then others during that time frame.
4. Dover cost would use a separate charge code. Rydberg handover took a few months due to the number of deliverables. The handover was completed August 2024.

Out of the 2,266 deliverables processed by BFP Topsides IM that month 924 ($19,495.664) were for Rydberg, 326 ($6,878.33) were for Dover, 541 ($11,414.66) were for Vito - Waterflood, all other cost were for smaller number of deliverables on other projects.

## Operator Response

Please refer to the responses provided under IR-18 for the related questions.

-  Supporting invoices requested in IR-18 (CJI3 tab) are included in the attached ZIP file.
-  WBS P.US.ITL.ES.23.028.BM241 is the Brownfield Topsides Information Management (IM) cost collector. The charges

mycm relate to document management services provided for Rydberg, including management of over 2,500 project deliverables.

-  Costs were allocated based on the number of project deliverables processed by the Brownfield Topsides IM team during the month.
-  Dover-related costs were charged to a separate charge code and were not included in the Rydberg allocation. Rydberg handover activities continued through August 2024 due to the volume of deliverables.
-  During the month in question, 924 of the 2,266 deliverables processed were related to Rydberg, supporting the allocation charged to the project.

Accordingly, the costs charged to the Rydberg WBS were allocated using the established deliverable-based methodology and are supported by the attached documentation.

011.short_description: Charges Not for the Joint Account
011.description:
Oceaneering invoice G0010-00030882, dated 2/29/2024 charged a total of $1,960,559.80 to WBS C.US.RYD.PD.22.001.1233F, Rydberg Jumpers. The charges relate to the offshore support vessel (OSV) Harvey Deep Sea's work on the Rydberg 1 well jumper installation during February 2024 - approximately 12.68 equivalent days from on-charter to off-charter. Of the total 12.68 days oncharter, the Harvey Deep Sea spend roughly 1.27 equivalent days performing work at Shell's 100% owned Dover well. The Harvey Deep Sea's day rate charges, while working at Dover, were excluded from the charges to the Joint Account. However, the auditor observed other charges billed on invoice G0010-00030882 should have been excluded as well.

The auditor observed other Oceaneering invoices associated with the Rydberg 1 well jumper installation which included charges that should have been excluded from the Joint Account:

- Invoice G0010-00031251, dated 4/17/2024, charged for additional personnel, an upgrade to bandwidth, and reimburseables during the 12.68 equivalent days; and
- Invoice R0010-00081216, dated 2/22/2024 charged for tool and equipment rentals during the 12.68 equivalent days.

The auditor appreciates the Operator's desire to optimize the OSV's usage in the field in joint campaigns, but certain ancillary costs were extended by the extra 1.27 equivalent days the OSV was working at Dover. Some OSV mob and prepwork may have related to the Dover work but was also charged to the Joint Account. Essentially, the Joint Account would not have incurred these additional costs if the OSV had not performed work at Dover.

The Operator is requested to credit WBS C.US.RYD.PD.22.001.1233F for $24,583.93 (as detailed in tab 'Exc. 11.2 Auditor Calculation') plus 2.5% Development Overhead for these charges that do not belong to the Joint Account.
